Strung Up by Regulators. [By telegraph to the Dispatch.]
[By telegraph to the Dispatch.]

NEW ORLEANS, February 9.—A Picayune's Ponchatoula (La.) special says: A negro attempted to assault Bud Turney's daughter six miles from here. He escaped, was pursued, captured, fully identified, and regulators strung him up in this place last night.

POINTED PARAGRAPHS. Topics of the Times Given in a Terse and Spicy Manner.
Ohio society has been incorporated in New York.

Lebanon, O., has availed herself of local option.

Adam Forepaugh is lying ill of typhoid pneumonia at Philadelphia.

The Daily Commercial Printing company, of Chattanooga, has assigned.

K. M. Q. Arbuckle has 200 girls picking coffee, who average over $12 a week.

Royal Templars of Temperance from Temperanceville are in session at Louisville.

Kate Ramey, aged sixteen, of Catlettsburg, Ky., cut her throat with a butcher knife.

A negro was lynched at Pontchatoula, La., for autraging a daughter of Albert Tunage.

Dr. McCosh will be succeeded as president of Princeton college by Professor Frances L. Patton.

Gen. William H. Gibson is now a regularly ordained minister in the Methodist Episcopal church.

Democrats in congress will send Senator Kenna's speech on the tariff broadcast over the land.

At Fort Smith, Ark., seven Indian Territory murderers have been sentenced to hang on April 27.

Louisville & Nashville railroad is trying to prove to the Newport, Ky., authorities that it is not a nuisance.

A Norwegian at Fergus Falls, Minn., has the leprosy. Another case is reported in Wilkin county, Minnesota.

Mrs. Charles Brookman, of Youngstown, O., deserted her children, corralled $600 and climbed for unknown climes.

The Kentucky legislature gives the Newport & Covington Bridge company just six years to complete that little job.

Chairman Mills' bill to invest the treasury surplus in United States bonds will be reported favorably by the committee.

Voorhees is annoyed because his great speech forninst the British extradition treaty was omitted from the senate report.

The body of Catherine Huelsman is under the ice in the canal at Dayton, whither its late owner went of her own free will.

Syndicate of Findlay, O., land owners hold a seductively jingling purse of $300,-000 to manufacturers seeking a location.

President and Mrs. Cleveland gave their closing reception of the season at the White House, Thursday night, to the army and navy.

Gen. Lew. Wallace has purchased a residence in Indianapolis, Ind., and will remove there from Crawfordsville, Ind., in the spring.

Chicago police have arrested Thomas Walters, Joseph Burke, George Needham and John Thornell, "suspects" in the Snell murder case.

Lucas, defaulting Auglaize county treasurer, concludes that honesty is the best policy when you can't help it, and condescends to compromise.

Dr. Donaldson, of Cambridge, O., was a physician who could not heal himself, and terminated his ill health with a dose of suicidal morphine.

Andrew Carnegie has sold his dozen newspapers in different parts of England. They were too much trouble to manage from this side of the water.

Coroner's verdict on the Urbana railroad disaster blames the employes for carelessness and violation of the running rules of the company laid down.

Sub-committee of the Republican National committee arranging for the convention at Chicago, is reported to be almost unanimously in favor of Blaine.

Mrs. Hendricks says that the monument to her late husband at Indianapolis suits to a dot, all rumors of her dissatisfaction to the contrary notwithstanding.

Happy Hoosiers at Indianapolis have a divorce case involving a big church scandal which supplies the entertainment demanded by an off year of the legislature.

James Redpath is recovering. He has written Louis E. Post as follows: "The doctors say I am going to die. I'll be hanged if I do until I see this thing through."

Gen. Moses Cleveland, founder of Cleveland, O., is to have a $5,000 granite monument there, to be dedicated July 22, under the charge of the Early Settlers' association.

Miss Grace Matthews, second daughter of Justice Stanley Matthews, and Mr. Cleveland, of Brighton county, Kentucky, nephew of Justice Harlan, of the supreme court, are betrothed.

Vines Hicks, of Whitehall, Ill., has just celebrated his one hundredth birthday. He was one of five brothers who enlisted in the war of 1812, and served under Gen. Jackson at New Orleans.

At Xenia, O., Henry Scott pleaded guilty to stealing Mr. Allen's diamond rings and is in jail. Mrs. Allen has just found the rings in her dresser drawer. There is a prevarication out somewhere.

"We Protect Our Women."
NEW ORLEANS, La., Feb. 11.—Twice within ten days negroes have been lynched in the parish of Tangapihoa for assulting white women. A negro, claimed to be an escaped convict, forced his way with a hatchet into the room of Miss Alberta Nash. The watch-dog sounded the alarm and awoke the girl's father. The negro was caught and identified. He was being taken to the train to be removed to the jail at Amita, when the party was overpowered by an armed gang of young white and negro men, who strung up the culprit to a tree. The customary placard was pinned to his breast: "We Protect Our Women."

LECISLATIVE ACTS.
The Senate has passed a bill to make 72 pounds of corn in car a legal bushel.

The Senate has passed the bill to pay jailers 60 cents a day for dieting prisoners.

Mr. Phelps has offered a bill to authorize the county of Casey to vote on prohibition.

Senator Harris is determined that if the circuit judge's pay is increased, the amounts for special judges shall be deducted from his salary.

A bill to make it a felony to draw or attempt to draw a pistol on another punishable at not less than one nor more than three years in the penitentiary is before the House.

The Senate has passed the bill granting the Louisville & Nashville to double track their road from Louisville to Cincinnati and to build a straight shoot from Shelbyville to Bagdad.

The House has passed a bill providing that all fines and forfeitures under the State laws shall be turned into the treasury, instead of to the trustees of the jury fund as at present.

The druggists have raised such a howl about Dr. Meade's bill, regulating the sale of patent medicines, that it is safe to assume that the Senate will not follow the House's lead in passing it.

Lawyer Davison presented bills to provide for repairing and keeping in repair the public roads in Lincoln county, and to authorize the county court to take stock in certain turnpike road companies.

The Lawyer's bill to prohibit the sale of morphine and other narcotics, except on the prescription of a physician, was strangled by the committee, perhaps on the principle that if a man wants to kill himself, this is a free country and he can do so.

The House continues to tinker with the concealed weapon law. The present document provides for both a fine and imprisonment—neither one without the other. This bill strikes out the imprisonment clause, and fixes the fine at $100, and if the fine is not paid the culprit is to be put at hard labor in the county jail. The bill passed by a vote of 41 to 39.

COMPRESSED NEWS.

Dr. Francis L. Patton, L.L.D., has been elected to succeed Dr.' McCosh as president of Princeton College.

The Richmond Register is mean enough to speak of Eugene Zimmerman as a regular old blower from Blowersville.

In the six days walking match at New York Alberts beat the record, making 621½ miles, and his next competitor about 40 miles.

A black brute who broke into her room and ravished a young lady at Ponchatoula, La., was taken from the jail and hung by a mob.

Berry, the English hangman, has executed 113 persons up to the present time, 16 of them having been in Ireland and two in Scotland.

While removing a clinker from his stove, Wilson Neal, an old man of Frankfort, inhaled coal gas and died before he could get relief.

Dr. William Munnell, brother of Eld. Thomas Munnell and father of editor W. H. Munnell, died at Brookville-Ind, last week, aged 73.

James Cooper, a prominent citizen of Pulaski county, died Friday. He owned 11,000 acres of land in one tract in Rockcastle and Pulaski counties.

By an explosion at Dupont's powder works at Wapwallopen, near Wilkes, barre, Pa, four men were killed and 40 others more or less seriously injured.

John Janauschek, a farmer, living near New Prague, Mich., murdered his wife, shot his daughter and then killed himself. The woman had just filed a suit for divorce.

Another very cold spell has prevailed in the Northwest. At Pembina, Dakota, the mercury went down to 62° below and at Montevideo, Minn., it is reported as frozen solid.

Gas was struck at Ft. Worth, Texas. at a depth of 380 feet. A rush of gas accompanied by a cloud of sand came from the well with a roar that could be heard a considerable distance.

Gov. Wilson, of West Virginia, has issued a requisition on Gov. Buckner for 28 men charged with participating in the killing of Dempsey in a fight between the Hatfields and McCoys.

Another terrible accident in Kansas City. One man killed and over 100 men, women and children bruised and mangled. The sole explanation is "the grip on the cable cars slipped."

Speaker Carlisle did a good thing when he ordered the bucket shop telegraph offices out of the capital. Their lines ran to Wall street, which speculates in a certain class of legislation.

A construction train on the Louisville Southern ran into the carriage of H. C. Bohon, cashier of the First National Bank of Harrodsburg, killing a fine horse and barely missing him.

Benj. Eggleston, a prominent figure in Cincinnati history, died after an illness of four years. He has been conspicuous in commercial pursuits and in local State and National politics.

Judge Parker, of the United States Court, at Fort Smith, Ark., sentenced seven Indian Territory murderers to be hanged April 27. He evidently believes in doing business by the wholesale.

Six white and seven colored persons were whipped as a punishment for crime at New Castle, Del., Saturday in the presence of 200 spectators. Samuel Long, the forger, also stood one hour in the pillory.

The liquor dealers at Lexington have organized for mutual protection and resistance of the laws prohibiting the sale of whisky to minors and on Sundays. A large number of them have been indicted by the grand jury.

It is now claimed that the negro Bob Crow, who asserts that Patterson confessed to him that he murdered Jennie Bowman, is instigated in the premises by a desire to have Patterson hung so that he can marry his widow.

Tracheotomy was performed on the throat of Crown Prince William Thursday. For two days his breathing has been difficult, and the operation was considered necessary to save him from strangling. It was pronounced a success.

Patrick John Hart was hanged at Helena, Montana, for the murder of Jno. Pitts, a miner at Elkhorn, who accused him of ruining his step-daughter. He said he only wanted to live to test a discovery that would prolong a man's life indefinitely.

William Kelley, the inventor of the process for making Bessemer steel and the first man to introduce Chinese labor into this country, died in Louisville Saturday.

The engagement of Mr. Cleveland and Miss Grace, daughter of Judge Stanley Matthews, of the Supreme Court, is announced. Mr. Cleveland is a resident of Bracken county, Ky., and has been studying law at Washington.

A new counterfeit, five-dollar silver certificate has been put in circulation. The bill is about three-sixteenth of an inch too short and there are no distinctive lines in the paper. The general appearance is good and calculated to deceive.

W. W. Corcorsn, the Washington millionaire philanthropist and art patron, is gradually sinking, and it is believed he cannot longer survive. He has been confined to his bed for a fortnight, and now takes little notice of what passes around him.

The Pineville Messenger says there were seven bids for its jail and court house, Eason, Wiggins, Brawner & Co.'s, of Richmond, being the lowest and the work was awarded them at $4,364 for the former and $17,887 for the latter. The amount appropriated for the two is $25,000.

Near Belleville, Ohio, two men were digging up dynamite that had been buried to keep it safe until needed. The pick of one of the men struck the explosive, and there was a shock that suggested an earthquake at Tiffin, Sandusky and other points. The men have not been discovered as yet.

THE SOUTHERN STATES.
A PONCHATOULA (La.) special says: "On last Sunday night a negro forced an entrance into the residence of Mr. Albert Tunnage and assaulted Miss Tunnage. In Edgiefie'D County, S. C., they have found a way to d'courage proselyting in the interest of Mormonism. Two elders who were passing through the county recently, and engaged in making converts, were tied up and flogged by citizens.

Governor Gordon of Georgia has written a lengthy article giving his views in reference to the appropriation of $8,000 for the education of the colored people. Burglar recently got away with $30,000 worth of watches and jewelry at Norfolk, Va.

Dr. E. Miles Willett, supreme medical examiner Catholic Knights of America, died suddenly at his residence in Memphis, Tenn., a few days since, of heart disease, aged sixty-one years.

Jake Fulton, a farmer of Bolivar County, Misa., shot and killed his son a few days ago for attempting to interfere when he was beating his wife.

albert-rossi-pittson-1888-05-18.A1:
Strung Up For a Lynching.
AN INFURIATED PENNSYLVANIA MOB NEARLY HANG AN ITALIAN.
WILKES-BARRE, May 19.—The suburb of Pittown known as Browntown came near witnessing a lynching yesterday. Three young girls had started into the woods to find several stray cows, when they were attacked by three Italians employed on the new branch of the Lehigh Valley Railroad from Pittson to Laurel Run. The girls resisted despately upon being seized and screamed loud and long. In their struggles the girls were much bruised and hurt and their clothing torn.

Their screams attracted the attention of a miner named Peter Mulderig, who was on his way to work. He ran to their rescue, and the Italians fled. Mulderig took the girls home to Browntown, and when their story was known a crowd of men and boys started out after the Italians, bent on a desperate revenge. They found the foreigners in company with a number of their kind at one of the shanties they live in, and at once attacked them.

A desperate fight followed. Knives clubs, and rocks were vigorously used. Many wounds were inflicted and blood flowed freely. The Italians finally fled in all directions, but one of those who had assaulted the girls named Alberti Rossi was caught. A rope was put round his neck and thrown over the limb of a tree, and in the midst of an excited and bloodthirsty crowd he was swung off his feet, begging and screaming for mercy. The better sense of some of the men returned, however, when they saw him in the air, and they interfered and had him lowered down. He was unconscious, but not seriously hurt.

A YOUNG DESPERADO KILLED
Alfred West, a Negro Work-House Prisoner, Murderously Assaults a Guard,
And, After a Desperate Fight, Is Shot Dead by the Man He Tried to Kill, and Whose Skull He Fractured with a Stone.
Albert West, a young colored man, until he was sent to the work-house, on Dec. 30, caused a great deal of trouble, not only in the family of his step-father, Wm. West, but in the Yandess-street neighborhood, where the latter lives. The young desperado's mother, as well as her husband, suffered from his abuse, and frequently, without any provocation, he would beat them severely. The act that led to his arrest arose from the step-father's objections to Albert bringing to his house a young woman with whom he associated. The last time this occurred was about the middle of December, when Albert, in his fury, cut the step-father about the head. Just after the affray, late at night, the injured man and his wife went to Mayor Denny's house and procured a warrant for the son's arrest. But they did not appear in court against the prisoner the next day, nor on other days to which several continuances had been made. Finally the prosecuting witnesses were brought in to court by an officer and gave evidence upon which Albert was sent to the work-house for thirty days, besides being fined $25 with costs. The prisoner's sweetheart was also a witness against him and all gave him a reputation of being a dangerous man. The Mayor says he ought to have been held for assault and battery with intent to kill, but the prosecutor, no doubt at the request of the witnesses, confined the charge to simple assault. The step-father, mother and sweetheart were all afraid of the fellow, who seemed to delight in affrays. After the trial Albert threatened to kill the prosecuting witness when he was released and this Mr. West dreaded. Day before yesterday West came to the Mayor to learn when Albert would be released and asked if some means could not be taken to keep the desperado from killing him. As far as as the father was concerned he would like to have had him kept in prison the balance of his life.

Albert had about a week more of his workhouse sentence to serve and the officers there were glad it was so near an end, as they say he had been a troublesome prisoner. He never worked willingly even at the lightest labor and he had such a strong objection to breaking stones that the guards were often compelled to threaten him with punishment. Two gangs of men are worked on the stone-pile, one in the morning and the other in the afternoon. Young West belonged to the morning gang, and yesterday was taken with the rest to the pile. The guard, Ananias Stewart, ordered him to break into finer pieces the stone on which one of the afternoon gang had been working. West refused. "Then I'll take you to the dungeon," said the guard.

"I you try I'll break your d—n head with this hammer," replied the prisoner.

"Come with me," said Stewart as he caught West by the arm. The prisoner did not attempt to strike him as he had threatened, but quietly walked along some distance. Suddenly he jerked away from the guard's grasp and ran towards the gate with Stewart following and crying out, "Stop, or I'll shoot:" West paid no attention to the warning, but just as he reached the gate Stewart caught him. West turned about, and before the guard knew what the prisoner was after, the latter was struggling to get possession of the Winchester rifle Stewart carried. Stewart wrested it from him, and stepping back a pace or two, covered him with it. West then threw several pieces of broken stones at the guard, two of which hit him on the head, one cutting the temporal artery, and the other fracturing the skull. Stewart then shot with direct aim, sending the ball into West's left side, about two inches below the shoulder. He dropped to the ground and died within a very few minutes. Stewart then fell and became unconscious, but under the treatment of Dr. Brennan and Coroner Wagner, who had been summoned, he recovered sufficiently to make an ante-mortem statement, in which the facts, as detailed above, were given. albert-west-indianapolis-1888-03.A2:
KILLED INSTANTLY.
INDIANAPOLIS, March 2.—Albert West, a young colored man serving sentence in the work house for assault upon his father, this morning attacked James Stewart, the guard in the stone house, crushing his skull with a stone. Although Stewart was severely injured, he fired on the prisoner as he attempted to escape and a bullet from his revolver took effect in West's heart, killing him instantly.

Bernhamer was taken to the Northern Penitentiary yesterday and Coy will follow as soon as he recovers from a spell of fever.

Amcs Bronson Alcott, founder of the Concord School of Transcendental Philosophy, and a well known author, died in Boston, Saturday, aged eighty-eight years.

Mr. Samuel Morrison, the oldest native Indianian, who claimed to have originated the plans for the capture of Vicksburg, died at Indianapolis, at the age of ninety years, last Friday.

Four hundred men took Tom Forsyth out of jail, at Carthage, Tex., last Thursday, and allowed him to jump off a limb. He was the Sheriff's son, who murdered the County Treasurer.

Congressman Butterworth has prepared a resolution appropriating $300,000 to enable the several Executive departments of the Government to make an exhibit at the Cincinnati Centennial Exposition.

The venerable banker, Valentine Winters, of Dayton, O., at a family dinner recently, distributed a half-million dollars among six children and the heirs of two others. Six years ago he gave them $400,000.

The scenery and costumes at McVicker' Theater, Chicago, belonging to Mrs Langtry, were seized at the suit of Mlle Dore, for $420, and her car was seized, on the suit of James Creighton, an Edinburgh jeweler, for $241.

Albert West, a colored tough in the Indianapolis workhouse, was shot and instantly killed by Guard Stewart last Monday. West assaulted the guard and inflicted several injuries before the fatal shot was fired.

The throttle of an engine standing in the Missouri Pacific round-house at St. Louis, Saturday, became opened in some mysterious manner. The iron horse forthwith made a dash through the yard at terrific speed. Result, three engines wrecked.

The strike of the locomotive engineers and firemen on the C., B. & Q. system is still in progress. The railroad company is moving trains with some degree of regularity, but practically the freight traffic has been suspended. The probability is that the strike will spread to other roads.

Railroad Accident in Iowa.
DETROIT. January 29th.—The express
Railroad Accident in Iowa.

DETROIT, January 29th.—The express on the Detroit, Grand Haven and Milwaukee Railroad, which left here yesterday afternoon, was thrown from the track about sixty miles west of here by a broken rail. Everything but the locomotive left the track, the baggage, express and smoking-cars overturning and catching fire, but the flames were speedily extinguished. All the passengers were badly shaken up and several were seriously injured. The worst one hurt was George Thomas, of Owosso, who is probably hurt internally.

A Great Cigar Industry.

[Copyright, 1888, by the California Associated Press.]

KEY WEST, January 29th.—The Cuban disturbances are causing Havana business houses a deal of trouble. An agent of E. H. Gato, the great Cuban cigar manufacturer, is at Key West making arrangements to build here the largest cigar manufactory in the country. Gato's intention is to employ 1,000 hands, who will turn out over 200,000 cigars a day.

Modjeska's Last Season.

NEW YORK, January 29th.—The present season may be Modjeska's last on the American stage, though the matter will not be decided for some time. She goes to Europe next month to sell her property preparatory to investing in California, where she intends to settle for life. The recent death of her mother, a constant pre-application of war and the settlement of her only son in this country have induced her to this course.

Brutal Wife-murder.

ST. JOSEPH, January 29th.—Louis Bulling, who had been forced to marry about two years ago and had separated from his wife, went to the Herbert House, where she was working, locked her and himself in a room and shot her three times, killing her instantly. He was arrested, and narrowly escaped lynching. The people are reported as much excited, and trouble is feared to-night.

A Fiend Quickly Disposed Of.

AMITE CITY (La.), January 29th.—Ben Edwards (colored), who so grossly assaulted Miss Catharine Hughes, a white girl living near here, on Friday last, was captured by the Sheriff and lodged in jail on Saturday night. Subsequently a hundred citizens compelled the Sheriff to give them the keys of the jail. They took Edwards out, carried him about a hundred yards from the jail and hanged him to a tree.

A Mismatched Switch.
A Misplaced Switch.
CAMBRIDGE (Neb.), January 29th. — "Flyer No. 1" on the B. and M. road was wrecked by a misplaced switch this afternoon. The following were severely injured: C. F. Born, Granville, Ia.; Mrs. H. G. Terrill, McCook, Neb; Miss Fannie Bloom, Denver; K. Gallagher, Granite, conductor Odell and engineer McNhrey.

Suits for Nearly a Million.
CLEVELAND, January 29th. — The papers in two important suits, growing out of the collapse of Ives, Stayner & Co., were filed in the Common Pleas Court yesterday. The plaintiff in each case is J. H. Wade, trustee for a number of persons, and the sum involved in both suits is $720,000.

A Sensation Promised.
CINCINNATI, January 29th. — Sensational developments are promised in the Fidelity Bank matters, and the Government intends to prosecute all connected with the misappropriation of funds. Briggs Swift, the venerable President, and Josie Holmes are to be prosecuted.

Should Be With Herr Most.

FOUR LYNCHINGS IN KANSAS. The Citizens Disgusted by the Law's Leniency Toward Murderers.
KANSAS CITY, June 28.—A mob at Minneapolis, Kan., took Chubb McCarthy, murderer of Mike Dorsey, from jail early this morning and hanged him to a tree. This was the last of four lynchings in the State within twenty-four hours. The others were Wallace Mitchell, who was strung to a telegraph pole at Syracuse, and John Risbee and Wyley Lee, negroes, who died together at Chetopa. The State law in Kansas in relation to capital punishment is a peculiar one. According to the statutes, a person convicted of murder in the first degree is sent to the penitentiary for one year, and at the expiration of the period is liable to be hanged at any time the Governor sees fit to sign the death warrant. No Governor has ever signed a warrant under such circumstances, and as a result there are fifty-four murderers under sentence of death in the State prison. To-day's record is the logical outcome of the situation.

About two weeks ago Wallace Mitchell assassinated a man and boy at Syracuse. He escaped to Colorado, but was captured and brought back on Tuesday. He confessed his crime with coolness and deliberation. This so enraged the citizens that they took Wallace from the officers, and, dragging him half dead to the scene of his crime, hanged him to the cross beam of a telegraph pole and riddled his limp body with bullets. The news spread from village to village, town to town, throughout the State, and the sentiment of the commonwealth seemed to be that lynch law was the only remedy at hand.

At Minneapolis Chubb McCarthy was in jail awaiting the action of the Grand Jury. His crime had been most flendish, and he had been caught in the very act. There was no question about his guilt, and no circumstances tending to extenuate the crime. At midnight an armed band numbering 200 silently rode into the streets of the town. Guards were posted at the doors of the residences of all the officials, and the streets leading to the jail were thoroughly patrolled. A squad broke the doors of the prison and the jailer was compelled to give up the keys to the culprit's cell. The murderer was taken to the bridge crossing the Soloma River and suspended high in the air over the swollen stream.

At the same hour at Chetopa, another scene was witnessed. John Risbee and Wyley Lee had been arrested by the Marshal and his deputy. In making a desperate attempt to escape they had shot both officers. The Sheriff captured them and held them in the City Hall until the arrival of the train which was to carry them to the county seat. A turbulent crowd gathered about the hall. At 12:30 word was brought that the deputy was dead and the Marshal diving. A special guard had been placed about the building. Suddenly the electric light went out. The officers were speedily overpowered by a quiet but irresistible mob of 300 men. The prisoners were dragged from under a table, where they had crawled in a vain hope of saving their wretched lives. They begged for mercy. For a reply they were dragged into an adjoining room, the windows kicked out, and the doomed men placed on the sill. Ropes were fastened to heavy timbers and around their necks, and against the muzzles of Winchester rifles they were ordered to jump into the street. The strong rope was slack, and as they tumbled from the window they fell a distance of thirty feet, almost to the ground. Bisbee's neck was broken. Lee strangled to death. Then the crowd dispersed. The dead bodies hung from the ropes until 9 o'clock this morning, when they were cut down by the Coroner.

Chubb McCarthy Hanged at Minneapolis, Kansas, by a Mob.

The Sheriff and Marshal Made Prisoners During the Execution.

Revenue Officers Worsted in a Fight with Arkansas Moonshiners.

A Lunatic Boards a Train Bent on Exterminating the Hands.
MINNEAPOLIS, Kan., June 28.—At 2 o'clock last night a party of forty or fifty masked men from Foontain township, this county, neighbors of Mike Dorsey who was murdered in his bed a few days ago by Chubb McCarthy, came into this city and with a sledge and a bar of railroad iron proceeded to break down the jail doors to get at McCarthy. The outside and one inside door were broken open and then finding greater resistance than expected they overpowered the jailor and after a lively fight took away the keys. Not being able to find the one which opened the cell door, the mob then compelled the jailor to unlock the door. McCarthy was quickly taken out and hung to the Geisen bridge across the Solomon river, about three miles from town. But very little noise was made by the mob, which was well organized and heavily armed. The city marshal hearing the noise went up toward the jail, but was stopped by the guards and held up until the mob got away with the prisoner. The sheriff was confined to his room by armed guards, and other citizens who were on the streets were held as prisoners until the mob got away. The body of McCarthy was found hanging to the bridge timbers at 7 o'clock this morning by the sheriff and city marshal. While deprecating resort to mob law, there is rather openly expressed sympathy with the action of the mob.

VA., June 28.—For some time there has been trouble brewing in the congregation of Latter Day Saints near Penn Easton, twenty-five miles east of this city. Last evening, while the congregation were holding a meeting at the house of Aaron Farris, an aged member of the flock, the trouble culminated in a riot in which two women were probably fatally wounded and six or eight others stabbed or otherwise hurt. Tom and Leroy Wait are in danger of death from their wounds, the first being stabbed in the left side, and the flesh on the latter's arms, hands and head being literally slashed into strips, and his throat cut from one ear to the chin. Jasper Wait was stabbed in the stomach, and Harvey Court-wright had his head cracked, and the bone laid bare from the top of the head to his eyes. Tom Chanibers was badly beaten with a club. Some of the Wait boys are looking for the Courtwrights with rifles. Another Lynching Bee in Kansas. MINNEAPOLIS, KAS., June 28.—At two
Another Lynching Bee in Kansas.

MINNEAPOLIS, KAS., June 28.—At two o'clock this morning a party of forty or fifty masked men from Fountain Township, this (Ottawa) County, neighbors of Mike Dorsey, who was murdered in his bed by Chubb McCarthy, came into this city, and with sledges and a bar of railroad iron proceeded to break down the doors of the jail, where McCarthy was confined. The outside and one inside door were broken open, and then, finding greater resistance they overpowered the jailer and compelled him to open McCarthy's cell. McCarthy was taken out, bound, removed to the Geisen bridge across the Solomon river, about three miles from town and then hanged.

Battle With Moonshiners.

St. Louis, June 28.—A special from Little Rock, Ark., to the Post-Dispatch says: A desperate battle occurred between revenue officers and moonshiners near Black Springs, Montgomery County, yesterday. Internal Revenue Collector Fry and a posse raided the moonshiners' camp in the vicinity, destroying three distilleries. Shortly afterwards the posse was attacked from ambush by an armed band of moonshiners. A regular battle ensued, in which Deputy U. S. Marshal Trammel was killed. Collector Fry has telegraphed to Port Smith for reinforcements.

Innocent Man Lynched.

ALTAMONT, Ill., June 28.—The people

Innocent Man Lynched.

ALTAMONT, ILL., June 28.—The people here are very indignant over the lynching of William Moore, at Charleston, Ill. The facts are that the girl, Mary A. Bumgardner, upon whom it is alleged the assault was made, lives some two miles from this place, and is not so very young, being about nineteen or twenty years old, and the people here who know her doubt the truth of her story. It is the general opinion that the people of Mattoon and vicinity were deceived, and, in acting hastily, have put to death an innocent man.

Canadian Outrage.

WASHINGTON, June 28.—The Secretary of State has officially called the attention of the British Minister resident at Washington to the case of the American ship Bridgewater, unlawfully seized by the Customs officials of the Dominion of Canada a year ago, and detained for eighty-one days at Sheinburn.

Oregon's Official Vote.

PORTLAND, June 28.—The official canvass of the vote of the State on the Congressional election resulted as follows: Hermann, Republican, 32,820; John M. Gearin, Democrat, 25,413; George M. Miller, Prohibitionist, 1,974; Herman's plurality, 1,407.

She Must Hang.

BOSTON, MASS., June 28.—Justice Field

She Must Hang.

BOSTON, MASS., June 28.—Justice Field and Knowlton, of the Supreme Court at Cambridge, this afternoon refused to entertain the motion for a new trial in the case of Mrs. Mary Jane Robinson, convicted of murder in poisoning her sister's husband in 1885, and sentenced her to be hanged November 16.

Death of a Sensitive Creature.

BOSTON, MASS., June 28.—George H. Gibson, who shot himself last evening rather than to appear at his wedding without the suit of clothes his tailor had failed to finish in time, died at the hospital this afternoon.

A Costly Experiment.

NEW CASTLE, DEL., June 28.—The pattern shop and bending mill of the Delaware Iron Works, at this place, operated by Morris Tasker & Co., limited, of Philadelphia, were destroyed by fire last evening. The fire was caused by an experiment in painting pipe with a mixture of benzine, coal tar and oil. A spark fell into the composition and instantly the place was in flames. The loss on patterns is $40,000 to $50,000 and on building $5,000. The lores are partially covered by insurance.

Chicago Newsboys Cleansed.

CHICAGO, June 28.—The Waifs' Mission

Chicago Newsboys Cleansd. 
Chicago, June 28.—The Waifs' Mission took five hundred newsboys to a bathhouse, where six barbers cut their hair short with clipping machines. They were then plunged into the water and scrubbed from head to foot. To-day the mission will give each of the boys a new suit of clothes, and then take the five hundred on a picnic. 
Got Twenty Thousand For Potts. 
Pork Huron, Mich., June 28.—In the suit of Alice Potts vs. Emily Williard for $50,000 damages for alienating the affections of her husband, Lewis Potts, the jury brought in a verdict this morning for $20,000.

FIFTIETH CONGRESS.

First Session.

WASHINGTON, June 25.—Nothing of Importance was transacted in either branch of Congress to day, the exciting news from the Chicago Convention being too much for the Senators and Representatives remaining in this city.

WASHINGTON, June 26.—SENATE. The Senate proceeded with the consideration of the legislative, executive and judicial appropriation bill. After some debate, there being no quorum present, adjourned.

HOUSE.—Consideration of public land bill was resumed. Most of the amendments which were adopted were in the nature of corrections. Mr. Herman offered one, however, which was accepted, allowing entry men six instead of three months in which to erect a habitable dwelling. There was a long discussion over an amendment offered by Mr. Weaver (la.), reserving title in the Government to alternate strips of public land along water courses and the sea shore. Mr. Laird (Nea.) indignantly resented the attacks which had been made on the cattle-breeders and other Western citizens. La. said that on the cross, only there were three instances of them. Those settlers were thieves and the cattle men were thieves, and the syndicates were thieves. Mr. Weaver (la.) replied that the thieves on the cross repented and these people did not. Mr. Laird retorted that they did not repent, for they did not admit that they were thieves. Mr. Weaver wanted to know what aled Mr. Laird. Was it worms? But the gentleman made no reply. The amendment was rejected, as were also several others. No quorum present, adjourned.

Insecurity of Human Life.
Four men were lynched in one day in Kansas last week, two in Minneapolis, one in Syracuse, two at Chetopa and one in Illinois, making five in all, three whites and two negroes. There is no country in the world where human life is so insecure as in several of the United States of America. It is a reproach upon the state and national government. It is a damnable outrage, not possible anywhere but in this boasted civilization of the 19th century in a free country. —The Iowa Citizen.

Nothing in the world makes human life as insecure as war, and nothing is a greater reproach to a State or Nation than to go to war, and nothing is a greater standing disgrace than a standing army, and nothing is more opposed to Christianity than the teaching, the spirit and practice of war.

WASHINGTON CRITIC.
NEWS OF THE DAY.
Recent Happenings of Interest Boiled Down for Hasty Reading.
The old Burlington trouble broke out anew
The old Burlington trouble broke out anew in Lincoln, Neb., Saturday, in the shape of a small riot. It was decided by the railroad officials to send an excursion train over the Burlington tracks. The Brotherhood men and adherents insisted that the train should not pass over the line. A fight ensued, revolvers were drawn and several dozen shots fired. One man was shot through the thigh and another had his ankle shattered.

Mary Olsen, 26 years old, the wife of a waiter employed in Harlem, jumped out of the window of her home in New York Saturday night to end her life. She struck on the sidewalk and sustained injuries that resulted in her death shortly afterwards. She had been drinking. Her three young children witnessed the fatal act. She had attempted suicide earlier in the evening by jumping from the roof, but struck on a balcony and only sustained slight injuries.

The body of Joe Lewis, charged with the murder of Miss Auxier, in Morgan County, Kv., last spring, was found Friday with two bullet holes in the back of his head. He had been dragged a hundred yards from his home and thrown over a precipice seventy-five feet high. Two of his cousins, Dave and Al Lewis, and a brother, aged 16, 18 and 20, respectively, are suspected and have been charged with the crime.

A permanent organization of the survivors of the Chatsworth Railroad disaster has been effected at Peoria, Ill., by electing Dr. O. B. Will, president; F. A. Vansant, secretary, and Pearl Adams, Robert Kennedy and Ezra F. Parker executive committee. In the near future a meeting of the officers will be held to further perfect the organization and find out if any of the number are in need of pecuniary assistance.

The Italian Government is arranging railway excursions from all parts of Italy in order to bring together a large concourse of people at the demonstrations in honor of the visit of Emperor William of Germany, and other preparations are being made for his entertainment, including public fetes, a naval review, etc. It is stated that the Kaiser's visit will cover six days.

A freight train on the Mobile and Girard Railroad, while going into Columbus, Ga., Friday, struck a sand bar six inches deep caused by heavy rains. The engine was overturned and four cars telescoped. The boiler of the engine exploded. Engineer Hoffman escaped with slight scalds and Fireman Pickeron with a dislocated shoulder.

At Galveston, Texas, Saturday, John Lovejoy, a prominent attorney, shot and instantly killed Aaron Williamson. The difficulty originated over a debt of $20 owed Williamson, by Lovejoy since the fall of 1884 when
joy, a prominent attorney, shot and instantly killed Aaron Williamson. The difficulty originated over a debt of $20 owed Williamson by Lovejoy since the fall of 1884, when the latter ran and was defeated for District Attorney of that Judicial district.

James A. Wright of Philadelphia, C. A. Hall of Marshall, Texas; A. W. Wright of the Labor Reformer, Toronto, Canada, and Morris L. Wheat of Colfax, Iowa, have been selected by General Master Workman Powderly to compose the Traveling Educational Board of the Knights of Labor.

The big raft Joggins passed under the Brooklyn bridge on Saturday afternoon and rounded the battery twenty-five minute later, amidst the tooting of steam-whistles and cheers from large crowds assembled on the piers. The raft was securely moored at her destination in the Erie basin.

John Callahan, aged 30, a former resident of Carbondale, Pa., was found dead in Mill Creek, near Wilkesbarre, Pa., Saturday. His arms were phiononed behind him with a rope made from a woman's skirt, and his neck was broken. It is believed that he was murdered.

The finding of a body near Natick, Mass., has caused considerable commotion because of the fact that his head was detached and the body unclothed and badly decomposed. No trace of any wearing apparel can be found.

An old woman named Lizzie Miller has been arrested in New York on the charge of luring young girls to their ruin. The Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children has taken charge of the prosecution.

Hon. Richard L. Spofford died at Amesbury, Mass., Saturday, aged 56 years. He was a lawyer, and practiced in Boston and Washington. He married Harriet Prescott, the writer, who survives him.

The members of the Holland Society of New York visited the Zoological Gardens and the University Library at Amsterdam Saturday.

General Boulanger, while driving, was shot at five times by Professor Perrin of the Lycee yesterday, but was not injured.

Ignaz Brull has written a new opera entitled, "Dassteinerue Herz." It will be produced in Vienna and New York next season by a German opera company.

The estimate of this season's wheat crop in France has been reduced to 80,000,000 hectolitres, the same as the crop of 1879, when the summer was wet and cold.

The Emperor of Germany is feeling well. The young prince is also progressing favorably.

The English Parliament ended its regular session Saturday.
The Parnell Commission bill passed its third reading in the House of Lords.
The artist, James Whistler, was married in London to Mrs. Godwin, widow of the architect.
A elections for Councillors-General throughout Greece Saturday two-thirds of the successful candidates were adherents of the government.
The new-born Prince of Greece will be named Christopher.
The Paris strikers decided to continue the contest, but show signs of weakening.
Mr. Parnell will probably sue the London Times through the Scotch courts.
The dory Dark Secret is thought to have foundered.

POINTED PARAGRAPHS.
Topics of the Times Given in a Terse and Spicy Manner.

The Lancaster, O., camp-meeting is drawing immense crowds.

Mrs. Robert Hasall committed suicide at Cleveland, O., by hanging.

Hon. Isaac LaFollette, prominent Indiana politician, died at Oakland.

William Howard, shot by his brother-in-law at Hopkinsville, Ky., is dead.

The new bridge in process of construction at Cedarville, O., fell and killed Dan Haley, a workman.

Near Wellington, O., Fred Battle fell off a stack of oats, running a pitchfork into his bowels. He will die.

On the site of the property destroyed in the great Chattanooga fire, a block valued at $150,000 will be erected.

Thomas Hendricks, of Portsmouth, O., is a heavy villain. He is in jail for stealing a derrick from a stone quarry.

A one-cent-per-mile-rate will be charged by the railroad companies during the Grand Army entertainment at Columbus.
An escaped convict named Smith Sloan shot Wesley Waultlaeve and fourteen-year-old son at Pittsburg, Tenn. Both will die.

Mat. Badcliff, Buchtel, O., saloonkeeper, is invited by the grand jury to appear and explain why he assisted in breaking the Owen law.

William McLin sues John Morgan for $5,000 because he, McLin, came out second best in a fracas with Morgan at Washington, Indiana.

Miss Ella Ganson, of Logansport, Ind., took a suicidal dose of carbolic acid, and has gone to tell his life's failures to the tenderest Judge of all.

Annual reunion of soldiers and sailors of northern Indiana and southern Michigan at Elkhart, Ind., was addressed by Gen. W. H. Gibson, of Tiffin, O.

An interesting session of the Northern Ohio German Lutheran Evangelical church is being held at Bucyrus, O. Many ministers are present from all over the state.

At Mount Carmel, Ill., Herbert Zimmerman, aged eleven, was shot and killed by an eight-year old companion. The weapon was a "thought-it-wasn't-loaded" one.

Postmaster Hurley, of New Albany, Ind., is sued by the Federal authorities for $228. The squabble arises from a misunderstanding as to who should pay the rent.

At Hall's station, Alabama, Gid Blackburn, aged six, and Lewis Davis, aged three, played with an "empty" gun. The baby, Lewis, lost one side of his head and died instantly.

James Scanlan, of St. Paul, Minn., was shot and killed by his mistress, Pearl Wilson, while asleep in a room at Minneapolis. The girl then shot herself through the head, and will die.

Moerehead, Ky., people have caught Dave and Albert Lewis, who murdered a young lady and their cousin, Henry Lewis. On the theory that "like cures like" they are threatening to mend the fracture in their laws by making another lynching bee.

WOMAN in her natural sphere is God's greatest and most sacred gift to man, but when she descends from that sphere, which is but a little lower than the angel's, hell itself could not furnish her counterpart. The woman "Buggy" Burns, who was the cause of the murder of the two policemen in Louisville last week, is but a fair example of the fallen angel. Born of good parents, she received all the accomplishments they could bestow upon her, grew to beautiful womanhood and married a worthy young man. The fatal gift of beauty was hers and she took delight in displaying her charms to other men than her husband. Scandal soon attached to her name and the man she had promised to forsake all others for catching here in a compromising attitude one night on his sudden return home, killed the man who had been ensnared to his death. The husband was acquitted but the slaying of his fellowman made him a wreck and a wanderer upon the face of the earth, while his wife sank from bad to worse and drifting to Louisville, became one of the lowest of the brutal prostitutes who haunt LaFayette street. The hearts she has made to bleed, the families she has made to suffer and the souls that she has sent to hell can never be fully enumerated till she stands up for final sentence in the court from which there is no appeal. She is in jail now, charged with being accessory to the murder of the two policemen and let us hope that her criminal career is at last at an end.

The awful tragedy in Louisville where in a miserable cut-throat killed two policemen who tried to arrest him for beating his woman, makes one almost wish the double murderer could suffer at the hands of an outraged people the justice that the courts will be months in meting, if the scoundrel does not finally escape under some such technicality as the omission of the word "feloniously" or other as flimsey pretext for reversal as are sometimes made. We have never advocated mob law, the Lebanon Standard to the contrary, but there are cases of such outrageous deeds that nothing but the most summary methods of dealing condign punishment seem to be applicable. The slow process of the law amounts almost to aggravation in such instances and Judge Lynch is in a measure excusable for taking a hand.

The terrible disaster at sea, mentioned in our news notes, is enough to make the blood run cold. Two ships heavily laden with human souls, crash into each other in a dense fog and in five minutes one of them goes down and with her 105 persons meet a watery grave. They were mostly Danish-Americans returning to the fatherland to see loved ones and recant upon the scenes, adventures, the hardships and the successes of life in the land of the free. As broad as is the Atlantic, it would seem that such a horror might be averted. But fate willed otherwise and so far as known no human agency is to blame.

MARSHALL FIELD, of Chicago, the largest merchant in the west, has declared his intention to vote for Cleveland, although he has been a life long republican, on the ground that President Cleveland's administration in its policy on the tariff question is distinctly on the side of the business interests of the country. He says that there is no free trade at all to be apprehended from it, but that there is just that wise and moderate reduction of the rate of duties which is needed at this juncture and which must be had if the nation is to escape serious difficulties.

THE harmless pastime of putting up presidential tickets continues. With 7 already in the field, the "American Party," after a row and a rumpus, succeeded in naming a ticket at Washington last week, and now comes the National Greenback party with a call for a convention at Cincinnati, Sept. 12, likewise to nominate candidates. These little side shows are diverting and amusing. The real fight is between the democrats and the republicans with cheap necessities against free luxuries and liquor the issue.

FLEMING county has the most iron clad prohibition law ever adopted, even the giving of liquor being unlawful. The advocates of the law had a druggist arrested for selling on a physicians' prescription, but Judge Cole at a special term of his court instructed the jury to acquit, and they are very hot in the collar.

The old sinner who edits the Covington Commonwealth hesitates to pray for us because he is in doubt as to whether we seek prayers for forgiveness or for recovery. For the latter, of course. Let yourself loose now, old fellow, and see if for once the prayers of the wicked can avail.

WOMAN suffrage gets a back set in the Supreme Court of Washington Territory. It is declared unconstitutional on the ground that the legislature exceeded its powers granted by Congress and that the word "citizen" in the organic act can only mean a male citizen.

NEARLY everybody feels a desire to see how the man looks about whom they have heard so long and after whom they have read so much, hence we present a picture of Col. E. Polk Johnson, the able managing editor of the Courier-Journal, which, while not doing the right royal old fellow justice, still gives a pretty good idea of him, especially of his cranium, which has no capillary substance upon its summit, at least none to brag of. The Colonel lays the loss of his "har" to early piety, but constant work of a massive brain has had very much more to do with it, we opine. His fort is not confined to writing alone. He is an unusually versatile man and withal carries a heart in his honest old bosom that is as tender and as true as a woman's. May his restoration to health be permanent and his days of usefulness be long upon the earth.

Dr. Woods, of the Frankfort Capital, suggests that while prayer may be very good for boils, shoemaker's wax is equally as reliable, especially when the former is put up by a wicked and perverse individual who is unfamiliar with the approach to the throne of grace. The trouble with us is not boils, O! sapient physician, carbuncles—mean, malignant, measly carbuncles, is the trouble. Send us a remedy for them and do it p. d. q., for in the language of the Psalmist, the tortues of hell have gat hold upon us.

On the first page of this issue will be found an admirable article on the church and the third party movement from a leading Southern church paper, which we commend to the earnest perusal of our readers. It seems to so fully cover the question that comment is unnecessary. Preachers should heed the note of warning and not degrade their sacred professions by dabbling in politics, while the priest-ridden people can find food for solid reflection which may benefit them and the cause they profess.

The national surplus is a constant menace and incentive to extravagance. Pension bills are now pending in Congress that call for an expenditure of two and a half billions; public building bills call for $150,000,000; fortifications and ships demand $50,000,000, while the river and harbor bill just become a law rakes out a cool $22,000,000. Down with the war tariff and its consequent wringing of millions, needlessly, from the people!

JUDGE DURHAM thinks that the Senate will delay the tariff bill as long as possible, so as to keep the democratic members at Washington and prevent a discussion of the question at home till late in the fall. Then they will endeavor to frighten the labor vote by misrepresentations about free trade. For this reason the judge very wisely advises the democrats to inaugurate an early and as aggressive campaign as possible.

Gov. McCreary added further laurels to his fame in the House Saturday by a telling speech on the Chinese question. His arraignment of the republican party on its disposition to flood the country with the miserable refuse of China to compete with honest home labor was very strong and his speech will furnish much campaign material on the question.

de-ashley.A3:
AN ATROCIOUS DEED.
BELVIDERE, Kan., April 26.—The murder of Dr. W. E. Ashley and Eugene Grove, of this place, in the Indian Territory has been confirmed.

They hired a team and buggy to go to the nation on a hunting and prospecting tour. When a few miles below Englewood in the Indian Territory they were met by vigilantes who called Grove to their camp and without warning or ceremony hanged him to a sapling.

Ashley drew his Winchester and opened fire, but they murdered him at once, fifteen balls piercing his body.

The victims had two women companions and what has become of the remains of the murdered men or the unfortunate females can not be conjectured. Sheriff Oleson has returned from the scene and says he can not find any trace of the people nor the team.

This is the most atrocious deed inflicted in a country where crime has full sway. The vigilants are, in most cases, worse than those whom they seek to kill.

de-ashley.A8:
Murdered by Vigilantes.
Kan April 26 - The
Murdered by Vigilantes.
BELVIDERE, Kan., April 26.—The murder of W. E. Ashley and Eugene Grove, of this place, in the Indian Territory has been confirmed. They hired a team to go to the Nation on a hunting and prospecting tour. Near Englewood, I. T., they were met by vigilantes, who took Grove, and without warning, hanged him to a sapling. Ashley drew his Winchester and opened fire. They murdered him at once, fifteen balls piercing his body They had two women companions, and what has become of them and the bodies can not be conjectured. Sheriff Olesen says he can not find a trace of them.
de-ashley.A13:
BRUTALLY MURDERED.
Two Kansas Men Murdered in a Cowardly Manner by Vigillantes. BELVIDERE KAN April 26. The murder
Two Kansas Men Murdered in a Cowardly Manner by Vigilantes.

BELVIDERE, KAN., April 26.—The murder of Dr. W. A. Ashley and Eugene Grove, of this place, in the Indian Territory, has been confirmed. They hired a team and buggy to go to the nation on a hunting and prospecting tour. When a few miles below Englewood, in the Indian Territory, they were met by vigilantes who called Grove to their camp, and without warning or ceremony, hanged him on a sapling. Ashley drew his Winchester and opened fire. They murdered him at once, fifteen balls piercing his body. They had two women companions and what has become of the remains of the murdered men or unfortunate females cannot be conjectured. Sheriff Oleson has returned from the scene and says he cannot find any trace of the people nor team. This is the most atrocious deed inflicted in a country where crime has full sway. The vigilantes are in most cases worse than those whom they seek to kill.

event.A1:
Notes From the North.
PORTLAND, January 9.—The dwelling of J. Waggy in Powder River Valley, Oregon, was totally destroyed by fire yesterday. His twelve-year-old daughter perished in the flames.

A dispatch from The Dalles, Ore., reports a double homicide in Harney Valley, Oregon, resulting from a quarrel between cattle and sheep men. One of the latter killed one of the former and was in turn lynched. His sheep are scattered all over the country.

fannie-garrett-goodlettsville-1888-06-27.A1:
A BLACK DEVIL.
Horrible Treatment of a Girl Whom He Lured From Home.
Horrible Treatment of a Girl Whom He Lured From Home.
Special Dispatch to The Appeal.
NASHVILLE, Tenn., June 27.—Fannie Garrett and Irvin Holder (colored) were granted a marriage license yesterday. At 2 o'clock this morning some one came to Fannie's house and called to her, telling her that Holden was dying of hemorrhage, and said for her to get ready to go to him immediately. The man then told her that he would go for a doctor. The girl got up and dressed, and on going out found a negro man, whom she claims not to have known, waiting for her. The two then started for Holder's house, which is just over the Sumner county line. The negro man walked in front until the bridge dividing Sumner from Davidson county was reached. At this point the man allowed her to pass him, and after crossing over the bridge, the man seized her and accomplished his purpose. The negro had an open knife in his hand, and during the struggle the girl received several ugly cuts on the face, one behind the ear and one across the hand. After outraging the girl the negro allowed her to go, and told her if she stopped or screamed he would kill her. Her clothes were torn and muddy, and showed evidence of a severe struggle. A posse of citizens are looking for the negro today. If he is caught he will probably be lynched.
fannie-garrett-goodlettsville-1888-06-27.A2:
WASHINGTON CRITIC
NEWS OF THE DAY.
Important Events of the Past Forty eight Hours.

Its history has been traced to a collection owned by Earle, the well-known painter and companion of President Jackson, who died at Jackson's home, leaving many valuable works.

In Chicago yesterday Mrs. Meckie Rawson, wife of the millionaire banker, who attempted to murder in court her husband's lawyer, Whitney, was permitted to give bail for that offense. Whitney is still in a serious condition, but it is thought will recover. Mrs. Rawson will be compelled to remain in jail thirty days yet, notwithstanding the bail, to atone for her contempt of court in continuing to shoot at Whitney, though the judge was loudly calling for order.

Early yesterday morning a negro called at the house of Charles Smiley, near Goodettsville, Tenn., and told his servant girl that Irwin Holden, to whom she is engaged to be married, was dying and that he wished to see her immediately. She accompanied the negro toward Holder's house, but when they reached a secluded spot the man assaulted her. During the struggle he cut her severely with a knife. She escaped and gave the alarm. A mob of whites are searching for the brute, who will be lynched if captured.

It has been decided to open the exercises pertaining to the celebration of the centennial anniversary of the settlement of Ohio and her sister States of the territory northwest of the river Ohio at midnight of July 3. The Cincinnati Centennial Exposition will open at 9 a.m. July 4. It is proposed to have Mrs. Cleveland start the machinery, if it has to be done by electricity from Washington.

Yesterday morning, as the south-bound express on the International Railroad was approaching Milano, near Austin, Texas, a white man entered the smoking car, and, without any provocation whatever, walked up to where Sam. Arnold, a colored porter, was sleeping, and shot him through the head, causing instant death. The man then attempted to shoot Conductor Corcoran, who overpowered and disarmed him. He proved to be a raving maniac.

Joseph Greenfield, son of D. Greenfield, a furrier at 679 Broadway, New York, was arraigned in court yesterday, charged with theft by his father. Last Monday young Greenfield, it is charged, stole a trunkful of furs, valued at $2,500, from the store. He was arrested at Rochester and brought back.

Charles Deckler, a farmer of Buena Vista, Ill., sent his children from the house Wednesday, and then crept up behind his wife and shot her through the brain. Deckler then went into the sitting-room and sent a bullet almost through his heart. The cause of the tragedy is unknown.

The Master Plumbers' Convention at Boston yesterday, elected as officers for the ensuing year: President, John Trainor, Baltimore; vice-president, E. J. Hannon, Washington; secretary, J. J. Carr, Baltimore; financial secretary, Enoch Emmerick, Philadelphia; treasurer, J. J. Hamlin, Chicago; sergeant-at-arms, D. J. Collins, St. Louis.

Mrs. Keese, a respectable woman of Anderson, S. C., who was charged with attempting to burn the city, and who disappeared two days ago, has been found. She is a raving maniac, and had attempted to drown herself. Gustav Frank, the Pinkerton detective, who was arrested on a charge of subornation of perjury, has been released.

At the closing of the session of the Hungarian Delegations, yesterday, Count Kalnoky, Imperial Foreign Minister, conveyed to the Delegates the special thanks of Emperor Francis Joseph for their devotion and for the patriotic unanimity with which they had fulfilled their important and difficult duties.

In Walton County, Ga., on Wednesday night, there was a church festival, at which some colored people got into a dispute as to who had done the most for the church. Pistols were brought into general use, and Sam Alexander was shot dead. Charles Cooper, who is supposed to be the murderer, is in custody.

E. Bradley, the teller of the Union National Bank of Chicago, who disappeared some months ago on the discovery of a shortage in his accounts, voluntarily returned to Chicago from Canada and surrendered to the authorities. Bradley says he hopes to make good his indebtedness to the bank.

Theodore Castor, a farmer, was attacked on his way home from Kingston, Mich., Wednesday night, by three brothers, named Drost, who demanded his money. He shot one dead and fatally wounded another, and thinks he hit the third, who escaped.

There was no announced change in Chicago yesterday in the East-bound rates situation. The Wabash and Chicago and Atlantic, it is understood, will make a rate of 35 cents on dressed beef from Chicago to New York, Boston and seaboard points.

In Minneapolis, yesterday, W. H. Truesdell was appointed receiver for the Minneapolis and St. Louis Railroad in the suit of Henry Seibert, trustee, successor to the Central Trust Company of New York, against the Minneapolis and St. Louis Railway Company.

A fire in McCrann's fat-rendering establishment, Paterson, N. J., yesterday, communicated to the sale and boarding stables of Hopper & Ackerman, which were destroyed, with thirty-two horses, including several valuable trotters. Loss, $25,000.

In the suit of Alice Potts against Emily Willard for $50,000 damages for alienating the affections of her husband, Lewis Potts, the jury, at Port Huron, Mich., rendered a verdict, yesterday, awarding Mrs. Potts $20,000.

The Mexican freight depot and adjoining buildings in Paso del Norte were burned Wednesday night. About seventy freight cars were also destroyed, a large amount of freight being burned. Loss about $200,000.

The grand jury of the Franklin (Ky.) Circuit Court has returned four indictments against James W. Tate, late State Treasurer, for embezzlement of $404,085.85. Embezzlement is not an extra-ditable crime.

While ex-Mayor M. A. Smith of Philadelphia was taking a bath in Chicago last Saturday a sneak thief entered his room and stole a diamond stud, valued at $600, and a gold watch and chain, valued at $500.

Gus. Clifford and William Tremlin were killed and Dick Thorn fatally injured in Kansas City yesterday by the giving way of a scaffold.

The two-mile boat-race between Columbia and Harvard was rowed at New London, Conn., in wind and rain. The New Yorkers won easily. Columbia's time was 11:54; Harvard, 12:08.

The indications are not favorable for a settlement of the wages of the iron workers, and it is feared that a big strike will take place in Pittsburg and Western mills, beginning next Saturday.

farris-avon-1888-04.A1:
IN COLD BLOOD. Dastardly Murder of Stephen McGehee in Buckheart Township Yesterday Noon. The Murderer, John Farris, a Former Husband of McGehee's Wife, Arrested and in Jail.
brutality, deliberateness of design and fiendish cold-bloodedness of execution was committed yesterday in Buckheart Township, about two and one-half miles south of the city.

The victim was Stephen McGehee, and the murderer was John J.—better known as "Bud"—Farris.

McGehee lived with his wife and her two children by a former marriage—boys aged twelve and six years, respectively—in a small tenant house on the farm of Samuel Wilcoxen. He was a hard-working man, of good reputation, and about thirty-six years of age. He was married not quite two months ago, to the divorced wife of John J. Farris, and for four weeks had resided at the place of the murder, removing there from the farm of Peter Bowman, his wife's father, four miles south.

Mrs. McGehee's first husband, Farris, to whom she was married some fourteen years ago, was a drunkard and a spendthrift. She endured his abuse and bore with his bad habits until he had squandered nearly all of her property, but about four years ago, he being at that time in the calaboose at Havana, she yielded to her friends' persuasions and returned home, with her children. Two years later she procured a divorce. Before and since that time Farris had visited her and the children, and had frequently importuned her to return to him, but she had lost confidence in his often-broken promises, and steadfastly refused. In March of last year, to escape prosecution for stealing timber, Farris quitted the country. He was back for about a week the last of December. At that time McGehee was paying some attentions to Mrs. Farris, but "Bud," though cognizant of the fact, made no protest and no threat. He had, however, frequently said that should his former wife ever marry another, he would kill him. Last week the older boy, Eddie, received a letter from his father, dated at Raritan, Illinois, and on replying, Saturday, mentioned the marriage of his mother. Monday Farris come to Canton, was in the city, drinking and threatening, the next day, and on Wednesday went down to carry out the mission on which it would appear that he had expressly come.

When he entered the house he found the family at dinner. They had heard of his return, but McGehee had expressed, and evidently felt, confident belief that he would make them no trouble. Farris gave his victim no opportunity for self-defense, but before McGehee could arise from the table fired at him two shots from a revolver, the second passing into the brain at the left temple and causing almost instant death. There were no words between the men, excepting the murderer's announcement as he walked in, "This is what I have come to do," and the victim's cry of "Don't" just after the first shot.

He threatened, and appeared to have purposed, to kill Mrs. McGehee, but yielded at last to the entreaties of his children, and after holding her under the cover of his branished pistol for an hour, he permitted the trembling woman to depart, upon her promise not to impart information of the murder until she should reach the city. She started with the children, on foot, stopping nowhere, in fear lest the murderer should be following, and it was after three o'clock when she reached the home of her parents, near the northeastern limits of the city, and told her story. Farris, before he left the scene of the murder, shook hands with her and the children, gave the eldest boy his revolver and cartridges—the weapon is a new one, thirty-two caliber, of cheap workmanship and invited them to his funeral, saying that he was going over to a neighbor's barn to hang himself.

However, he did not carry out that purpose, if ever he entertained it. Constable Wilson found him at five o'clock in the hollow near Thomas Hornett's, with a keg of beer, and arrested and conveyed him before Magistrate Armstrong for examination. The hearing was postponed until Friday morning, the prisoner being taken to Lewistown on the evening train and placed for safe-keeping, meanwhile, in the County Jail.

A party proceeded at once to the premises, finding McGehee dead, as they had expected, although his wife had not been permitted by his slayer to examine his injuries nor even to go back into the house after the shooting.

The Coroner is holding an inquest today. There is, however, not much that is doubtful to be cleared up. The murderer does not deny, but seems rather to exult in, his desperate crime. The account of it he gave to the officers does not materially differ from the version of the woman and children. Neither the pistol shots nor the after tumult in that quiet little hollow seems to have attracted the attention of any neighbor, although there are three houses within 300 or 400 yards. But the case is clear enough, even without the murderer's confession.

Farris is about thirty-four years of age, and of unprepossessing and rather brutal appearance. He has respectable family connections in South Fulton, being originally from Isabel Township.

LATER—The evidence at the inquest, heard this afternoon at the City Hall, gives the crime an aspect of yet deeper blackness. The fiend outraged the person of the woman, after the murder, dragging her into an old log house adjoining the dwelling, and sending away the children by the bribe of the revolver.

The brute probably will not be brought back for examiation to morrow, as intended. It would scarcely be safe.
farris-avon-1888-04.A2:
A Cold Blooded Murder.
CANTON, ILL., April 19.—A man named Farris walked into the house of M McGill, south of this city two or three miles, yesterday afternoon, deliberately drew a pistol and shot McGill, killing him instantly. Farris then threatened to shoot McGill's wife and two children. The woman begged for her life, and Farris then drove the woman and children from the house. Word was brought here and officers went out and arrested Farris.
farris-avon-1888-04.A3:
GUARDS AND THEIR GUNS
STAVE OFF A LYNCHING THAT WAS ALMOST DESIRABLE.
Particulars of a Recent Devilish Crime in Illinois—Bloody Sequel to the Work of the Divorce Court—The Divorced Husband Kills His Successor in the Presence of Wife and Children.

CANTON, Ills., April 21.—The crime perpetrated near this city on Wednesday afternoon by John J. Harris was a fiendish one. Thirteen years ago Farris married Miss Dibbie Bauman. Two children, boys, aged respectively 12 and 5 years, were born to them. Four years ago, on account of brutal treatment, Mrs. Farris procured a divorce from her husband, who had squandered her fortune in dissolute living, the court awarding to her the custody of the children. Two months ago Mrs. Farris was married to Stephen McGehee, a farmer. Mr. and Mrs. McGehee took up their residence on the Wilcoxen farm, about three miles south of Canton.

On Saturday, April 14, Eddie, the eldest boy, wrote Farris, his father, that his mother was married again. Farris was engaged at the time with a party of railroad surveyors in Henderson county, west of here. News of his former wife's marriage seems to have turned him into a human devil, for immediately after receiving his son's letter he come to Canton, arriving here on Monday. His whereabouts on Tuesday are unaccounted for, but it is known that he was under the influence of liquor and threatened to kill McGehee and his wife. On Wednesday morning he was seen going south toward the residence of McGehee. It is probable he went direct to the premises and remained in hiding, awaiting the appearance of McGehee, who
About 1 o'clock McGehee came home. While he and his little family were at the dinner-table, Farris opened the door and walked in, revolver in hand. Approaching the table he fired at McGehee, exclaiming: "I have come to kill you and her, and I'll do it." The first shot McGehee received in his right arm. He begged Farris not to kill him, but Farris fired again, the second bullet crashing through the brain. Farris then turned upon Mrs. McGehee, telling her that she had to die, too. Mrs. McGehee caught his arm and pulled the pistol aside, and Eddie also caught hold of him, begging piteously for his mother's life. In the struggle that ensued Farris tripped and fell, and was held down for a time, being allowed to arise upon his promise to spare her life. For an hour he kept the woman terrorized, refusing to allow her to enter the house. Finally he gave the revolver to Eddie, and told him to get his brother and go to the barn and play. The little fellow, thinking he was saving his mother's life by getting away with the revolver, promptly took it and went as requested.

As soon as he had gone Farris seized his former wife and outraged her. This accomplished he called the children to him, compelled them and their mother to shake hands with him, and promise to attend his funeral. He then informed them that he intended hanging himself, first ordering them to go to Canton and not to say a word about what he had done until they arrived there, under pain of instant death. With her children Mrs. McGehee started for this city, not knowing whether her husband was dead or not. It was after 3 o'clock when she arrived at the residence of her parents, and it was then the alarm was given.

A physician was dispatched to the scene of the tragedy. Word was also sent to the city and search for the murderer began. At about 5 o'clock he was in the vicinity of a beer garden near the city, in company with a number of companions, drinking beer. Officer Wilson arrested him and brought him to the city. His examination was set for Saturday, and he was taken to Lewistown and placed in jail. Friday afternoon at the coroner's inquest, in addition to the above facts coming out, certain unmentionable testimony was given in relation to the flend's outrage upon his former wife. As soon as this became known threats were made of lynching the devil in human form, and the excitement became intense. At the adjournment of the inquest the sheriff at Lewistown was notified to look out for a lynching party and a guard was placed at the county jail.

During the night about seventy-five masked men from south of the city marched to Lewistown for the purpose of executing summary justice. Arrived at the outskirts of the town, a runner was sent in to reconnoiter the jail. He came back and reported a heavy guard armed with Winchester rifles. For some reason, probably the lack of a leader of nerve, the mob concluded not to make the effort that night and went away.

During the night Sheriff Smith slipped away with Farris and drove across country to Cuba, where at 6:30 Friday morning he boarded a train for Peoria, safely lodging his prisoner in the jail there.
