farris-avon-1888-04.A11:
To Be Hanged for Murder. PEORIA, Ills., Dec. 22.—In the case against John J. Farris, for the murder of Stephen McGee, the jury to-day brought in a verdict of guilty, and fixed the penalty at death by hanging. The murder was committed in Fulton county, in April last, and was one of the most cold-blooded on record. The victim was the husband of Farris's divorced wife. The evidence showed that Farris, while under the influence of liquor, went to the house where the couple were living and deliberately shot McGee. After committing the murder, Farris outraged his divorced wife. The murder created the most intense indignation, and Farris was threatened with mob violence. He was brought to this city for safe-keeping, and the case was brought here for trial on a change of venue. Editors Ordered to Divulge Certain Things.
PHILADELPHIA, Dec. 22.—Judge Biddle, this afternoon, issued a decree directing Wm. M. Bunn, editor and proprietor of the Sunday Transcript, and Hugh A. Mullin, editor and proprietor of the Sunday World, to testify in the Select Council bribery investigation, and answer the question as to the sources of information upon which they based editorials in which they charged that attempts had been made to bribe councilmen in the interest of the Northeastern Elevated railroad project. The witnesses, when before the committee, refused to divulge their sources of information on the ground that it was contrary to newspaper ethics and the honor of their profession. The city solicitor then appealed to the court, with the above result.

Mrs. Whitling Must Hang.

PHILADELPHIA, Dec. 22.—Judge Allison to-day overruled the motion for a new trial in the case of Mrs. Sarah Jane Whitling, convicted of the murder of her little daughter Bertha, by poisoning, and sentenced the woman to be hanged. Mrs. Whitling received her sentence with apperent indifference. The death of little Bertha was the indictment on which she was convicted, but had conviction failed she would have been tried for the murder of her husband and infant boy Willie. The husband and two children died within a period of three months, and after her arrest Mrs. Whitling confessed to having poised them all for a few hundred dollars insurance which was carried on their lives. The defense was insanity.

Father Shot by a Son.

WILKESBARRE, PA., Dec. 22.—James Warner, aged forty-five, and his son John, aged eighteen, residents of Dorrance township, a few miles from here, who have been at work chopping in the woods for several days, had a quarrel this morning. The father made a lunge at the boy with an ax, but the latter dodged and ran to his home near by, barring the door as he entered. The father going to the front door commenced to batter it down with the ax, when the son poked a shotgun through the opening and sent a load of buck-shot into the father's breast. The injured man died in a few minutes. There is not much sympathy heard for the deceased, as his conduct toward his family has been bad.

"Artemus Ward's" Will in Court.

NEW YORK, Dec. 22.—Charles F. Brown (Artemus Ward) died in Southampton, England, in 1867, leaving a will which was admitted to probate there. Today, a decree of the Supreme Court was filed, ordering that the surrogate of this county admit a copy of it as the original will. The humorist left property in Yonkers, and legatees, in this country. He made his mother his residuary legatee, and provided that at her death the greater part of the principal should be devoted to founding an asylum for worn-out printers in the United States. The children of John G. Gerry, of Waterford, Me., were also to receive $1,000 each, and it was in their behalf that the proceedings here were taken.

Panic on Board a Train.

TUSCOLA. Ill., Dec. 22.—The explosion of a hot-water pipe in a day coach on the Illinois Central train last evening, filled the car with steam and created a panic. Every passenger attempted to run out of the car at the same instant, and many were trampled upon and more or less hurt. Mrs. Ida Pierce, of this city, was among the passengers, and she alone retained self-sufficient nerve to pull the bell cord and stopped the train. A number of ladies attempted to jump from the train before it stopped, but were held back by men passengers.

frank-gillam-1888-09.A1: Two horse thieves were caught and lynched in Routt county the fore part of this week.
frank-gillam-1888-09.A2:
A Reported Lynching.
For two day past rumors have been circulated to the effect that Frank Gillam, until recently a resident of this city, and one George Elliott had been lynched in Routt county near the Utah line, about five days ago. The story as reported here has the wild sensational features that such matters generally take on the frontier when horses are the subject of the stealing. The rumor says that Mrs. Gillam accompanied her husband and Elliott and was present when the lynching occurred. It is through a letter from her that it is claimed the news was conveyed to this city. Mr. K.R.Bowles and Mr. Plumb missed a horse, each, the night Gillam left Aspen and Mr. Plumb has sent a man to Routt county to see if his horse is among the herd that were captured from the men whom it is alleged were lynched. This band of horses consisted of eighteen animals, part of which we stolen from Piceance creek, and it is said that the cowmen from that section pursued the thieves to the Utah line, captured them and strung them up to the handiest pine tree that had a limb strong enough to serve as a gallows. It is also reported that the two men were buried near the spot where they were lynched.

From another, and what seems to be an entirely different source, comes the same account of the affair coupled with the allegation that Mrs. Gillam who has a baby scarcely a month old, made such a desperate fight to save her husband's life that she was threatened with the rope also. The latter rumor is traced to a prominent cattleman from the White river country who sojourned over Sunday in this city.—Aspen Times.
frank-gillam-1888-09.A3:
Hanged by Cowmen.
Hanged by Cowmen.
Says the Ogden "Argus": The cowmen of Piceance creek pursued and overtook Frank Gillam and George Elliott, alleged to have stolen some horses, in Routt county, Colorado, near the Utah line.
Mrs. Elliott, who was present with her baby a month old, fought like a tiger to protect her husband, but in vain; the self-constituted executioners hung both men to the branch of a fir tree.

george-mitchell-1888-03-18.A1:
WEST WASHINGTON.
A Murderous Assault.

A murderous assault was made at the Virginia end of the Aqueduct by George Mitchell, a constable of Alexandria County, upon Roger Fields, a young man living at 3010 M street, about 5 o'clock yesterday afternoon. Fields, accompanied by a friend named Rowland, was walking along the road when they met Michell, who invited Rowland to play a game of cards. Thereupon a scuffle ensued for the possession of the cards, Rowland claiming them as his property. During the scuffle a friend of Mitchell approached with a club and attempted to strike Rowland. At this time Fields started to the rescue of his friend, and Mitchell drew a forty-two calibre revolver and fired one shot, the bullet striking Fields in the left side and lodging between the ribs.

Mitchell, after the shooting, was threatened with lynching by the large crowd present, and he was taken to the stable of John Clark, who locked him up and turned a bull dog loose to keep off intruders. Fields' wound was dressed by Dr. Suter and the ball extracted. It was pronounced a serious but not dangerous wound.

At the Churches

Rev. Dr. Stuart, rector of Christ Church, occupied the pulpit at St. John's Church yesterday morning.

A memorial window has recently been placed in St. John's Church to the memory of Rev. Mr. Addison, who held the first Episcopal service in Georgetown in 1794. It is an imported window and very beautiful.

Rev. Mr. Regester of St. John's preached at Christ Church yesterday morning. He took his text from the 138th Psalm, 8th verse, "The Lord will perfect that which concerneth me." Mr. Regester is an eloquent divine and his delivery is good.

Rev. Dr. Bates of the Congress-Street M. P. Church took his text at the morning service from Matthew 21st chapter, 42d verse.

The supper given by the ladies of Congress-Street Church was a success socially and financially. At the annual meeting Mr. Richard Young was elected as delegate to the annual conference, with Jas. Martin as alternate. The old boards of trustees and stewards were re-elected.

Rev. Father Welsh of the Georgetown College occupied the pulpit of Trinity Catholic Church yesterday. He took his text from the 8th chapter of the gospel of St. John, "But Jesus went out of the temple and hid himself." The sermon on Wednesday night will be delivered by Rev. Father Gillespie, S. J.

Notes About Town.

The President and Mrs. Cleveland drove through town yesterday and crossed the Aqueduct, whence they drove to Fort Myer and Arlington Cemetery.

The official date of the parade and celebration of the free bridge is the 11th of April.

Mr. John Drill, an old ex-member of the police force, is lying dangerously ill at the residence of his son on Prospect avenue.

On Saturday night the barn of H. C. Stroman at Langley, Va., was burned with its entire contents, including two valuable horses. The same night the barn of General W. W. Mackall was also burned with its contents.

The weighmaster at the hay-scales reports a small quantity of hay coming in, with prices as follows: Good timothy, 75@80c. per hundred; clover, 55@60c. per hundred and mixed hay 55@65c.

Mr. Robert Arlow, living at No. 1019 Thirty-second street, while under the influence of liquor, attempted suicide on Saturday night at his residence by cutting himself in the muscle of the left arm. He was discovered by Acting Sergeant Volkman and Officer Hall. Dr. Ritchie was called in, who dressed the wound.
george-mitchell-1888-03-18.A2:
Affairs in West Washington.
HOOTING AFFAIR ON THE VIRGINIA SIDE — BO
SHOOTING AFFAIR ON THE VIRGINIA SIDE.—Roger Fields, a young man who resides on M street, near 30th, was shot by a colored constable named Mitchell, near the Aqueduct bridge, on the Virginia side of the river, yesterday afternoon, the shot taking effect in Fields' left side. Fields was seen by a STAR reporter this morning, and stated that while he and a companion, named "Bud" Roland, were returning to West Washington from Roslyn, Va., by way of the road leading to the free bridge, they were accosted by two colored men, one of whom said, "Do you want to play a game of cards?" to which Roland replied "Yes," and taking the cards from the man he (Roland) asked, "Are there 52 here?" While Roland was handling the cards, showing the colored men a trick with them, a white boy came up and said: "Keep them cards; that man took them away from me this morning." The colored constable made a grab for the cards when Roland threw them upon the ground, telling him if he wanted them to pick them up. This, one of the colored men did, and after picking them up dared either one of the white men to touch them, which Roland did, when suddenly the negro caught Roland by the coat collar and began shaking him. Fields says he then interfered, whereupon he was seized by the other colored man who refused to let go his hold. Fields then drew a small penknife and opened it, and threatened to cut the colored man if he did not let him go. Fields then made a motion as if he was going to cut him, when his captor quickly drew a revolver and fired at him, the ball striking him in the left side. The men then escaped, followed by a large and angry crowd. The ball was removed by Dr. Suter.

ATTEMPTED SUICIDE.—Robert Arlow, who resides at 1019 32d street, and who has been on a protracted spree for several days, returned home Saturday morning at 4 o'clock and drove his wife from the house. She was compelled to seek shelter in a neighbor's house and remained there during the day, fearing to return. Later in the evening Mrs. Arlow desiring some clothing, applied at the station for protection. Acting Sergeant Volkman and Officer Hall accompanied her to her residence, and found the house locked up. After entering by forcing the door, the officers had to climb through a window to get to other parts of the house, and then found the door leading into Arlow's bed room locked. This door was also forced, and there the officers found Arlow lying upon the bed, which was saturated with blood, which was flowing from a cut on his left arm, about four inches long and about two inches deep. The flow of blood was checked until the arrival of Dr. Ritchie who dressed the wound and sewed it up. It is thought by his wife that her husband cut himself with suicidal intent, as he has on previous occasions said he would commit suicide. Mr. Arlow was resting easy this morning.

THE PRESIDENT CROSSES THE FREE BRIDGE.—The opening of the free bridge at this place has caused a great influx of visitors to West Washington on each pleasant Sunday. Several thousand persons visited the bridge yesterday. In the afternoon, about 3 o'clock, the President and Mrs. Cleveland, accompanied by a restroom driver,
a great minuus of visitors to west washington on each pleasant Sunday. Several thousand persons visited the bridge yesterday. In the afternoon, about 3 o'clock, the President and Mrs. Cleveland, accompanied by a gentleman, drove across the bridge in an open carriage.

THE CANAL. The water was turned on in the canal to-day, and many of the boats which have been here during the winter started for Cumberland. The water was turned on in the upper levels some days ago.

AT EACH MEETING of the M-street Christian Union Temperance Association there is an increase in attendance. The meeting last night at the Market-house Hall was a largely-attended and spirited one. Addresses were made by Messrs. Cox and Giles urging those present who had not signed to do so at once. Several persons signed the pledge.

INCENDIARY FIRES IN VIRGINIA.—A large hay barrack, containing 5 tons of hay, the property of Gen. Mackall, at Langley, Va., was totally destroyed by fire Saturday night about 11 o'clock. Shortly afterward, about 12 o'clock, a large barn belonging to Mr. Henry Stroman, also at Langley, was destroyed by fire. There were in the barn at the time of the fire three horses, a cow, and a lot of agricultural implements, which were destroyed. It is generally thought that these fires were the work of an incendiary.

FINED FOR PROFANITY.—Wm. Massey was before the Police Court to-day, charged with profanity, Officer Cotter appearing as complaining witness. The defendant denied the charge and said he could get witnesses to prove his innocence. "What witnesses can you call to prove that you did not use bad language?" asked the judge. "Mr. Cotter, if he will tell the truth," replied the defendant. "You know I told the truth," said the officer. "You are fined $5," said the judge to the defendant.

ACIDENT TO A LADY.—While Mrs. O'Neal was returning to her home, near Green Springs, on the Conduit road, Saturday afternoon, she was knocked down by a horse attached to a buggy in which were seated two drunken men. Two of her ribs were broken. Dr. Ritchie attended her.

NOTES.—During the past few days there have been many pike, perch, mullets, and alders caught in nets in the wide water near the club-house.—John Drill, an old resident of this place and one of the original members of the metropolitan police force, is lying dangerously ill at his residence, No. 1240 32d street.

SHOOTING AFFAIR.—Roger Fields, a young man living in Washington, was shot by a colored constable named Mitchell near the Aqueduct bridge, in this county, on Sunday afternoon, the shot taking effect in Fields' left side, inflicting a slight wound. Fields says that while he and a companion, named "Bud" Roland, were returning to Washington from Rosslyn, they were accosted by two colored men, one of whom asked him to play a game of cards. While Roland was handing the cards a white boy came up and said: "Keep them cards; that man took them away from me this morning." The colored constable made a grab for the cards, when Roland threw them upon the ground. He then caught Roland by the coat collar and began shaking him. Fields says he then interfered, whereupon he was seized by the other colored man, who refused to let go his hold. Fields then drew a small penknife and opened it, and threatened to cut the colored man if he did not let him go. Fields then made a motion as if he was going to cut him, when his captor quickly drew a revolver and fired at him, the ball striking him in the left side. Mitchell, after the shooting, was threatened with lynching by the large crowd present, and he was taken to the stable of John Clark, who locked him up and turned a bull dog loose to keep off intruders. He afterwards e-caped. Fields' wound was dressed by Dr. Suter and the ball extracted.

An account of the affair furnished by a resident of the county is as follows: Since the free aqueduct bridge has been open between Georgetown and Alexandria county, great crowds of people from Washington and Georgetown come across on the Virginia side, especially on Sundays, and while the great majority are quiet, law adding people, yet some presume to disregard the law by being boisterous, gambling, &c. On Sunday last George Mitchell intercepted a party of young men playing cards, and took the cards away from them, telling them it was against the law. In a short time these young men got another party with them and assaulted the constable with a knife and struck him with what he thought to be brass knuckles, whereupon the constable shot one of them in the side. The crowd then attempted to lynch the constable, but assistance coming to him the crowd dispersed, taking the young man to Georgetown, where the ball was extracted. It is understood the next county grand jury will investigate the matter.

executive committee.
Alexandria Affairs.
d for THE EVENING STAR.
THE SHOOTING IN ALEXANDRIA COUNTY.—The next grand jury of Alexandria County, at this place, will hear witnesses, as to the shooting of Roger Fields, of West Washington, by the colored constable, Robert Mitchell, last Sunday, near the Aqueduct bridge. The constable claims that he found a party of young men gambling and took the cards away from them, and that these men, with others, came back and assaulted him, and that he fired in self-defense. The next county grand jury will meet here on the fourth Monday of May.

CIRCUIT COURT.—The Circuit Court, Judge Keith, did not try the coupon cases to-day, as was expected, the judge having postponed them to the May term. He will devote that entire term to the coupon business, and if necessary will ask the assistance of other circuit judges, and hold continuous terms until all the coupon suits are disposed of. The court has heard arguments in the suits of Swansbury agt. Lucas, and Artcheson agt. Summers, and has ordered a sale in the case of Daniel Young agt. M. E. Jones.

Notes.—The city collectors are pressing for the payment of the tax bills in their hands. No coupon question arises in relation to city tax bills.—The agents of Chataigne's new Alexandria directory are now making ready for their canvass here.—Thos. Dalley, charged with obtaining goods under false pretenses, has been sent to jail for ten days by the mayor.—Several parties are prospecting for the establishment of fruit canneries here.—Objections have been made by residents of the neighborhood of the Pioneer Mills to the erection of the United Oil Co.'s tank-house in that section. The street committee will hear all parties and the permission will probably be granted.—The ship Syren, which has discharged part of her cargo of lumber here, has gone on to Washington.—The suit of the late Lewis Hipkins against the city council for damages to his property on Cameron street by change of street grade has been sent on to the next term in the Circuit Court.
george-mitchell-1888-03-18.A6:
SMOOTING SCRAPE.
A Fight with a Constable-Other Alexandria Notes.
[Special telegram to the Dispatch.]
ALEXANDRIA VA. March 20. Anoth

ALEXANDEIA, VA., March 20. — Another shooting scrape is reported from Rosslyn, near this end of the Aqueduct, it having occurred Sunday. It appears that George Mitchell, a village constable, interrupted a game of cards of some boys, taking the cards away; whereupon they, obtaining a number of others, principally toughs and blacklegs that infest there on Sundays, went back to thrash Mitchell, who being surrounded and threatened by one Roger Fields with a knife, fired, the ball making, perhaps, a serious wound in Fields's side. This so infurred the mob that they made threats of lynching, and it was with the greatest difficulty, it is said, that Mitchell was gotten to a stable near by, where he was guarded by bulldogs until night.

Judge Keith has decided to let the "coupon-crusher" cases go over this term. There are some thirty-five on the docket.

General Mackall's haymow, containing five or six tons, and the barn of Henry Slowman, containing several horses, cows, and a number of implements, situated near Langley, were totally destroyed by fire Saturday night. It is believed that the fires were the work of an incendiary. Slowman was partially insured.

John Johnson, the negro horse-thief of the upper counties, has been given fifteen years.

Charles Harris, for slaughtering Albert C. Harrison's fine cow for its hide, was yesterday given four years.

Daniel Jett is held here for the Fredericksburg authorities, who want him on the charge of stealing a $100 gold watch and some money.
Rev. W. L. Young has been ordered to the Southern Methodist church here vice Mr. Rumsey Smithson, who goes to Winchester.

george-washington-1888-05.A1:
A negro boy with n wooden leg, age
A negro boy with n wooden leg, age about 17 years named George Washington, way laid, shot and killed W. H. Taylor, white, a citizen of Catahoula parish while he was plowing in his field. The boy was caught, and as the following account from the Harrisonburg News would indicate, neither his wooden leg nor the distinction of passing under the name of the Father of his Country saved him:

The boy was captured by the constable of the ward and a possee who started for this place with him—but up to this writing they have not reached here. It is some distance from here, the roads are bad and the woods are thick and it is conjectured that he might have escaped from the posse.

He probably escaped a trial by jury but the crime was a horrible one and if he got "lost" in the thickest of those thick woods his fate was well merited.

It will be remembered the great fuss that was made over the alleged rape case in which Miss Angeline Herbert, white, and Mingo Jack, black, were the parties. On account of the color of the alleged rapist he was duly lynched, not because he had committed rape, but because the alleged victim was white. White men are very particular about protecting white females from black ravishers and they need only to think a black man guilty to be ready and willing to hang him higher than Haman. Even up here, in the free Northwest, they have that same fiendish prejudice. Only a short time ago, a Colored man was accused of raping a white woman in Grand Forks, Dakota, he escaped and came into Minnesota but was followed by a mob and taken from this state back to Grand Forks, a team of horses was attached to his arms and another to his feet and he was literally drawn asunder. It afterward transpired that he did not commit rape at all, the woman confessed that he did not, but that she thought he intended to do so when she gave the alarm. Nothing was ever done in vindication.

It now seems that Mingo Jack was murdered by the blood thirsty mob who sent him to his eternal home.

The following was sent out by the Associated Press last Monday:

"Richard Carney, a Negro under sentence of death in Freehold, N. J., for the murder of Mrs. Margaret Purcell, has confessed that he assaulted Miss Angeline Herbert, a white girl, two years ago, for which crime Samuel Johnson, an old Negro known as Mingo Jack, was lynched."

We have always believed that a majority of these alleged rape cases were without foundation and that a thorough investigation before a legal tribunal should be had when such would be found to be the case. We do not wish to shield criminals, black or white, but we wish innocent black men saved from death at the hands of unprincepled prejudiced mobs of white men. Lynch law must go.

Assassinated His Successful Rival.
OLNEY, Ills., Feb. 13.—Joseph F. Leaver, a bridegroom of a week, was shot and killed Saturday night while seated at his fireside twenty miles southwest of Olney, and his brother-in-law, Washington Osterman, a boy of 17, was shot and wounded slightly. The shot was fired from a shotgun through the window from without about 8 o'clock. The load entered Leaver's heart, killing him instantly. Leaver's wife and her mother were seated about the fire at the time, but escaped. Harper Meadows, aged 21, who was an unsuccessful suitor for Miss Osterman's hand, and who threatened to kill whoever she married, has been arrested.
harper-meadows-1888-02-14.A2:
The Assassination Near Olney.
St. Louis, Feb. 13.—Late information from Olney, Ill., near where Joseph F. Leaner was assassinated, last Saturday evening, by being shot through a window while sitting beside his young wife, is that Harper Meadows, a member of a highly respected family of the neighborhood, has been arrested on suspicion of being the murderer. Mrs. Leaner makes a statement that she rejected an offer of marriage from Meadows, and that he threatened to dispose of the man who should marry her. This has aroused strong feeling against him. Meadows is in jail at Fairfield, and the people are in a state of high excitement.

THE WEEK'S NEWS.
Congressional Proceedings for the Week Miscellaneous News Items. Monday, April 2- In the senate the house
A bill was passed appropriating $150,000 for the purchase of quarters for the signal office at Washington. The house bill to authorize the construction of a bridge across the Mississippi river at Memphis was considered and passed, with amendments. In the house the Mills tariff bill was reported and referred. Notice was given that it would be called up Tuesday, April 17. Under the call of states bills were introduced. A motion to suspend the rules and pass Crain's joint resolution, proposing a constitutional amendment changing the time for the annual meeting of congress was defeated—nays 80, yeas 154—not the necessary two-thirds.

Tuesday, April 3.—In the senate Mr. Riddleberger's resolution to consider the fisheries treaty in open session was taken up' and an executive session was ordered to cut him off. After the doors were opened, Palmer's motion to recommit the bond-purchase bill was lost—yeas 20, nays 31. In the house 5,000 additional copies of the tariff bill and reports were ordered printed. The direct-tax bill was called up. Mr. Foran opposed its consideration with the pension appropriation bill, which was defeated—yeas 95, nays 144. The direct-tax bill was then considered until adjournment.

Wednesday, April 4—In the senate a bill was reported withdrawing public lands in Mississippi from sale. A resolution was agreed to asking information of the secretary of the treasury in regard to lead ore smuggling from Mexico to Canada. A bill was passed granting right of way to the Billings, Clark's Fork & Cook City railroad through the Crow Indian reservation. The bill to reimburse the Freedman's bank depositors was taken up, but laid over on a demand for the regular order, which was the bond purchase bill. In the house, after the reading of the journal, the direct tax bill being the regular order, it was proposed to fix a time for taking a vote, but the opposition objected. E. B. Taylor (O.) moved to limit debate to an hour, whereupon filibustering was resorted to until adjournment late at night.

Thursday April 5.—In the senate Senator Wilson of Iowa spoke at length against the president's message. In the house the entire day was spent in filibustering against the passage of the direct tax bill. No agreement was reached.

Friday, April 6.—In the senate a message from the president was received with the draft of a bill for the revocation of the withdrawal of certain lands for railroads. The house joint resolution appropriating $25,000 for the international exhibition at Barcelona, Spain, was passed. The bill to authorize the sale of mineral lands to aliens was considered and postponed until Monday. A preamble and resolution were offered by Riddleberger calling for copies of the correspondence on the subject of territory reported as recently acquired by Great Britian from Venezuela. It was referred. One hundred and twenty-seven private pension bills were considered and passed, sixty-five being house bills. The bill for a bureau of animal industry was considered and then postponed until Thursday. House bills were passed for public buildings at Greenville, S.C., and Texarkana, Ark. In the house filibustering continued.

Saturday, April 7.—The senate was not in session, and there was nothing of importance done in the house.

THE END OF A QUARREL THAT AROSE FROM TALKING POLITICS.

The quiet village of Belleville, on the Passaic River about four miles from Newark, was the scene of a murder at 11 o'clock on Saturday night, William Henry Harrison, colored, fatally stabbing William Barnett, with whom he had an altercation growing out of a political dispute. Harrison is about forty-eight years old and Barnett was thirty. The two men met in a beer-shop kept by Andrew Reinhard, in the main street. Barnett was engaged in discussing politics with several men, when Harrison joined in with a remark derogatory to Irishmen. Barnett replied that his father was an Irishman and asserted that he would not permit any man to say anything against him.

The dispute waxed warm, and the two men exchanged blows. Reinhard thoreupon interposed between the combatants, receiving a blow in the face intended for Harrison. Reinhard put Harrison out the back door, and then took hold of Barnett and ejected him from the front door. Immediately afterward the two men encountered each other in a little street near the beer shop leading to the bridge across the Passaic. The quarrelling was renewed and the men clinched and pounded with each other until they reached the house of the bridge tender, where witnesses from the beer shop saw Harrison crowd Barnett on a low back plaza of the house.

The men unclinched for an instant and then Harrison drew away and walked off. Several men ran to Barnett, who was staggering on the porch, and gathered about him, when he fell and a stream of blood gushed from his neck. Doctors were hastily sent for but Barnett died before any help could be rendered. The body was laid on a bench and an examination was made. It showed a deep stab in the left side of the neck, severing the jugular vein and penetrating to the right side. News of the murder soon spread, and Justice of the Peace Sandford, with a constable, hastened to the spot. On their way thither they saw a man crossing the street and recognized Harrison, whom they took into custody.

A crowd soon gathered and threats were made to lynch the prisoner, who preserved a cool demeanor. Justice Sandford opened his court and informed Harrison a statement.
A crowd soon gathered and threats were made to lynch the prisoner, who preserved a cool demeanor. Justice Sandford opened his court and informed Harrison that he was at liberty to make a statement. Harrison thereupon related what had occurred in the beer shop and his encounter with Barnett after being ejected. He said: "Barnett came up to me and asked if I had enough. I said I didn't want anything to do with him, and then he tripped me up. I fell down and when I got up we both clipped and I hit him, but I couldn't fight him: he was a stronger man than I. When we got to Mr. Mulligan's (the bridge tender's) stoop I got my arm around the post and caught hold of his neck and choked him a little. I didn't have a razor or knife. I never carry a knife." Harrison was committed to the jail in Newark yesterday. He has a wife and five children in Belleville and worked as a laborer. Barnett lived with his parents on a small farm in Washington ave.

MURDER DUE TO POLITICAL TALK.
William Henry Harrison, a negro, and William Barnett quarrelled in Reinhardt's saloon, Belleville, N. J., Saturday night over a disparaging remark which Harrison made about Irish voters. They came to blows, and Reinhardt put them out through opposite doors. The fighters met in the street soon after and struck several blows, and then clinched and fell. The negro walked away, but Barnett did not stir, and several witnesses found blood gushing from a stab wound in his throat. He died before a physician could help him. Harrison walked into the hands of a constable before midnight, and was committed to the Newark jail by Justice Sandford for murder. He denied using any weapon, but said he choked him.

Harrison has the reputation of being a pretty hard man, and has been in trouble many times. Barnett was popular and inoffensive when sober. Both were laborers. Harrison was born on the 4th of March, 1841, the day of President Harrison's inauguration, and he was named after the President.

A Wife Murderer Lynched.
ORT COLLINS, COL., April 5.--Tom Howe.
A Wife Murderer Lynched.
FORT COLLINS, COL., April 5.—Tom Howe, a la borer, who had been on a protracted spree, Monday evening brutally murdered his wife by cutting her throat with a jack-knife. He then kicked the body into the street and went to bed to sleep off the effects of the liquor. At 8 o'clock last night 300 masked men took possession of the jail where Howe had been placed, and in a short time Howe's lifeless body was hanging from a barrack in the court-yard.
j-h-howe-fort-collins-1888-04-04.A2:
A Murderer Lynched.
FORT COLLINS, Col., April 4.—At noon to-day J. H. Howe, a prominent citizen, murdered his wife by cutting her throat with a pocket-knife. He was at once arrested, and this evening a mob took the prisoner out of the jail and hanged him. On account of continued abuse, Mrs. Howe had threatened to procure a divorce. To-day Howe found his wife packing her clothing, preparatory to leaving him, and he cut her throat. Howe was about forty years old, and came from Fredonia, N. Y.
j-h-howe-fort-collins-1888-04-04.A6:
Howe's Awful Death.
DENVER, April 6.—A Fort Collins special to the Republican says: The lynching of J. H. Howe Wednesday night pricked the bubble of public suspense and excitement, and to day a feeling of relief pervaded the community. It is a singular fact that there is little conflict of opinion as to the propriety of the awful deed which launched a human soul from time into eternity. Unlike similar occasions, usually—where the law-and-order elements of society favor upholding the dignity of the law and allowing courts of justice to assume the responsibility of deciding the matter, the aggravated and causeless nature of this case was so evident that the outraged people took justice into their own hands.

Not only laboring men and merchants, but professional men, doctors, lawyers and clergymen, strange as it may appear, attended the execution, and none opposed, with the exception of the sheriff and his posse, the execution of the unwritten warrant.

A meeting of citizens was held early in the evening in a vacant business room on Linden street, where the murder and the details for the lynching were discussed and plans formulated. Shortly after 8 o'clock the electric lights were extinguished by disconnecting the wire from a lamp and this was the signal for opening the ghastly programme. Sheriff Davy apprehended trouble. He had guards stationed about the jail and five or six men of nerve within, but the attack was so sudden and the darkness so intense that resistance was impossible.

About thirty men advanced at a double quick across Oak street to the front door of the stone jail, and while three or four pinioned the burly sheriff, the balance forced the outside door, and in two minutes they had broken the huge lock which fastened the strong door of the jail.

The attacking party had all the necessary tools, and their entrance was almost unimpeded. As Howe heard the door being broken down he cried for mercy, and continued his beseeching till at the scaffold. As his cell door opened he walked into the arms of his executioners, who speedily bore him to the rear of the new court house, where stands a scaffold about thirty feet high, used for hauling up mortar for the workmen. A rope dangled from the pulley, just as it had been left by the masons. Howe was placed under it, his feet and hands pinioned and a noose adjusted about his neck, in less time than it takes to describe it.

At this juncture a voice cried, "Let him speak!" As the opportunity was given, he only said: "Gentlemen, once more I ask you to spare my life!" His request was greeted with a howl of derision, and a moment later he leaped into the air, as two scores of strong arms tugged at the further end of the rope. He kicked and drew himself up three or four times, and several minutes elapsed before life was extinct. The body was cut down and taken to the hose house, which crowds visited to view the body during the day.

The poor wife's remains lie at Undertaker Ralph's and many have been attracted thither by morbid curiosity as also to the scene of the tragedy where the lifeblood of Howe's victim stains the carpet, door-sill, gate and fence for thirty feet.

Probably no community in the West is more disposed to be law-abiding and peaceable than Fort Collins, but the extreme cruelty and needlessness of Howe's act so inflamed the public mind that resistance was useless. Possibly after a few days elapse and sober second thought comes into action an attempt may be made to establish the supremacy of the law, but it appears doubtful whether any successful prosecutions can be made.
j-h-howe-fort-collins-1888-04-04.A7:
QUICK JUSTICE
Administered to a Colorado Wife-Murderer by An Infuriated Mob. FORT COLLINS, Col. April 6—J. H. Howe
Administered to a Colorado Wife-Murderer by An Infuriated Mob.

FORT COLLINS, Col., April 6.—J. H. Howe murdered his wife in cold blood at noon, Wednesday, and at 8 o'clock in the night a lynching party numbering several hundred took Howe out of jail and hung him. The town is wild with excitement. Howe came here from Fredonia, N. Y. For the past few years he has been dissolute, not properly supporting his wife and one child. Her friends have frequently counseled her to leave him, but this she refused to do, hoping to redeem him.

Tuesday he gave her a whipping while he was drunk. Wednesday noon he went home and found his wife packing her trunks, and she told him that she was going to her friends. Upon this he seized her and, taking out a pocket-knife, slashed her across the cheek, cutting a gash reaching from the mouth to the ear. He then took her to the door and pushed her out. Here she fell to the ground, and he then, planting his heels on her breast, deliberately cut her throat, severing the jugular. She managed to get to her feet, and staggered into the street, where she fell dead at the feet of a few spectators, who had been attracted by her screams.

Howe went into the house and waited for the officers. He did not resist. Within an hour a crowd of one hundred people had assembled around the jail, and lynching was freely talked of. The sheriff fought off the mob as best he could, but at 8 o'clock in the evening the jail door was forced, and Howe was taken out and strung up without ceremony.
j-h-howe-fort-collins-1888-04-04.A10:
A FORT COLLINS TRAGEDY.
A Man Named Howe Kills His Wife and is Promptly Lynched.

Special to the Denver Republican.

FORT COLLINS, Colo., April 4.—J. H. Howe, a millwright, murdered his wife at noon to-day in his own house by cutting her throat with a pocket-knife. He was partially intoxicated. He entered the house and found her engaged in packing her trunk preparatory to leaving him. He seized her by the hair, cut her face through with his knife, dragged her to the door, cut another gash in her throat, and kicked her from the door-steps. The victim ran out of the gate and a half-dozen paces, fell, and died in a few minutes.

So quickly was the tragedy over that the victim was already beyond human aid before the neighboring people, who were alarmed by her cries, arrived upon the scene. Quickly, though, they gathered, and as the news spread like wild-fire men came breathless with running, from all parts of the city. The now inanimate form of the lovely woman was tenderly borne to a neighboring residence. It was found that she had been cut twice. One gash was from the mouth through the right cheek to the ear. Another was on the left side of the neck and deep, severing the jugular vein. It was from the last cut that death came immediately.

Word was dispatched for Sheriff Thomas R. Davy, who soon came and entered the house in company with a deputy. He found Howe lying on a bed and arrested him without trouble. The murderer was taken to the county jail, escorted by the sheriff and several deputies. He was followed by a crowd of men, who needed but a leader to make a rush and tear him from the care of the officers. Howe was conveyed safely to jail and locked up.

As soon as the news of the terrible crime spread fully a thousand men gathered about the jail building and clamored for the swift execution of Justice. Lynching was loudly talked, but was prevented by the Sheriff who refused anyone admittance to the jail and surrounded himself by a strong posse. The excitement grew throughout the whole city, and the feeling of indignant demand for the quick retribution of outraged life swelled until it could be confined by no bounds.

At 8:30 o'clock to-night 300 men, all mounted, rode to the jail and demanded admittance. Some of them were masked and some were not. They were refused, when the leaders promptly knocked down the jailer, Sheriff Davy, and overpowered a posse of twenty men who made such resistance as was possible, but which was plainly futile. The masked men then battered down the jail door and obtained access to the jail.

Away back in the corner of a cell Howe was just discernible, crouched in abject fear. He pleaded piteously for mercy, but the battering ram was again brought in play and in crashed the cell-door. Out through the opening the begging, half-fear paralyzed wretch was dragged. He was pulled and pushed through the corridor and out of the jail and surrounded by the grim determined figures borne swiftly to the base of a derrick, which was standing near the new Court House building.

Quickly a noose was placed over his livid face and around his neck. He prayed for deliverance and cried for pity, but his cowardly cries were met with derisive shouts. The rope had been led over the top of the derrick and on the other side were a half hundred strong hands holding it. The leader of the masked men gave the word. The men at the rope called "One, two, three!" and Howe shot up in the air as if a ton weight had fallen on the other end of the hempen cord, which tightened with a snap and strangled the life out of his worthless body.

Howe was about 40 years of age and came from Fredonia, New York, a famous milling town, about eight years ago. He was then accompanied by his wife, whom he married in that state. They had a girl about 6 years old, born in Colorado.

SAM WILDY: The Career of Sam Wildy and His Silver- Tongued Partner.
Sam Wildy, the tall handsome Texan, who went crazy at Billings, by the whisky route, who was sent to the Warm Springs, released after a time and with $25 in his pocket given him by Dr. Mussigbrod, went to Spokane Falls and there tried to dispose of a forged draft on his kind benefactor, has left for parts unknown and Montana will know him no more. Wildy was an indifferent kind of a lawyer; but was a man of fine presence and when he made his appearance in Montana was not addicted to drink. He came first to Junction City, very close to the terminus of the Northern Pacific railroad. About the time of his arrival, Burns Smith, since dead, one of the old citizens of the northwest, who in the early days of his life had killed a negro at a point on the Missouri river near where Bismarck now stands, added another death to his list, under more favorable circumstances. Burus kept a saloon at Junction and was leader of affaction arrayed against another saloon man with an equally large following. One morning he became involved in a quarrel with a stage driver belonging to the other side. The drunken driver at once declared war and fortifying his courage with a copious supply of the villianous concoction called whisky sold principally to the Indians on the adjacent reservation, he took his gun, a rifle, and taking up his position across the street at a distance of about fifty feet, under the shadow of Paul McCormick's store, opened fire at Burns, who was close to the open door of his saloon. Several harmless shots were fired, Burns all the while standing immovable. But no sooner had the assailant stopped his firing when Burns reaching for his gun near by, took aim and as the man turned to leave, shot him in the back, killing him almost instantly. The affair caused the wildest excitement and for awhile it looked as if shooting would become general and the town depopulated; but fortunately the danger was averted by the sober and cooler citizens. It was at Burns Smith's trial before a justice of the peace that Sam Wildy first practiced law in Montana. In the case he was assisted by a person claming to be a lawyer, by the name of Farwell, and together they secured the acquittal, against big odds, of Burns Smith. Wildy soon after went to the new town of Coulson and as soon as Billings was established became a resident thereof. While he was not a well-grounded lawyer, he was a pleasant speaker and was withal, one of the most popular men of the lower Yellowstone. During the past two years he gave way to his desire for drink and that soon accomplished his downfall. Notwithstanding his loose habits however, he was elected to the important position of county attorney two years ago, and had Wildy been able to withstand the temptations that stood in his way he could have been a recipient of the highest honors the people of this section could bestow.

In this connection it is not inappropriate to speak of Farwell, mentioned above. This erratic genius commanded a flow of speech, and invective when needed, that was remarkable. In personal appearance he was slouchy and possessed a countenance that was almost hideous. In his habits he was also diametrically opposite to Wildy, as he would not even taste liquor and denounced a man who did with the strongest condemnation his wonderful vocabulary contained. Farwell carried his law library under his arm and relied entirely on his use of language to win his cases, and was generally successful as there were few jurys or judges in these new camps that could withstand his eloquence no matter how hard the lawless portion of the community endeavored to compel them to do otherwise. Farwell claimed to be a relative of the rich Chicagoan of that name and had at one time owned a large farm in Nebraska, upon which he raised corn. The price of corn went down and Farwell having family troubles coupled with this disaster left all behind him and struck out without money for the new northwest. In his younger days he had been a street "fakir" and from this experience he was indebted no doubt, for his wonderful powers of speech. While fighting the lawless in the courts at the new town of Coulson, "Dutch Charley," who has never been apprehended, killed a boy without the slightest pretext or provocation. There being no minister at hand Farwell was selected by those who wished to give the boy, who had been a waiter and a general favorite a "good send-off," to make a few remarks at the grave. ROPE JUSTICE.

J. H. Howe Brutally Murders His Wife at Fort Collins by Cutting Her Throat.

A Fort Collins, Col., despatch of April 5th says: J. H. Howe, a millwright, murdered his wife at noon yesterday in his own house by cutting her throat with a pocket knife. He was partially intoxicated. He entered the house and found her engaged in packing her trunk preparatory to leaving him. He seized her by the hair, cut her through the face, dragged her to the door, cut another gash in her throat, and kicked her from the door steps. The victim ran out of the gate and a half-dozen paces, fell, and died in a few minutes.

Howe is a worthless character, and has for two years been on a protracted spree. He had made his wife's life a burden for many years. His whisky-maddened brain harbored all kinds of suspicions, and his unprovoked jealousy incited him to all manner of brutality. Tuesday night, crazed with whisky, he attempted to beat his wife. The neighbors interfered, and Deputy Sheriff Stultz was found and went to the house to arrest him. When the deputy sheriff arrived he found Howe in bed, and was told by Mrs. Howe that her husband had taken an opiate and was quiet. The deputy sheriff advised Mrs. Howe to have Howe locked up, but she thought it would not be necessary. The night watch was told to watch the place and see that Howe did no harm. Nothing was heard of Howe yesterday morning, he being at home in bed.

At about 1 o'clock a scream was heard and Mrs. Howe was seen to run out into the yard with the blood streaming from a wound in her throat, and she fell dead at the gate. Her husband with his bloody hands still holding the large knife with which he performed the fiendish deed, threw himself on the bed, where he was found by the officers.

This forenoon Mrs. Howe consulted Attorney Love on the propriety of getting a divorce, and she was preparing to leave her husband and was getting her furniture and clothing packed preparatory to moving when he cut her throat.

Howe is a millwright, and when sober an excellent workman, but of late he has been more or less under the influence of liquor, so that his wife was obliged to support herself and little girl by sewing. The murdered woman stood high in the estimation of Fort Collins people, and was a lady of education and refinement.

April 7, 1888.

DEAR FREEMAN:

We have just been shocked with
the most terrible tragedy that ever
occurred in this city.

A man by the name of James H.
Howe, while in a state of intoxication,
killed his wife by cutting her

ky. Another High-license argu-
ment for Prohibition.

Wednesday, April 4th, James H.
Howe, a citizen of this city, re-
turning home from the saloons cut
his wife's throat, from which she
died in a few minutes. The mur-
derer was arrested by one of the

It was evident by the conversation that plans were being made to execute summary vengeance upon the wife-murderer. About 8 o'clock p. m. the electric light wires were cut, and the lights suddenly extinguished, when bands of men, some of them masked, began to gather from every direction, until there were about 500 about the jail. The Sheriff and his assistants were put under guard; then they proceeded to break open the jail doors, and in about 15 minutes the prisoner was in the hands of the infuriated mob. During the excitement which prevailed, the pastor of the Presbyterian Church ran out, and seeing what was going on, said: "You would better hang the saloon-keepers," whereupon, some of the mob cried out: "Better hang the preachers, and let the Saloon keepers alone." This is the element ni society, which breeds lawlessness and crime; and how strange, that so many of our preachers and church members will still vote with this very class, that would exterminate the churches and the preachers and foster the saloons, with all their corrupting and crime breeding influence!

When shall the Christian conscience be properly awakened to
the enormity of this awful curse!

Mr. Howe and his wife were both
of good families, and brought up
with care. They came to this place
from Fredonia, N. Y., in 1880; he
was a respectable citizen before he
began to visit the saloons. Both
himself and his wife moved in the
best society, until he started on his
downward course. He was a mill-
wright by trade, and is said to have
been one of the best mechanics in
the West. But how quickly
rum ruins all!

Fort Collins, the scene of this
double tragedy, has a $1,000 High
License law. This revenue can
never atone for this awful crime;
but it serves to deaden the public
conscience and so perpetuate the
iniquitous system.

"How long, O Lord, how long;"
until the Christian men and women shall rise up in their righteous indignation, and in the name and strength of Jehovah, wipe from the face of the earth this blackest and most damning curse! May God God speed the day when the Saloon must and shall go! Yours for Prohibition, National and Complete

A Barber Criminally Assaults His Ten- Year Old Step Daughter.
A Barber Criminally Assaults His Ten-Year Old Step Daughter.

Special to the Gazette.

WACO, TEX., March 24 — At about 1 o'clock today one of the most heinous attempts at outrage ever known in the criminal annals of this county or the state, took place on the public street and in a stone's throw of the court house. Joe Nebroes, a Spaniard, and a barber by trade, has a barber shop on the square near the courthouse. He has a little step daughter ten years of age in December last, and very small for her years. She goes by the name of Birdie Nebroes. It has always been thought that she was an own child of Joe Nebroes, and she thought so herself. She always brings the dinner to her father at his stop. To-day she came as usual with the dinner, when her stepfather attempted to outrage her, was caught in the act and taken to jail. An excited mob had gushed and the steel bars of his cage only saved him being lynched. Nebroes has been here for many years. He was in the habit of getting on sprees, and it is said he was drinking this morning. The little girl is very intelligent and is a student of the public schools. She did not know but what Nibroes was her own father. On examination she stated that she was in the habit of obeying her father implicitly and did not know what he wanted with her in the private house in the rear of the shop, or understood what he was attempting to do or wanting to do. It has caused considerable excitement in the city. Another Mexican was jailed this morning on three charges, carrying a pistol, resisting an officer and kidnapping.

The jury in the case of N.C. Elliot vs. Constable Kirk, for false imprisonment, gave the plaintiff $200 damages.
