John Braden Dead.
Special to the LEADER.

Special to the LEADER.

BUTTE, Mont., Dec. 10.—John Braden, who was assaulted by a Chinaman on Saturday, died today at the Sisters' hospital, where he had been tenderly cared for ever since receiving the fatal wound. The gash, it was found, affected the spinal column and its effects also extended to Braden's left leg, which was paralysed immediately. When the news of the death became known great excite-prevailed and a crowd of about 200 gathered on Main street with the intention of lynching a few heathens.

One crowd chased a Chinaman several blocks for the purpose of hanging him, but fortunately he managed to escape their clutches.

According to the statement of an eye witness Braden had struck the Chinaman repeatedly previous to the Chinaman's retaliation, and then entered a saloon with a friend. On returning he picked up a large piece of wood to again assault the Chinaman when the latter suddenly turned on him with the result stated. The Chinamen, who committed the murder, is still at large. The result of the inquest is kept secret for the present.
john-braden-butte-1888-12-11.A3:
LYNCHING IS FEARED.
A Chinaman Resents an Assault by Partially Wounding a White Bully.
A Chinaman Resents an Assault by Partially Wounding a White Bully.

Special to the Globe.

BUTTE, Mont., Dec. 10.—John Braden, last Saturday evening, while passing a Chinaman who was sawing wood, kicked him and also gave him an undercut under the chin, which sent the Mongolian sprawling several feet on the ground. The Chinaman merely arose to his feet and commenced sawing wood again. Shortly afterward Braden, with several others, passed the place again, when he made another lunge at the Chinaman, when the latter swung his saw around his head and hit Braden with it. Braden bled very feely from the wound, which was about four inches long and an inch deep. Hopes were entertained of his recovery, as no large vein had been severed. To-day, however, Braden died from injury, as his lower limbs had been paralyzed by the blow, which had affected the spinal cord. Threats are uttered against the residents of Chinatown, but the authorities have put on fifty extra police to keep out the hoodlums and the mob to-night, which, it is feared, will lynch the Mongolian murderer and his friends. An inquest is now being held on the remains of Braden.
john-braden-butte-1888-12-11.A4:
CUT BY A CHINAMAN.
The Consequence of Fooling With a Mongolian When He Has a Weapon Handy.
The Consequence of Fooling With a Mongolian When He Has a Weapon Handy.

Saturday afternoon a young man named John Braden was cut on the neck by a wood-saw in the hands of a Chinaman who was sawing wood in the alley between West Broadway and West Park street. He was carried into the rear room of Murphy's saloon on West Park street, where Dr. Leavitt was called, who examined the wound and found it not serious, though it was an ugly, ragged opening, being caused by such an uncouth instrument.

When a reporter obtained admission to the room where Braden was lying stretched out on a couple of tables, he was weak from loss of blood, but rational, though unable to converse above a whisper. The saw had struck him to the right of the back of the neck, and just missed the jugular.

From one of the friends of the man, the following account of the affair was given: "Braden and another man and myself had been in this saloon a little while, and went out by the back door leading to the alley. Braden was about ten feet ahead of us. As he walked by the Chinaman, who was sawing wood in the alley, he chucked him under the chin and said, 'Hallo, John, how are you getting on with sawing the wood?' Without a word the Chinaman drew the saw out of the log of wood and dealt Braden a blow on the neck with it. He fell and we ran up to him and carried him in here, never giving a thought to the Chinaman. We thought he was dead at first, as he was bleeding freely from the wound and looked as if an artery had been cut."

After the wound had been staunched, Braden was taken in an express wagon to the Sisters' Hospital.

From another party who witnessed the affair it was learned that as Braden was passing the Chinaman, who was stooping over his saw with the usual plodding industry of his race, he knocked him over on the ground with a blow, which the Chinaman resented immediately by springing up and dealing Braden the blow that came near taking his life.

Search was immediately instituted for the Chinaman, who was cutting the wood for the St. Louis Restaurant on Broadway, through which he passed and disappeared from sight. The Sheriff and Under Sheriff arrested several of the Chinese who own and run the restaurant, and took them up to the County Jail, as they refused or professed to be unable to reveal the fugitive's name or whereabouts.

The affair created a good deal of excitement in the neighborhood of its occurrence, and there were loud threats made of going down to Chinatown and hanging a few of the residents there to make them disclose the fugitive's whereabouts. But nothing came of this.

The police say that they are not surprised at the action of the Chinaman, as the Chinese residents here are daily subjected to such repeated and wanton insults at the hands of hoodlums, large and small, which in the main go unrescued, that they are goaded to desperation. Instances are of everyday occurrence where Chinamen passing along are treated to insults amounting to personal violence calculated to drive a white man crazy. The feeling among all classes is against the presence of Chinese, but as long as they are employed and patronized by the white people they should, at least, be free from personal violence.
john-braden-butte-1888-12-11.A7:
FROM OUR SPECIAL.
The Anaconda Smelters Resume Work.----
A Chinaman Wounds a White Man.----
Lawlessness Runs Riot.--AMarriage
in High Life at the Silver City.
Special Correspondence of the LEADER.
Special Correspondence of the LEADER.

BUTTE, Mont., Dec. 10, 1888.—Yesterday afternoon, after everything about the Anaconda smelters had put on holiday attire and many of the employees had bidden farewell to friends, perhaps forever, and taken trains for the east and west, a sudden telegraphic clicking was heard calling for Anaconda. It proved to be a

MESSAGE FROM J. B. HAGGIN,

in New York, to Marcus Daly, stating that all matters having been adjusted satisfactorily between the company and the railroad, the mines and smelters of the Anaconda company would at once resume work. The trains began to roll in their carloads of coal. The fires were started in the furnaces, the ore trains commenced pouring in, and by to-morrow the vast machinery will probably be in motion again as though no stoppage had occurred. How many hearts leaped for joy at this welcome news! How many hearths and homes will now greet the "Merry Christmas" with joy and gratitude that, but for this glad news, would have been shrouded in

DARKNESS AND DESPONDENCY!

The details of the arrangements by which this settlement was reached are with the parties themselves, and probably will not be given to the public. Sufficient has transpired, however, to justify the conclusion that the interests of the great Anaconda works will be no longer a secondary consideration with the Montana Union railway. In fact the road is practically in the hands of the smelter people, who. the public may be assured, while they will take good care that

THE WORKS ARE SUPPLIED

to their fullest capacity, will also see that the interests of the traveling public, merchants and all having business with or passing over the road will not be less promptly and faithfully served than under the former management. This new department is important in various aspects. It means faster time, better accommodations, greater celerity and security for the mails, closer connections with other territorial lines, more favorable rates for travel and traffic, and a general supervision and conduct of the line, with the other vast properties to be operated conjointly therewith, pre-eminently to the advantage of Butte and Anaconda and, in no merely passive sense, the upbuilding and development of the mining, agricultural and manufacturing resources of

OUR OWN GLORIOUS MONTANA.

Here in Butte, on Saturday, the streets were full of idle men. A careful estimate, by one who ought to know, placed the number at 5,000, and many of them without money and almost desperate. One can readily imagine the effect of an outcry or alarm upon such a fevered mass of humanity. As if the occasion was not to be wanting to arouse them to a pitch of madness, the cry was heard,

"A WHITE MAN'S HEAD CUT OFF
by a Chinaman!" The needed impetus was given and the pell-mell rush began for the scene of the tragedy. In was in an alley in rear of a saloon. There, sure enough, lay the man, the life current pouring from a frighful gash in his neck. But Chinaman! where, O where was he? It seemed that the whole city had assembled to avenge the bloody deed. A yell went up, "He's in that loft!" pointing to an old log stable near by; and it seemed for a few moments that the ancient pile would be razed to the ground. The

BLEEDING AND APPARENTLY DYING man was carried into the rear of the saloon. A doctor was immediately called. After an examination of the wound it was found that the jugular vein had not been cut, as was at first supposed. After the usual washing and taking up of arteries the terrible gash was sewed up and the doctor pronounced the wound not necessarily fatal. It was a close call verily. The effusion of blood was very great. The man's name was John Braden, a miner, about twenty-five years of age, a powerful young fellow. It seems that he had been drinking some, and going out at the rear of the saloon passed the Chinaman, who was sawing wood, saying something that

CELESTIAL LOVE DIDN'T LIKE.

Love spoke back, and Braden slapped him in the face; and lo! Love, in his most amiable manner, slashed his adversary's neck as though it had been a spruce pole; and the spruce young man failed to come to time. The jaundice-hued personification of Love took to his heels and made good his escape. Had he been found.
WOULD HAVE BEEN TORN IN PIECES as if by wild beasts. But a few hours later the dispatches gave an other horror at Bermingham, Alabama, about one o'clock yesterday morning, in which five men were killed outright and a large number wounded, several seriously, if not fatally. The trouble arose from an attempt to lynch a man named Henry Hawes, imprisoned in the county jail, who was supposed to have murdered his wife and two daughters, whose dead bodies were found. When arrested he was about leaving the country with a woman he had been intimate with. As the mob approached the jail Sheriff Smith and his guards warned them not to advance. Disregarding his warning, the sheriff ordered his men to fire upon the mob, and from a

GATLING GUN AND WINCHESTER RIFLES they poured volley after volley into the advancing mass, mowing them down as though they were but cane-brake. Among the killed were Postmaster M. B. Throckmorton and Adolph Shieb, of Louisville and Nashville railway. The postmaster was trying to persuade the crowd to disperse.
john-braden-butte-1888-12-11.A9:
JOHN BRADEN'S DEATH.
The Inquest Concluded—Search for the Chinaman Continues—His Description.
The Inquest Concluded—Search for the Chinaman Continues—His Description.

The inquest on John Braden was closed Tuesday morning. In accordance with the statutory requirements, nothing concerning its developments can be made public so long as the murderer is at large, but the information leaked out that the verdict reached by the jury was that Braden came to his death from the effects of a wound on the left of the back of his neck inflicted by a wood saw in the hands of a Chinaman (fanning him) with felonious intent. The jury could, of course, reach no other conclusion.

It is known that the police authorities made an ineffectual endeavor to discover a boy who, it was reported, had seen the dead committed on Saturday evening, and whose account of the affair differs materially from that related by the dead man's companions at the time. The impression, outside of certain circles, is that it was impossible that the Chinaman could exhibit such sudden and murderous resentment on such slight provocation.

A gentleman who has seen him frequently, passing him often at work on the spot where the fatal blow was struck, says he could tell him anywhere among a thousand others, as he resembles a woman in the face more than any other he ever saw. He describes the missing man as about 5 feet 4 inches in height, and weighing probably 130 pounds. His face is very fleshy and, contrary to the usual appearance of his race, he has very red cheeks. His shoulders are broad and he is stout. His age is put down at about 50. He was a well known figure in that neighborhood, cutting wood behind the restaurant three times a day, and always had a pleasant smile for anyone who spoke to him, though he apparently did not understand a word of English. His dress was poor, but even the women passing him had a word or two of kindness for him in spite of his poor appearance.

The search for him hitherto has been unavailing, but the police authorities still entertain the hope of being able to capture him. Yesterday evening about 8 o'clock Officers Layton and McLaughlin arrested a Chinaman on suspicion of being the man required and took him up to the Court House, followed by an immense throng of men who gathered on Main street at the sight of the two officers with a Chinaman under arrest. They had made the arrest from information received from a woman who professed to know where the man lived. It was a cabin in Chinatown between Mercury and Galena. When the officers rapped at the door for admittance they found difficulty in gaining entrance. The placed was very securely barred. At last they entered and found several Chinamen sitting in the room of the cabin, and McLaughlin selected one whom he thought he recognized as the man in the habit of sawing wood behind the restaurant on Broadway. He went with the officers without any resistance. As they passed the gambling house on Main near the bank, a few cries of "Hang him!" were heard, but no one offered the least violence to the prisoner. It may here be remarked that it was just as well that nothing of the kind was attempted, as the officers have received instructions to stand no nonsense, but to meet any indications of hoodlumism promptly.

Arrived at the Court House, the officers lost no time in getting their man behind the bars. The Court House steps were filled with people who pressed up to the doors through which admittance was denied to all after the officers and their prisoner had passed through. The Chinaman was inspected by several people who professed to know him, but all declared him the wrong man. Even Officer McLaughlin was now doubtful of his identity, and the conclusion was reached that he was not the man wanted. Certainly he bore no resemblance to the description given of him by the gentleman who professes to describe him so accurately above. He was, however, detained at the jail all night as a safer place for him then to let him out after being arrested.

The police precautions taken by Marshal Coulter have been excellent and have no doubt had much to do with repressing any tendency to acts of hoodlumism if contemplated by any of the friends of the deceased Braden. The Marshal himself has been up till a late hour every night since, in the Chinatown district. The district has been patrolled by a strong force of specials who are on duty all night there in addition to the regular officers. The men selected by Marshal Coulter are steady, trustworthy men, to be depended upon in an emergency. The Marshal's orders have been thoroughly impressed upon them and the first symptom of ruffianism will meet with a check that will make the perpetrators regret their rashness.

Two of the worst characters in town are credited with the intention of making trouble for the Chinese, and inciting their friends in the haunts they patronize to get even with the heathens. As they are well known they are marked men if they take part in any such expedition. They would never return from it alive. Everyone acquainted with Marshal Coulter knows his determined character and his utter fearlessness. It would be the worst rashness for any set of men to brave him and his force by any attempt at lawlessness. The expense to the community is a trifle compared with the necessity to assert the supremacy of the law at all hazards, and this is Marshal Coulter's justification, and will be willingly coincided in by the community.

At a late hour this morning all was quiet in town, with no indications of their presence by the rough element.

COLLECTING MADE EASY.
john-braden-butte-1888-12-11.A10:
The Chinaman Set Free.
BUTTE, Dec. 13—The Chinaman arrested Wednesday night, supposed to be Braden's slayer, was released yesterday, it having been proved to the entire satisfaction of the officers that he was the wrong person. Another Chinaman stated positively today that the murderer was not in town, but had skipped the country and is out of the territory. There was no disturbance at the jail last night.
john-braden-butte-1888-12-11.A11:
BUTTE EXCITED.
TALK OF LYNCHING A CHINAMAN SUSPECTED OE MURDER.
A Naval Encounter in Chester River --Joe Murphy Will Appear on the Helena Stage-- Annexation.
Butte, Dec. 11—There is considerable excitement over the murder of John Braden by gashing him with a wood saw. The murderous Mongolian is still at large though every effort is being made to effect his capture. Sheriff Lloyd visited Deer Lodge yesterday and searched for the fugitive, but without avail. He returned last night, having heard that the mob would attack Chinatown. He stationed a large number of special officers to keep a look out and to preserve the peace. There was no violence attempted. Today a reward of $50 was offered for the apprehension of the heathen by the sheriff, he having heard that people knew where he was located, but were waiting to see if there was something in it.

The coroner's jury, which has been in secret session for two days, concluded its work this afternoon with a verdict that Braden came to his death by blows inflicted with a saw in the hands of A. H. Chee with felonious intent.

A CHINAMAN ARRESTED.

Later, 8 o'clock p. m.—The arrest of a Chinaman was made a few minutes since. He is believed to be the one wanted. The arrest was made by a policeman upon information given by Mrs. Hockett, who resides next door to the laundry on East Broadway where the capture was effected. No resistance was offered by the Chinaman. He has been placed in the jail. The Chinaman who slew Braden had gray side whiskers and a goatee. This fellow is shaved. Five or six persons have examined him but say he is the wrong party, while McLaughlin, the man who was with the deceased when he was killed, declared this is the right man. There is some talk of mobbing the jail tonight, taking out the Chinaman and lynching him, but Sheriff Lloyd is prepared to resist such an attempt. He has a strong guard stationed all around the jail and inside the doors. The sheriff says should any violence occur its probable that a scene similar to that at Birmingham, Ala., may follow. He does not feel alarmed.
john-braden-butte-1888-12-11.A14:
Killed by a Chinaman.
At Butte, John Braden, died from the effects of an injury received Saturday evening. He was passing through an alley where a Chinaman was sawing wood. Braden had been drinking, and must have done some act upon the Chinaman. His friends with him claim he chucked the Chinaman under the chin and said: "Hello, John! How are you coming on with your woodsawing?" He then drew his saw, and struck Braden on the back of his neck, missing the vertebra and the jugular vein. The blow caused a great loss of blood, and Braden was sent to the hospital, but the wound was not thought dangerous. Braden died at 10 o'clock Sunday night. The theory that Braden must have offered the Chinaman violence is generally believed except by the hoodlum element, to which Braden belon ed. Fifty special police were sworn in as it was apprehended that the tough element may make reprisals on the Chinese residents of whom a great many are in the city. The Chinaman was not found who did the deed, and it is suspected he has been spirited away by his friends and to be beyond reach. Accurate description has been furnished the officers surrounding the place, and the sheriff's officers are out in every direction, with little hope of catching him. Braden is a young man about twenty-three, unmarried, and a miner by occupation.
john-braden-butte-1888-12-11.A20:
NOT THE MAN.
EXAMINATION OF AH HEN ON
CHAEGE OF KILLING BRADEN.

Conclusive Testimony by a Host of Witnesses that Ah Hen, the Man Who Has Been in Custody for a Week, in No Way Resembles the Man Wanted for the Murder.

The preliminary examination of the Chinaman who has been held in custody on suspicion of being the man who slashed John Braden across the neck with a saw on the afternoon of the 8th instant took place yesterday afternoon in the Probate Court room at the Court House before Judge Engel. It was held there at the instance of Mr. Speer, counsel for the defense, because he expected that it would be necessary to exclude the witnesses from the room where the hearing was held while it was in progress, and there were more conveniences at the Court House for this purpose, and because there was more room there to admit the public to the hearing than in the Justice's office, and a large audience availed themselves of the opportunity. It was also a safer place to hold the hearing in from the fact that the officers of the Court House were present in case they should be needed.

County Attorney DeWitt examined the witnesses, and, their testimony being nearly all in favor of the man under examination, Mr. Speer had very little occasion to cross-examine. The first witness called was Michael Ward, who testified to the occurrences at the time Braden received his death blow as already published. According to him, Braden gave the Chinaman no other provocation than to tap him on the shoulder and inquire how he was getting on with his sawing wood. Asked if the Chinaman under arrest was the man who struck Braden he replied he was not so old a man as the prisoner. He was a few inches taller than this man. This was not the man at all. He could not remember whether the Chinamen had a beard or not. Michal Dugan was the next witness. After reciting the occurrences that took place ten feet away from him on the afternoon of the 8th inst., he too declared "That's not him, at all." The man who did the deed was a big stout man, taller than the prisoner, who in no way resembled him. Both Dugan and Wood were with Braden in Murphy's saloon, went out into the alley with him, and were only ten feet away when the blow was struck. They therefore had the best right to know whether the prisoner resembled the Chinaman who gave Braden his death wound, and both were emphatic in declaring the man under arrest not the man wanted.

It was evident that the case might safely rest here, but in order that the public mind might be satisfied that the murderer is still at large, a number of other witnesses were put on the stand and examined. A man named Stanley swore that he saw the murderer at work sawing wood in the alley five minutes before the occurrence, and knew him as Ah Chee. He was yoanger and taller than this man, meaning the prisoner.

Laughlin, the next witness, testified on direct examination that the prisoner was the man who was sawing wood at the place in question a few minutes before 3 that afternoon. He lives in a room overlooking the spot and about that time he got up, built a fire and looked out of the window when he saw the man sawing wood. He was dressed in different clothes to those he wore at the examination. He described him as dressed at the time of the occurrence in an old blue shirt, black pants stuck in stogie boots and wearing a kind of a Scotch woolen cap. He wore a goatette an inch or an inch and a half long then and had beard growing all over his face. To the best of his belief that (pointing to the prisoner) was the same man. Allowing for the difference between his appearance then and now, dressed in ordinary Chinese garb, without any beard save a week's stubble on his face, he thought he could identify him.

On cross examination, he admitted that the window of his room must be over thirty feet away from where the Chinaman stood at his work sawing wood. Finally, he wouldn't swear positively that this was the man, only that to the best of his belief he thought so.

Mrs. Hackett's testimony was to the effect that she could identify the prisoner as the man who was usually employed in sawing wood back of the restaurant in the alley. The last time she saw him there was on the Friday preceding the Saturday on which Braden was murdered. All her evidence was irrelevant as only going to show she believed she had seen the prisoner sawing wood on the spot where Braden fell at other times previous to the day of the occurrence, and her evidence was struck out.

The next witness was a man named Fox. Mr. Fox seemed to labor under the impression that this was a conflict of wit between himself and the County Attorney. He was a little how-come-you-so, besides, and was prepared to settle the case out of hand by the simple expression of his opinion. He replied impertinently to the County Attorney's questions and used cuss words pretty freely. The Justice ordered him under arrest for half an hour to convince him of the proper respect due to the presence he was in. The Sheriff and Under Sheriff hustled him out unceremoniously, took him upstairs, and accommodated him with a cell for a little while.

Doc Beal testified that he knew Ah Chee, the man wanted, and had known him for six or eight years. Saw him on the 4th or 5th inst., but was not in town on the 8th. Ah Chee is a man 5 feet 10, taller than the prisoner, and had worked for him, so that he could identify him anywhere. Had frequently met him on the street and recognized him. This was not Ah Chee.

Half a dozen other witnesses were put on the stand and one after another asserted positively that the prisoner was 100 An Chee, the Chinaman who sawed wood in the alley for the St. Louis restaurant. They all did business in the vicinity or passed by the place frequently while the man was at work, and in every case they described the man wanted as larger than the man under arrest. Some had seen him at work as recently as 3 o'clock that Saturday afternoon. A man named Anthony had worked beside Ah Chee frequently and talked to him, and was well acquainted with his appearance.

County Attorney DeWitt suggested that there was no use in going any further. He was satisfied that the identification was a failure.

The Justice remanded the prisoner to the custody of the Sheriff and directed that he be brought down to this office at 5 o'clock when he would give his decision. At that hour the Sheriff brought Ah Hen to Justice Engel's office on Main street when he was formally discharged.

SHORT TELEGRAMS.
LONDON, January 24—In the Divorce Court to-day in the case of an English woman named Turner, who had married an American named Thompson, and who had had the marriage annulled by an American court, the judge held that the woman having married and American and lived with him in America was entitled to the same laws as her husband; and therefore the decree pronounced in America was binding in England without a further decree from an English court.

WARSAW, January 24.—General Gourko presiding at a war council yesterday, declared that the sum of 20,000,000 roubles was required to complete the fortifications on the Russia frontier and build needed bridges, roads and railways. An offensive war in Russian Poland, he said, was impossible under the present conditions; a defensive war was possible if all railways and stores were destroyed.

KINGSTON, ONT., January 24.—The attention of the Dominion Government will be called to the lynching of John C. Wells, a Canadian, at Bad Ax, Mich. Wells killed a neighbor in a quarrel about a ditch, and the neighbor's friends lynched Wells.

LONDON, January 24.—Lady Sackville, sister-in-law of the British Minister at Washington, died suddenly to-day of heart disease.

DUBLIN, January 24.—A row occurred at the railway station at Galway to-day between a crowd, which was awaiting the arrival of Fathers Burke and Francis, and the police. The latter charged the people, using their batons freely, while the crowd retaliated by throwing stones and bottles. Several persons were injured, among them a member of the municipal council, who received three cuts on the head from a policeman's baton.

LONDON, January 24.—Lord Randolph Churchill has sent a dispatch denying Mr. Shaw Lefevre's assertions regarding himself and the Pernellites.

CHATHAM, ONT., January 24.—The house of Israel Evans, a license inspector, was shattered by dynamite early this morning. No one was hurt, but the house was badly damaged. The police have arrested a man who had a loaded revolver and fuse and caps for dynamite cartridges in his possession. Three other persons are also detained on suspicion of being implicated in the affair.

NEW YORK, January 24.—An Ottawa special says: A semi-official announcement comes from England that Hon. Joseph Chamberlain is likely to succeed Lord Landsdowne as Governor-General of Canada.

PITTSBURG, PA., January 24.—Edward Coffey, the murderer, died this morning at 6:10 o'clock from the effect of his self-inflicted wounds last Wednesday.

AUSTIN, TEX., January 24. The Hon. John T. Allen, ex-State Treasurer, died yesterday, aged 80. He bequeathed $300,-000 to the city for an industrial school for boys.

ST. PAUL, January 24.—A story of horrible inhumanity reached the Pioneer Press from Belgrade, Mont., where it is said a sick German laborer in the employ of a farmer was allowed to freeze to death. His employer owed him a large sum of money. His body was then removed to the woodshed, where it was partially devoured by hogs.

CLEVELAND, O., January 24.—George Kerns of Pittsburg and Charles Myers of Chicago fought with two-ounce gloves in a room here yesterday. Twelve hard and bloody rounds ended in Myers being knocked out. Two of his ribs were broken. Kerns was badly cut up.

LONDON, January 24.—Representatives of the oil dealers of Scotland conferred with a delegate appointed by the American producers at Glasgow to-day. It is considered certain that the Scotch delegates will report in favor of restricting the out, out of oil.

MELBOURNE, January 24.—Advices from Samoa say that the Germans are enforcing the payment of taxes, and that a German judge is soon to arrive at Apia. The proclamation of a German protectorate is expected.

NEWBURYPORT, Mass., January 24.—Three shocks of earthquake occurred in this vicinity about midnight Sunday night. Houses four miles from town were violently shaken.

CONSTANTINOPLE, January 24.—The Porte has prepared a reply to the recent demand of Russia for the arrears of the war indemnity. In this the Government states that the delay in payment has been due to a famine in the village, which made it necessary to divert the tithes from the indemnity fund.

DUBLIN, January 24.—An explosion of gas occurred to-day in the Bankruptcy Court here. The force of the explosion was so great that the roof of the building was hoisted from the walls, and windows were smashed. One workman was killed and another was injured.

BERLIN, January 24.—The statement is made by some officials that the military bill will involve an expenditure of 248,000,000 marks.

Strikers Returning to Work. NEWARK, N. J., Jan. 25.—Thirty-three girls and two men, who were among the striking employes of Clark's thread mills, returned to work this morning. All the strikers who applied for work were taken back without question and sent to their former places in the card and frame rooms. About one hundred and fifty of the strikers have not yet applied for work, but the probabilities are that all will soon do so. The company state they have no intention of reducing wages. The Breaker Boys Determined.
SHENANDOAH, Pa., Jan. 25.—There is not a sign of any of the collieries running around here or at Ashland. The situation is practically unchanged. No attempts will be made to start up the individual collieries. Both sides are determined to stand out, and the ranks of the miners are unbroken. The breaker boys, who are very necessary adjuncts, are more determined to stand out than ever, and as long as young America holds out the breakers cannot resume.

Preparing to Resume.

ASHLAND, Pa., Jan. 25.—The outside foreman of the North Ashland colliery claims he will resume operations at that colliery tomorrow. It is said on good authority that a meeting of the Amalgamated association will be held in Pottsville to-morrow to consider the advisability of cutting loose from the railroaders' strike.

Smallpox Appears at Detroit.

DETROIT, Mich., Jan. 25.—A few days ago William Johnson, a young colored boy, who had recently arrived from Buxton, Ont., was found by the authorities to be suffering from a mild case of smallpox and was removed to the pest house. To-day another case was discovered, the victim being a young lady from the south, but whose name and address the health officer refuses to divulge. She was also taken to the pest house. Her case is regarded as much worse than that of Johnson, and the spread of the contagion is feared.

Express Train Wrecked.

SOUTH ROYALTON, Vt., Jan. 25.—As the Boston & Montreal express, due here at 2:30 p. m., was nearing the station, the rear car broke from the train on account of a broken switch rod, left the track and rolled over an embankment fifteen feet, landing bottom side up. The train was running with considerable speed and the air brakes failed to work. Seven passengers were aboard the car, two of them sustaining slight injuries—F. H. Churchill, of Lebanon, and a man from Buffalo.

Both Legs Cut Off.

CHICAGO, Jan. 25.—At the Meagher street crossing of the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy railroad yesterday afternoon Mrs. Catherine Hogan, a lady fifty-seven years old, living at 121 Barber street, was struck by an engine and both her legs cut off. She died two hours later at the county hospital.

Fought About Five Cents.

MOUNT STERLING, Ky., Jan. 25.—Jim Lawson and John Jonett, negroes, stable hands, quarreled and fought over five cents. Lawson broke Jonett's head with a pitch fork, and Jonett cut Lawson with a knife, inflicting a serious wound in the breast.

Canada Will Investigate.

KINGSTON, Ont., Jan. 25.—The attention of the Dominion government will be called to the lynching of John C. Wells, a Canadian, at Bad Axe, Mich. Wells killed a neighbor in a quarrel about a ditch and the neighbor's friends lynched Wells.

Death of Frederick C. Brightly.

PHILADELPHIA, Jan. 25.—At 12:42 o'clock this afternoon, Frederick C. Brightly, the author of Brightly's Digest and other notable law books, died at his residence in this city, at the age of seventy-six years.

[Special to the Greenville News.]

UNION, S. C., August 6.—John Gist, colored, last week committed an assault upon Mrs. Smith Wood, white of this county. Gist was lodged in jail Saturday and an attempt was made by a mob of 75 strong on Saturday night to lynch him, but they were repulsed by Sheriff Long and Deputies R. W. Long, T. J. Vinson and L. Moore. The Johnson Rifles were ordered by the Governor to protect the prisoner. It is rumored a raid will be made to-night by 200 men with the purpose of lynching. SOUTH CAROLINA.
Prof. A. W. Long has been elected to the chair of English in Wofford college.

The new Episcopal church at Darlington was dedicated a week ago yesterday.

The colored people propose holding a base ball tournament at Laurens at an early date.

Rev. T. D. D. Clarke has assumed pastoral control of the Baptist church at Marion.

There is not a vacant house in Cheraw, and there is a steady demand for dwellings and stores.

There is some talk of the woolen mills now located at Hamlet, N. C., being moved to Cheraw.

The interstate farmers' encampment at Spartenburg during the past week has been a big success.

The farmers of Fairfield are making arrangements for the holding of an institute in that county.

The Presbyterians of Cheraw have sold their parsonage and will build another on the adjoining lot.

The Richland Volunteer rifle company of Columbia celebrated its seventy-fifth anniversary Wednesday.

The dwelling of Zack Pearson of Marlboro county was set on fire by lightning on July 29 and entirely consumed with all its contents.

J. W. Mack of Orangeburg county recently lost his gin house, mill and several outhouses by fire from an incendiary torch. Loss $2,000.

At Aiken, Bradwell & Lamar are building a livery stable on Curon street, on the site of Chapin's stables, that were burned last summer.

T. G. Lamar recently sold his plantation on the "levels" near Aiken, to Messrs. Holley and Coward. It contained 313 acres, and brought $8,000.

A new postoffice to be known as Dibble has been established on the old Charleston road, between Orangeburg and Connor's, with Thomas Riley as postmaster.

One of the arguments used for the building of another hotel at Aiken is the fact that last season over 500 people were unable to secure hotel accommodations there.

During a severe storm at Walterboro on Tuesday John Graham, a respectable colored man, living on the outskirts of the town, was struck by lightning and instantly killed.

J. B. O'Neall Holloway of the Pine Grove section of Orangeburg county says that a large salmon has been caught out of the Santee river. Mr. Holloway saw it and says it was quite a large, fine fish.

Quite a number of new dwellings are in course of construction at Laurens, and a still larger number will be built in the near future. This is due in a great measure to its successful building and loan association.

Sheriff Long of Union brought to Columbia Tuesday afternoon and lodged in the Richland jail for safe keeping John Gist, the negro accused of criminal assault in Union county and threatened for several days with lynching.

While the Rev. J. W. Kilgo was driving on the road between Wadesboro and Chesterfield, a few days ago, his horse was struck and instantly killed by lightning. Mr. Kilgo was much affected by the shock, but it is not thought that he will experience any serious injuries.

It is understood that at Darlington Thursday a contract for the largest cotton ginery in the state was given out. The ginery will be operated by a company in the town of Darlington. There will be six gins in the ginnery, and all the other machinery will be of the most improved kind.

A white man named William Martin from Anderson county was accidentally shot while examining a pistol in West Greenville Thursday. The ball entered the right breast and penetrated under the shoulder bone, whence it was extracted. Martin was sent home, but he may die.

It seems that Laurens county's triangular fight for senatorial honors is destined to continue. Senator Crews is opposed by Col. John W. Ferguson and Lewis W. Simkins. There appears to be little difference of opinion between the candidates, as all are in favor of the Clemson college. Not having a clear-cut issue, the election will probably turn on personal preference.

The regents of the State insane asylum met at Columbia Thursday and it was decided to reconstruct a number of rooms in the basement of the old asylum building, which have heretofore been used for storage purposes. When enlarged these rooms will be formed into wards and the capacity of the building will be so increased as to accommodate twenty-five additional patients.

Taking the whole Pee-Dee section of country into consideration, there have been very few complaints this year as to bad crops. Of course there are sections here and there that have suffered from drought, etc., but the general crop is good, and farmers seem to be cheerful. A good crop this fall will put many of them who are behind even with the world, and should the seasons be good again next year many will have some money ahead.

At 6 o'clock Wednesday afternoon a very severe wind, rain and hail storm passed over Fairfield county, between Blackstocks and Winnisboro. The wind is said to have nearly approached a cyclone. Trees and telegraph poles were blown down, and it is probable that considerable damage was done to corn and cotton. The hail stones were as large as one's thumb. The effect of this storm was felt in Columbia. The temperature fell considerably between 6:30 and 7 o'clock, and a pleasant breeze sprung up.

An electric storm followed by rain passed over St. Matthew's Thursday afternoon. Lightning struck the large oak tree in front of Banks & Wimberley's store, tearing off the limbs and bark and killing one of a team of two mules standing beneath the tree. The driver, a colored man, was shocked, whirled around and thrown several yards away. He is not seriously hurt, and will soon recover. Mr. Ed Wimberly was thrown from his chair and slightly stunned, while a number of others standing around were shocked. On the outskirts of the town a negro by the name of Zeigler was killed while in the act of picking up his saddle from the roots of an oak tree.

At the primary election held at Belton Friday there were 156 votes cast, of which M. F. Ansel for solicitor received 113, W. C. McGowan 12 and R. A Cailds 28. For the house of representatives H. R. Vandiver received 113, J. Perry Glenn 132, J. Belton Watson 119, J. E. Breazeale 125, and a small scattering vote for others. For clerk of court M. P. Tribble received 110. For probate judge, W. F. Cox 145. For school commissioner, C. Wardlaw 87, R. W. Todd 46 and D. H. Russell 20. For coroner, R. Y. H. Nance 134 and J. J. Dodd 17.

COLUMBIA, S. C., August 7—[Special.]—Sheriff Long, of Union, brought here to-day for safe keeping John Gist, the negro charged with criminally assaulting Mrs. Woods in the absence of her husband on last Wednesday. LYNCHERS AND LYNCHING.
Conflicting Opinions in Union County-Vindication of the Law.
[Special to the News and Courier.]
[Special to the News and Courier.]

UNION, August 10.—This community is again resting in the blissful reign of peace with all the world, and the people, both of the town and country, breathed easier when it was learned that Sheriff Long had decided to carry the prisoner, John Gist, to Columbia. There has been some mistake as to the right name of the prisoner, and in justice to Robert Barnwell I beg leave to correct the same.

It is admitted by all that the Union County jail is the place to imprison and keep a Union County prisoner, but in this case the feeling engendered by keeping the prisoner here has been bitter in the extreme, and at once was the cause of arraying bitter feeling between different sections of our otherwise peaceful county. The keeping of the prisoner here in jail after Sunday, when the authorities had the time to take the prisoner away, acted like a dare to the people in whose neighborhood the dustardly criminal assault was perpetrated and not only was the feeling in that immediate neighborhood intense, but in every section of the county and in town, and even across Broad River in Chester County. When the whole truth was learned and there was no doubt as to the prisoner's guilt, the feeling of the people was wrought up to such a pitch that innocent lives were put in great danger by keeping the prisoner here.

It has been learned by good authority that on Monday night a party of seventy-eight men, with seventy-eight Winchester rifles, crossed Broad River from the Chester side and met a party on this side, and proceeded towards town, stopping four miles out waiting to be joined by similar crowds from the surrounding country, who were rapidly gathering, when a party of Pinckney men, who remained in town all day Monday until 10 o'clock Monday night reconnoitering, met them and told them the condition of affairs at the jail. It is also known that the party meeting the lynchers had a hard time in their efforts to turn the lynchers from what they had set their heads and hearts upon doing. It is also known that the party did not want to hurt the sheriff and the rifle company, although the party was "armed to the teeth" with rifles, muskets and shotguns.

Among the arguments used, so far as your correspondent has been able to learn, were: That they did not wish to hurt or kill the brave sheriff, or a single member of the Johnson Rifles; that they only found out that the Rifles were there under the orders of Governor Richardson, and had no alternative but to protect the sheriff; that the sheriff and the rifle company were not protecting the dastardly negro, but the law and the sheriff in the discharge of his duty and his oath of office; that the sheriff and the military company had all the law on their side; that the military company wore the United States regulation uniforms, and if they, the riflemen, were murdered or killed, there would be a hereafter, and all for "a nigger" that would be hung anyways.

It was also learned that some of the party were of the best people of the county—brave and determined. They had reason enough to listen to arguments, and went back home, but very reluctantly. So far as can be learned the lynching parties have all labored under two very great errors. The first was that the rifle company was only at the jail to guard and protect the prisoners, that one hundred onstitutes Car the law, and whatever date for their right and lawful. When restored out that the rifle company ordered there by the Governor to protect the sheriff and not to "to stand up" for the black scoundrel of a prisoner, they had no desire to hurt one of them.

The second error was the result, so far as can be learned, of a charge made to the grand jury of York County, by Judge Pressly when, (they are informed and they believe it implicitly,) he charged the grand jury not to find a true bill against the lynchers of that county, and said that public opinion was the law, and law could not be enforced, and men could not be found guilty when the act of so many of a county's citizens joined them together. I do not know the truth of the charge, and only judge from what they tell me and what they believe. A great many certainly believe and say it openly that a hundred men constitute the law, and it is an innocent but fatal mistake with them.

The papers of the State should do all they can to educate the people against such a mistake, as the consequences of such beliefs and reports are obliged to be terrible to all concerned, and the safety and tranquillity of a people and State can be easily affected by it.

Now for the mistakes the riflemen labored under. They could not understand why lynchers would come into town to run "rough shod" over them and maybe murder and annihilate the whole company in which they take such great pride. It was daily reported to them that men from the neighborhood had sworn vengeance against them, that they had bought five bags of buckshot on Monday to shoot them down, that some of the lynchers wanted to wear our pretty and new "blue coats," as they called them. All this for a negro, whom the majority of the riflemen would have liked to hang, but who was in the custody of the sheriff, and they themselves ordered by the Governor to protect the sheriff and vindicate the law. Such reports were calculated to inflame the "boys," who had no alternative, and, should the final issue have come, there would have been an awful tale to tell; but, fortunately for all concerned, wisdom, counsel and natural affection intervened between brave men, and the affair was settled to the best advantage of all concerned.

joshua-anderson-owensboro-1888-06.A1:
SOUTHERN GLEANINGS.
Philip D. Bennett, a prominent citizen of Muhlenburg County, Ky., died at his home several days since, after a lingering illness, aged sixty-two years.

Henry Walton, colored, has been sentenced to be hanged at Dawson, Ga., June 23, for the murder of Tink Daniels, also colored.

The trial of five men of Sumter, S. C., for the murder of Justice Haynesworth, has resulted in the acquittal of the parties. These men are among the most influential in the county. They represent two factions who had been fighting among themselves, and they were summoned into court to give peace bonds. While the justice was preparing the papers pistols were drawn and firing begun by the opposing sides. Three men were wounded and Justice Haynesworth was instantly killed.

Jack Barfield, a desperado of Miller County, Ga., was shot and killed by Deputy Sheriff Adams a few days ago while resisting arrest.

Two barges loaded with pig-iron were sunk in the Tennessee river, near Clarksville, Tenn., recently.

A fakir recently took in a crowd at Franklin, Ky., for $250 on the bogus jewelry dodge.

Chas. Young, colored, was recently captured near Helena, Ark., and taken to Holly Springs, Miss., where he is wanted for murder.

A terrible cyclone passed near Milton, N. C., a few days ago, doing immense damage to crops and fruit, but no lives were lost.

Raleigh, N. C., has voted to license saloons.

Henry Mahony, of Evansville, Ind., was murdered by Frank Green, of Paris, Ky., at Nashville, Tenn., a few days ago.

Colonel C. M. Cason, county register of Chester County, Tenn., died a few days ago of ulceration of the throat.

G. B. George, manager of the Joseph Davis Shoe Company, of Linn, Mass. (contractors for convict labor in the Virginia penitentiary), committed suicide recently in the penitentiary yard by shooting himself in the temple.

John Holloman, a young man residing near Marion, Ky., was run over by a wagon a few days ago, and his recovery is doubtful.

Michael Duffy, the oldest member of the Montgomery, (Ala.) police force, is dead. He had been in the service of the city for thirty years, except while in the Confederate army. He was buried with military honors.

Helena. Ark., has quite a sensation. Recently T. J. Simmons was put on trial on the charge of murdering a man named Nicholson in 1872. He has been residing in that vicinity for six years past, and was arrested last January as the man Sparks who committed the murder. He was put in jail, and while thus imprisoned his wife and two children died and the remaining children were placed in the county poor house. He was put on trial, but not a single man of the vast array of witnesses for the State was able to identify him as being the Sparks that they knew at the time of the commission of the crime, and the jury without retiring from the box returned a verdict acquitting him. It was clearly a case of mistaken identity and overzealousness caused by a desire to capture a reward offered by the State.

Fourteen hundred bales of cotton at Columbia, S. C., owned by Jones, Robertson & Co., were burned a few nights ago. Loss, $60,000; insured.

Near Salem, Livingston County, Ky., an old farmer met a horrible death. He was hauling rails with a yoke of oxen when they started to run away. The old gentleman undertook to check them, but was thrown from the wagon. His head was caught between the bolster and wheel, and his skull was crushed into a jelly.

Mrs. Amelia Bolton, one of the oldest residents of Sharpe, Ky., died a few days ago of general debility. She was in her eighty-second year.

Captain J. L. Harris, a prominent cotton merchant of New Orleans and owner of the Hurstbourne stock farm, near Louisville, Ky., died suddenly a few days since of congestive chill.

Mrs. Davinney, of Columbia, S. C., died during a heavy thunder-storm, after being terrified to unconsciousness by the thunder.

United States officers report a desperate state of affairs in Clay County, Ala. A few days ago a dastardly attempt was made to murder Allen Rigsby, who had been a witness in several cases against moonshiners at the present term of the Federal Court. His wounds may prove fatal: The revenue officers report that the fruit crop in the upper counties is abundant this year, and the moonshiners are killing or intimidating witnesses so that they can have a big run in the illicit distilleries. Rigsby's house was burned by incendiaries last winter, and his life had frequently been threatened by moonshiners, who charged him with being a spy and informer.

Buck and Jerry Rasher, John Burns and James Holderman disguised themselves as "White Caps" a few days ago, and took Joshua Anderson, a quiet farmer living near Owensboro, Ky., out and thrashed him, at the same time ordering him to leave. He did not heed the warning, and subsequently he was enticed to the vicinity of Holderman's house, where arrangements were made to whip him again. Whisky the Cause of a Double Tragedy.

LOGAN, June 24.—Logan was thrown into a state of excitement by the news that James Phillips had killed his wife and then killed himself. The Coroner, accompanied by a number of citizens, repaired at once to the scene of the murder and suicide, four miles from Logan, on the Krider farm, where the news was confirmed by finding Phillips and his wife both lying dead in a poorly furnished room of a small log cabin.

The woman lay with her head near the stove, her left arm spread out on the floor. In her side near her heart was a knife stab, and her throat was cut from ear to ear. Phillips, the murderer, lay by her side, with his right arm over. Under his head was a small pillow and his hat. His body was yet warm when the Coroner arrived. Phillips' body showed three stabs on the left wrist, and his juglar vein was severed. On a table in the scantily furnished room was a nearly empty whisky bottle and a letter, in which he confessed to having done the killing.

Mrs. Byerly screamed and cried out, that her husband, who was at work in a field a quarter of a mile distant, was coming. Stewart went to look out of a window, when Mrs. Byerly started to run. A FIGHT BETWEEN POLICE AND HORSE THIEVES FOLLOWED BY WHOLESALE LYNCHING.

Oklahoma, I. T., April 10 (Special).—A courier from Shawneetown, forty miles from here, in No-Man's Land, on the north fork of the Canadian, brings the report of a fight between outlaws and a posse of the United States Marshal, which was followed by an uprising of the farmers on the border of Kansas, who meted out summary justice to four horse thieves and have the rest of the band besieged in the hills. Three colored horse thieves stole a bunch of horses from Long Tom, a Shawnee Indian. When the theft was discovered a deputy United States marshal, with some Sac and Fox Indian police pursued and caught up with the thieves, who at once opened fire upon the officers with Winchesters, unhorsing one policeman at the first round. A regular pitched battle then followed in which two of the negroes were killed and one policeman mortally wounded, dying soon after. The marshal was also badly wounded. The horses were recovered.

This section of the country is overrun with desperadoes, who have made life a burden for the farmers along the border for a long time, and when the report of this affair became known a party of fifty ranchmen congregated and started for the haunts of the outlaws. They had hardly crossed the line before they were met by a band of the thieves and succeeded in capturing four of them, who were immediately strung up to the nearest tree. The remainder of the band, six in number, was then so hotly pressed by the avengers that they were compelled to run to earth in a dugout, where they were held at bay when the courier left.

a Message.

NEW YORK, April 10.—Mayor Hewitt today transmitted to the common council a stirring message, disapproving of the resolution taking from the mayor the power of directing what flags shall be displayed upon the city buildings. In it he shows while the Irish born population amounts to 16.45 per cent, 27 per cent of the board of aldermen are Irish; more than one and one-half times the normal ratio of representation prevails in all the departments except the police, where 28.10 per cent are Irish born, nearly double the normal per centage. This he declares is at the expense of the German element. He gives a tabulated account of the national representations in office and in the charitable institutions. He states he does not publish the tables to invoke comment, but declares that under our free government and boundless resources, the Irish malcontents should exhibit a modest restraint in claiming new privileges not known to the law and not desired by the more conservative portion of the nationality in whose favor the exception is demanded. He advises the board of aldermen to adopt a measure whereby the vexed question may be made squarely an issue before the public.

OKLAHOMA, I. T., April 10.—A courier from Shawneetown brings word of a desperate fight between officers and desperadoes. GUARD CRAZED.
JOHN SHARP KEPT FOR EIGHTEEN HOURS UNDER CONTROL OF CRAZY MEN
And Becomes a Raving Maniac From the Terrible Ordeal—Horse Thieves Crops in the Southwest.
On the train with him was a man whose condition excited the greatest commiseration from all the passengers. His actions showed plainly that he was a raving maniac. He had to be tied down, both hands and feet, to the seat. From the man in charge, Pat Maloney, Mr. Van Denberg learned the strange and interesting story of how he came to his present condition.

"It was," said Mr. Van Denburg, "a strange and terrible effect of fright which had occurred near Blue Grass, No Man's Land, April 7. A Mr. Stanley, the postmaster of Blue Grass, and another man had become demented, it is supposed, from fright by vigilant committees who are now scouring that country for horse thieves. They took possession of a farm house and proceeded to smash up everything and to hold possession in spite of every effort that could be used to oust them.

On Saturday, John Sharp, a settler who had had some experience in handling said people boldly entered the house in the hopes of quieting the two men. No sooner had he gotten within than the two demented men covered him with revolvers and for eighteen hours held him a prisoner. They compelled him to dance for hours while they in maniacal glee stood by, pistols in hands to enforce their bidding. Then they would require other actions from him; anything and everything that the muddled brain of the crazy men could conjure up. For hours he remained in this house alone but at last the settlers commenced to come from the neighborhood and after he had been under this terrible ordeal for eighteen hours they had arrived in sufficient force to enter the house and overpower the two maniacal captors and tormentors. This ordeal, however, had been so long continued and was such a terrible strain upon Mr. Sharp's mind that when rescued he, too, was but a raving maniac. His mind seemed entirely gone, though formerly he was a man of strong mind, used to dealing with insane people are familiar with their curses and threats. He was taken to Englewood, Kan., in a wagon, with hands and feet tied. There the citizens raised funds to send his half-crazed wife and five little ones to their relatives near Pleasanton, Lane county. Mr. Malone, an old acquaintance, took him in charge and was coming east yesterday over the Mulvane extension to place him in an asylum.

He is about 40 years of age, and a strong muscular man. The terrible calamity appears to have likewise affected the mind of his wife and she too manifests symptoms of mind affection."

When Mr. VanDeuberg was asked regarding the hanging of the horse tieves by the vigilance committee he gave the particulars of the affair, a report of which was sent to the EAGLE shortly after its occurrence.

"In the past two weeks" he said, "an organized band of horse thieves have been operating in Clark county east of No Man's Lands and the Indian Territory, running and stealing stock from Kansas down into No Man's Land, and then stealing horses and running them back to Kansas. Last week the citizens of the vicinity of Ashland, Englewood and the settlers of No Man's Land formed themselves into a ca-operative vigilant committee to break up the gang and proceeded to raid their stronghold. In the southwestern part of No Man's Land on Saturday, the 17th inst., they captured two notorious horse thieves of the Chitwood gang, and one George Montgomery. The latter had in his possession four stolen horses. The thieves were taken to Neutral City where the vigilants assembled on Sunday, the 8th, and strung up Montgomery in the presence of seventy-five or one hundred men. He was hung to a pole projecting from a shanty. He made a full confession as to who composed the gang where the stolen stock was kept and other particulars. The other two men were released upon promises to return a certain amount of stolen stock. They were before being released required to put a number of good horses as a guarantee of good faith. The vigilants then started for the strongholds of the thieves in a body, vowing vengeance upon the miserable wretches. At last account they were moving upon the thieves' rendezvous where were kept most of the stolen stock. A hard and bloody encounter is expected when they meet. The thieves are strongly barricaded and the settlers are equally determined and well armed. All the law-abiding people in No Man's Land, and there are many of them, are acting heartily in accord with the people of Clark county, in breaking up this gang, and they will no doubt succeed."

The county is in an excellent condition, Mr. VanDenberg says, and there is a fair prospect for large and bountiful harvests.

"The rainfall in Clark and adjoining counties the first of the week was the heaviest and most continuous since the settlement of the county. Crops of all kinds are now most promising. The oat crop is up and covering the ground with a nice mat of green.

The greater portion of the corn is planted and much of it is coming up. A large area of cane, millet and forage crops will be sown. The Ashland board of trade has purchased three tons of cotton seed for the farmers in that vicinity and what has heretofore been an experimental crop, will, it is now thought, be an important product.

The Ashland coal gas and water company has been organized with a capital stock of $15,000; and the machinery for sinking a well 2,000 feet is on the ground. Everything, in fact, is bright and hopeful."

FARGO, Dak., Aug. 28.—Lynching of the two brakemen accused of ejecting a tramp from a train yesterday, whereby causing his death, was averted to-day only through the coolness of the officers conveying the men to Mapleton to attend the inquest. City Marshal Burdick, of Mapleton, rushed excitedly up to Sheriff Barnes and District Attorney Pollock, who had the train bearing the brakemen stopped a short distance from Mapleton, and proceeded in advance of the brakemen and demanded them, saying, "I want them and demand their release to me immediately."

This the officers refused to do, and after assuring the large and excited crowd gathered at the depot that they had come to Mapleton to ascertain the facts in the case, and that if the men were found guilty they would be dealt with according to law, succeeded in satisfying them enough to conclude it safe to advance with the two brakemen and proceeded with the inquest. It was shown that the brakeman had warned two men to keep off the train at Haggart, but on approaching Canfield noticed the men aboard and started toward them. When about two car-lengths from them they noticed one man suddenly disappear between the cars. The partner of Bejamin substantiated this statement, and the verdict of the jury was that deceased came to his death through no fault of the railroad company. It transpires that the excited pitch to which Mapletonians had been raised was caused by a highly colored story alleged to have been told by Benjamin's partner on the train.

POINTED PARAGRAPHS.

Topics of the Times Given in a Terse and Spicy Manner.

Wabash, Ind., is lighted by electricity.

Cars killed James O'Hara at New Philadelphia, O.

A runaway team killed William Lyons at Marion, Ind.

A home will be built at Wabash, Ind., for the little Hoosier orphans.

Members of the Canadian parliament favor the abolition of bucket shops.

Jessie Campbell died at Springfield from the scratch of a pin on her nose; blood poisoning.

George Johnson, colored, has confessed to the murder of Jake Myers, at Hopkinsville, Kentucky.

George Schinnerer had both legs cut off by the machinery in the cerealine mills at Columbus, Ind.

Patsy O'Leary, ex-champion featherweight, has blown out of the Dayton jail. A reward is offered for his return.

Lafayette, Ind., locomotive firemen offer aid and sympathy to their striking brethren of the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy.

Jewish congregation at Hamilton, O., has discharged Rabbi Bauer because he enforced wifely obedience by the beating process.

In a quarrel of prohibition at Uptonville, Ky., J. D. Upton silenced his opponent, Dr. Overstreet, with the ever ready blue grass bullet.

Andrew Thomas, of Warsaw, Ind., donates $50,000 for the purpose of sending flannel undershirts and tracts to the far away heathen.

Henry Colston, of Georgetown, Ky., murdered his uncle, and the jury awarded the bereaved nephew three and a half years in the penitentiary.

At Ironton, O., Mrs. Willis, aged sixty, shot herself because the gay lothario to whom she was wedded years ago, left her and married a woman in Texas.

William Hof, of Evansville, Ind., lost his position and immediately fitted himself for a permanent one of another kind by shooting himself through the head.

The Columbus, O., base ball club has filed suit for the appointment of a receiver, alleging that under the present management it is rapidly approaching financial ruin.

Mrs. Ellen Tupper, known as "the bee woman," and one of the foremost entomologists of the world, died suddenly Monday at El Paso, Tex., where she was visiting her daughter.

The managers of the Knights of Pythias conclave at Cincinnati have notified the Terre Haute, Ind., division that it has been assigned to lead the international drill this summer.

J. A. Pickett, a Lexington, Ky., tea agent, is cited to appear before the the court and explain why his customers failed to find the promised gold watches and diamonds floating in their cups.

At Roost, Ky., in one of those pleasant little before-breakfast exterminating tours, Bill and Jim Givens left George Sageer dead on the ground, after emptying their rifles into his heart.

Bricklayers at Findlay, O., already getting $4 per day, have struck for twenty cents more. The Nypano managers, for whom they worked, have notified them that they will give no quarter.

Unhappy Mr. Weimer jumped into the river at Augusta, Ky., found it wet, hallooed for help and being fished out, declared he would never try to make a moist, unpleasant body of himself again.

Mrs. Mary A. Holloway, of Chicago, IH. gets $2,000, done up in a cast-iron provision, out of the $400,000 distributed by her father's will. She brings suit in the Columbus, O., court to fracture the will.

John Puckett, of Calhoun, Ky., violator of the prohibition ordinance, made a spirited resistance to arrest by Sheriff Stateler, and is now only a demi-John, being half killed by a shot from the officer's gun.

The office of the Scioto valley depot, at Portsmouth, O., was broken into last Sunday night, and the money drawer rifled. Thirty-five dollars and a few checks, payable only to the company, were taken.

The Masonic fight at Columbus, O., between the Cerneau and Northern jurisdiction, Scottish rite, has again broken out and each side calls in the aid of the law to compass the task of making the other to act upon the square.

Gus Williams, the colored desperado who killed Hardin Venable at Indianapolis, March 6, kindly consented to surrender himself, and the terrified policemen are notified that they can come out from under their beds and resume work.

Josephine Blann, the missing heiress, of Cleveland, for whom the sheriff of Cuyahoga county has been searching for nearly three months, was brought into court and delivered to that official. She had been concealed in a farm house near Painesville, about forty miles east of Cleveland. She still insists that T. H. Johnson, her guardian, wanted to poison her, so as to obtain possession of her property.

The murder of the young woman, Margaret Auxier, near Yocum, in Morgan county, Kentucky, is still being discussed in the neighborhood where it occurred. On Friday night a party of men rode up to the house and called to her father to come out. Instead of doing so, he sent his daughter, who asked the men what was wanted. In answer, they opened fire on her at short range, and her body was literally riddled with bullets. The neighbors are completely at a loss to account for any motive for the cowardly murder of the young woman. Joseph S. Amos, David Lewis, and Noah and William Long are still held on suspicion,

His cousins, Dave and Al Lewis, and a brother, aged sixteen, eighteen, and twenty, respectively, are suspected and have been charged with the crime.

The district includes all that territory now embraced in the Lakeview, La Grande and Dalles districts.

LIMESTONE, Ind. Terr., Jan. 23.—Four masked men, all heavily armed, entered the Citizens Bank Saturday and presented a pistol at the head of Cashier W. T. Reynolds and demanded that he hand over the cash. While pretending to comply Reynolds slammed the door of the safe to and turned the lock. He was at once laid out by a bullet from the pistol of one of the desperadoes, which killed him instantly. The bank was then ransacked and all the money in the cash drawer, some $2300, was taken. An attempt was made to open the safe, but in this the robbers were foiled, as the sounds of pistol shots were heard and several people came rushing toward the bank. In a few minutes the town was aroused and twenty or thirty armed men hurried to the bank. The robbers were just mounting their horses, and a hot fire was began, in which Thomas Evan, a ranchman living near town, was killed. In the melee four citizens were wounded, but not fatally. The surviving robbers then rode away with the booby, followed by a posse, which after an hour's chase, caught the desperadoes and took them back to Limestone. The leader was found guilty of murder and strung up. The other two were placed in charge of a strong guard and started for Fort Washitt, where they were turned over to the United States authorities. The stolen money was recovered.

oscar-carmichael-sunnyside-1888-11-19.A1:
MURDERED BY A CONVICT.
An Unsuspecting Guard Butchered Near Griffin with an Ax.
GRIFFIN, GA., Nov. 16. — The plantation of T. G. Manly, Jr., about four miles from town, was the scene of a cold-blooded murder this morning. Mr. Manly works a few convicts on his farm. This morning he had seven convicts under a guard named W. J. Gresham clearing up new ground. Oscar Carmichael, one of the convicts, was cutting down a tree, when Gresham happened to pass in reaching distance. Carmichael suddenly turned and struck Gresham over the right eye with his axe, knocking him senseless.

COLD-BLOODED MURDER.

Not satisfied at that he hit his victim two more blows on the head and once in the breast, his skull being scattered some distance. He then took Gresham's pistol and gun and marched the other convicts ahead of him fully a mile from the scene. He then turned them back at the point of his gun, thus giving him a two-mile start. The other convicts returned and gave the alarm, and a large posse went in pursuit. At 2 o'clock they were close on his track, and found where he had stopped and tried to get off his shackles. He will be lynched if caught.
oscar-carmichael-sunnyside-1888-11-19.A3:
A CONVICT'S CRIME.
Speedy Vengeance Overtakes a Prisoner Who Murdered His Guard.
Who Murdered His Guard.

GRIFFIN, Ga., Nov. 19.—Four convicts in the camp near Sunny Side were sent on a detail under Guard Gresham. As soon as the squad was outside of camp one of the convicts, Arthur Carmichael, picked up a stone, and, throwing it with unerring aim, sent it into the guard's temple, killing him almost instantly. The four prisoners then escaped, and it was an hour or two before the body of the guard was found. The sheriff, with a posse and two bloodhounds, took the trail, which they followed through the swamps into Henry county. There the pursuers secured information of the fugitive murderer, who had sought the house where his wife lived. Friday night the posse surrounded the house, when fire was opened. After several volleys between the posse and the murderer the latter opened the door, and, rushing out, brandished his revolver over his head. He was riddled with shot from the sheriff's officers. His face was unrecognizable, so mutilated was it.

GEORGIA.

Macon's cold storage company has just begun operations.

Toccoa merchants complained of dull trade and collections last week.

The republicans of Atlanta will probably nominate a municipal ticket this week.

At Ochlocknee M. V. Chastaine has made an assignment to Ferst & Co. of Savannah.

A movement is on foot to establish a furniture factory in Americus at an early day.

The friends of Capt. T. M. Allen of Americus are urging him to make the race for tax receiver.

The city council of Americus is feeling around and figuring on establishing an electric fire alarm system.

H. S. Glover will now run between Macon and Savannah as postal clerk, instead of between Macon and Montgomery.

The hailstones of Friday evening killed nearly every bird in the Howard district of Bibb county. One farmer had two pigs pelted to death.

Mr. Stoney, a gentleman of experience in street railways, is in Americus for the purpose of making an estimate on the cost of a street railroad in the city.

At Waynesboro, Saturday, Frank, little son of Mr. Malone, was playing on some cotton bales at the railroad, and one of them fell on him, breaking a leg.

Jack Morris, who lived on H. A. Tompkins' place, in Heard county, was thrown by a Texas pony on Sunday last, and died the following day from injuries received.

Hattaway had his commitment trial at Griffin Saturday before Judge Beeks for the killing of Willingham at Sunnyside a few days ago, and was found guilty of murder.

Hon. T. S. Davis had on exhibition at Toccoa Thursday an enormous radish. It had the appearance of a turnip, but had the radish taste and flavor without doubt. It was eighteen inches in circumference, and weighed three pounds and four ounces.

A. M. Culpepper, one of Hart county's most successful farmers, made this year, on an old plantation, with two mules, 350 bushels corn, 3,200 bundles fodder, 6,000 pounds lint cotton, 70 bushels wheat, 75 bushels potatoes and a large quantity of oats.
A little negro about 10 years old was up before Judge Pilsbury, at Americus, Saturday, for stealing $2 from a colored woman. On account of his age he was turned over to the ordinary to be bound out. No one would have him, so he can go and steal again.

W. T. Blackwell, who for several years has been conducting a profitable mercantile business at Waynesboro, has suspended, with liabilities, at $5,000 and assets $7,200. William Neill, on Wednesday, bought out the stock in trade, and C. V. DeLoach of Millen is now in charge of the store.

Edgar Perkins, a young man whose father lives four miles from Georgetown, was killed Saturday afternoon while packing cotton. He was standing on the platform of the screw and one of the levers caught him on one of the upright posts, breaking his neck and crushing his head almost to a jelly.

The greatest sensation of Jasper county now is created by what is called a dog-eater. It goes at night to different houses, and wherever it finds a small dog, or one it can easily conquer, it kills it and eats its head off. No one knows what the thing is, and there is considerable excitement over it.

Marion county held its nomination Friday for candidates for county offices to be voted for next January. All of the old officials were nominated for re-election except J. M. Lowe, ordinary, who was defeated by Joseph J. Dunham. Judge Lowe has been ordinary of that county for twenty-five years.

At Covington Elija Cooksey, driver of O. S. Porter's factory wagon between that place and Cedar Shoals, while returning on horseback to the factory with Mr. Porter's mail during a heavy rain, lost his hold on the umbrella, and in trying to recover it the saddlegirth broke and he fell to the ground and broke his neck, dying in a few minutes.

The dwelling on W. S. Walton's Mitchell county plantation, near Baconton, was entirely consumed by fire on Friday night. The building was one of the old style southern country residences, commodious and comfortable, and was for many years the home of Mr. and Mrs. Walton, who now reside at Albany. The building was worth about $3,000, and was insured for $1,500.

Charles Hall (colored) who lives on the Huff place in the Warrior district of Bibb county, was in Macon Sunday, mourning the loss of his 17-year-old son, a mule and wagon and a load of wood. The son came into Macon Saturday morning and has not been heard from. Hall has no idea as to what could have become of him, especially when incumbered by the mule, wagon and wood.

The convict, Oscar Carmichael, who killed W. J. Gresham near Griffin Friday, is reported to have been killed at his wife's house, near the line of Henry, Friday night by a posse that went in pursuit. The sheriff came back to town, but the posse went to his wife's house and watched for him, and when he was seen approaching he was fired on, and according to reports was literally riddled with bullets.

At Milledgeville there has been considerable kicking by the farmers and citizens generally over a bill advertised in the legislature at an early day regarding the road and revenue commissioners of Baldwin county. A petition signed by several hundred voters of the county has been circulated, and will be forwarded to the county's representatives protesting against the bill. The local papers are against it.

Tom Harrison (colored), is a noted character in Stewart county. He was convicted of burglary once and sent to the penitentiary for four years, which time he served out. He was again convicted for a similar offense and sentenced for eighteen years. He served four years of this term, when Gov. Gordon pardoned him out. He had not been home more than six months before he was caught stealing again. He was tried, convicted, and sentenced for one year this time.
