The report that five men had been lynched by "Bald-Knobbers" in Christian County, Mo., was on Friday pronounced false.

In a fit of insanity the son of Porterfield Brooke, a farmer near Staunton, Va., shot and killed his father and then committed suicide.

The trustees of Columbia College, in New York, have sanctioned the request for an annex to the college, which shall be for women.

Mike Reinhart was convicted on Saturday of the murder of Joseph Robinson at Winnamac, Ind., and sentenced to life imprisonment.

John Hodell, a native of Switzerland, confined in the State prison at Weathersfield, Conn., on a life sentence, killed himself Monday.

A heavy fall of snow, the first of the season, was reported on Monday from points in Northern Illinois, Indiana and Western Iowa.

T. Matthews and J. R. Woodruff, prominent citizens of Point Cooper, La., killed each other on Thursday in a quarrel over a land purchase.

Mrs. Henry Jones died suddenly on Friday at Bridgeport, Conn., aged 90 years. She was the daughter of Noah Webster, of dictionary fame.

The famous Doris mansion at St. Louis, lately utilized as a public resort, was burned Monday morning. The insurance is about $25,000.

Wilson Arnold (colored) was taken from the jail at Yazoo City, Miss., on Monday and lynched for the murder of Captain Robert Johnson.

The Woman's congress closed its sessions at Detroit on Friday after the election of officers. Mrs. Julia Ward Howe was re-elected president.

Sheep belonging to C. J. Myers, living near Cincinnati, O., died of hydrophobia Friday, three weeks after they had been bitten by a dog.

A bill granting the right of suffrage to women was defeated in the Vermont House of Representatives on Thursday by a vote of 192 to 37.

Frank, the 5-year-old son of William Mason, of Terre Haute, Ind., who was bitten by a dog a few weeks ago, died of hydrophobia on Monday.

Rear-Admiral Charles H. Baldwin (retired) died in New York on Saturday. He was born in that city in September, 1822, and entered the service early.

The treasurer of Indiana filed his annual report on Monday, showing that the total domestic debt of the State was $383,783, and the foreign debt was $6,770,668.

Oscar Carmichael, a convict at Sunnyside, Ga., who escaped after killing a guard, was surrounded at his wife's house on Monday and riddled with bullets.

The Illinois Supreme Court on Friday reversed the decision of the Cook County criminal court and granted Ed McDonald, the Chicago "boodler," a new trial.

Fritz Anschlag, who was to have been hanged at Garden Grove, Cal., for the murder of Mr. and Mrs. Hitchcock, of Illinois, committed suicide on Thursday.

The Christian World, a London journal of immense circulation and influence, and hitherto stoutly advocating Unionist principles, has been converted to home rule.

At the Dudley poor-house in London a woman named Sarah Wright, who had been a pauper for thirty years, died on Sunday at the advanced age of 110 years.

Mlle. Gaudart, a French governess in the family of Mr. Bonnell, at Youngstown, O., committed suicide Monday by jumping from a window, fifty feet to the pavement below.

Thirty converts in charge of a Mormon elder passed through Montgomery, Ala., on Monday en route for Utah. All were from that neighborhood. Most of them were women.

William Davis, of Damascus, Md., committed suicide on Saturday through worry over his mother's illness. The news of his death proved such a shock to the mother that she died in a few minutes.

Fred S. Simpson, who absconded from Tacoma, W. T., a few days ago with $12,-000 of the Northern Pacific Express Company's money, was caught in British Columbia and the entire sum was recovered.

LYNCHBURG, VA., November 21. It is reported that the Chesspeake and Ohio Company, now that they have control of the Richmond and Alleghany, will build a belt railroad around the city. If this be true, Lynchburg will get up a big boom.

D. B. Payne, one of our oldest citizens and the oldest merchant here, died yesterday; aged seventy-six. He had been in business since 1836.

A dispatch was received to-day reporting another clash between whites and blacks at Pocahontas. A policeman shot and killed a negro Saturday night while the negro was resisting arrest, and last night a large crowd of negroes endeavored to lynch the policeman who did the shooting. A fight ensued, and one negro was killed and several wounded. A great deal of excitement exists.

A Highly Colored Elopement.
JACKSONVILLE, Ills., Sept. 18.—Miss Hattie B. Flack, daughter of C. E. Flack, of Schreiner, Flack & Co., commission merchants of St. Louis, eloped with Preston Sands, a colored man, and was married. Mr. Flack's family live in this city and Sands has been in their employ for a number of years, until recently, when he was discharged for stealing. The marriage license was secured in Springfield and the parties secured a carriage in the night and drove over the line and were married.

Nine of the colored men in the Washington post-office are graduates from the city high school.

There are three colored men elected to the Legislature in Phillips County, Ark., by the Fusionists.

Of Ascension parish, Hand Watson, colored, sent the first bale of cotton to New Orleans, this season.

Louis V. Kelley has been appointed messenger by the Republican campaign committee of Cincinnati, O.

The "Cuban Giants" won a ten-innings game from the "Athletics," of Brooklyn, there September 19. Score 2 to 1.

Mrs. Carrie Wilson, of Los Angeles, Cal., recently gave birth to four children, three boys and a girl. Mother and children are well.

A baby born to Mrs. Jacob Hagen, of Logan, has no legs, but one, arm and the hand of that is deformed. It's healthy and will live.

Walter S. Brown, at one time Pittsburgh correspondent of THE GAZETTE has been appointed a postal clerk between the Smoky City and New York.

Miss Annie C. Hawley, who has taught with great success in the white schools of Portland, Me., has taken the chair of history in the Tuskegee (Ala.) Normal school.

Rev. James C. Clumes, of the diocese of Trinidad, was recently ordained priest by Archbishop Riordan, at Louvain. He is the second colored American, who has been ordained to the priesthood.

The first bale of cotton ginned this season at Arnite City, La., was raised by Robert Virion; the first bale at Baton Rouge, La., by Alfred Neldar; the first at Jackson, Miss., by J. M. Nixon, all colored farmers.

The colored man who refuses to subscribe for a colored paper that is endeavoring to elevate him, and at the same time subscribes for a white paper from which he derives no benefit, is not only devoid of race pride, but is wonderfully deficient in common sense. Ex.

J. E. Stevens, a leading member of Zion church, at Bridgeport, Conn., has by economy and industry accumulated a fortune variously estimated from $75,000 to $100,000. He was mainly instrumental in the erection of the fine church there of which Rev. G. L. Blackwell is now pastor.—Star of Zion.

The attendance in the branch (colored) schools of Cincinnati, O., has exceeded the expectations of the many teachers engaged in them. The prospects are that these schools will continue this term at least. There are, however, grave apprehensions that the High School will not continue more than a few months.

The citzens of Oglethorpe have in contemplation a dummy line between Crawford and Lexington. This is a splendid project and the best part about it is that the colored citizens of that section, under the lead of Mr. Hiram Maxwell and Mr. M. G. Gilham, have called a meeting and mean to take a large share in it.—Athens (Ga.) Clipper.

That is what George W. Clark, a colored man formerly of this city, but now of Cleveland, O., says: There is not a man, woman or child in this State who could conscientiously say that this is true.—Louisiana S. W. C. Advocate.

The intolerance of Southern Democrats may be inferred from the following incident: By special invitation A. F. Judson, of Colton, Cal., addressed the colored Republican club of Hot Springs, Ark., on the issues of the day. After leaving the hall he was assaulted by three white men, knocked down and stabbed. His only warning was the remark, a second before he was hit: "We'll teach you Republicans how to speak to niggers."

Every (colored) business enterprise creates a position for your sons and daughters who are qualified for them. Hence, the more the race patronizes such enterprises the more positions you are helping to create for our worthy young men and women. We must get up in the world by helping each other. The race must have a market within itself if it would demand any trade. These are facts.—Messenger.

Will Roberson, formerly of St. Louis, and later of Oberlin, who has been employed as shipping clerk at North St. Paul for the Holland & Thompson Manufacturing Company, in St. Paul, has been promoted to the position of traveling salesman and started on the road recently, representing the above firm and the St. Paul Iron Company. Mr. Roberson is an intelligent young man with good business habits, and he will score a success in his new field.

George W. Cable is quoted as saying: "Here and there in the South a county, village, or a Congressional district where the colored people have for a long time been allowed, an unusual fullness of simple freedom, yet in most if not all these cases this condition has been attended by an exceptional degree of great prosperity, peace and good order, contrasting most creditably with other regions not far distant where the old idea has been made to prevail of holding the Negro under by main force."

Jacksonville, Ill., society has been convulsed by a social sensation. Miss Hattie Flack, daughter of Chas. E. Flack, of the firm of Schrewin & Flack, commission merchants, has married one John Sams, a coal black Negro and her father's hired man. The groom has some education and considerable natural shrewdness. The bride is a very pretty young lady, eighteen years of age, and a graduate of a famous seminary. She has for some time been a prominent figure in society circles there, and had scores of friends and admirers. The couple are now said to be in Springfield.

The way they do it down South: A pair of white church goers met a pair of colored church goers on a plank walk at Utica, Miss. They were going in opposite directions. Because the colored pair did not give up the sidewalk entirely, the white man put his hands on the shoulder of the colored woman to push her off. The colored man resented this. Next day "the intention was to give the Negro a sound thrashing and then let him go." The Negro refused to be thrashed. Result, a white man shot down dead in self defense, and a Negro lynched.

A Mr. Smith, of England, is creating quite a sensation among white society of Atlanta, Ga., by visiting at the home of the Rev. C. R. Carter, pastor of the largest colored church in that city. Mr. Smith is a traveled young man of thirty, and the son of a large blanket manufacturer of Halifax. He has been in India and visited almost every part of the world. When Mr. Carter was in England this summer, Smith took him to his house and treated him as one of the family, hence the present visit is simply an exchange of courtesies.

James Shells, of New York, is a boss bricklayer and contractor, and the only man of color belonging to the union of mechanics of that profession there. He is a young man, about twenty-six years of age, and is making rapid strides in North Carolina, where he learned his trade. He had to board himself on $150 a year, or fifty cents per day. In New York he demanded five dollars per day, and recently he passed a Civil Service Board examination, and has been appointed inspector of the Great Aqueduct at a salary of $2,100. It is, without a doubt, one of the greatest pieces of engineering and masonry work ever attempted in the city. It is a large tunnel, 200 feet in circumference, 100 feet in diameter, and is fifty miles long, extending from Croton Lake to New York City.

St. Louis, Oct. 1.—Miss Hattie Flack, the St. Louis girl who married a notorious negro in Jacksonville, Ill., two weeks ago, was arrested yesterday in Moscow, Ky., and returned here in charge of an officer. The girl was 18 years of age, and was on a visit to her father, from whence the elopement occurred. The negro, Press Sams, proves to be a horse thief, and is now a fugitive in Kentucky.

SHE MARRIED THE NEGRO COACHMAN, AND HE HAS PROBABLY BEEN LYNCHED.

Says a special to the Philadelphia Press from St. Louis, Oct. 1: D.C. McCoy, a deputy sheriff, who left Jacksonville, Ill., last week on the trail of Press Sams, the negro who was married to a white woman, Miss Hattle Flack, about two weeks ago, near Jacksonville, arrived with the woman in his custody and turned her over to her father, Charles E. Flack, of Schreiver, Flack & Co. commission merchants, of this city. McCoy, who is an old friend of the family, found the couple at a log cabin in the mountains, near Clinton, living with the family of Sams' brother-in-law. The girl at first refused to go with McCoy, until he convinced her that Sams had another wife from whom he had never been divorced. McCoy refuses to say what became of Sams, but intimates that he was lynched to save the state the expense of his trial for bigamy. The report given out at Clinton is that Sams has left the country. The Flack family live near Jacksonville, and Sams was their coachman.
pres-sans-jacksonville-1888-10.A5:
She Repents Her Folly.
St. Louis, Mo., Oct. 1.—Hattie Flack, the nineteen year old daughter of Charles E. Flack, of the St. Louis commission house of Shirmir & Flack, who married a mulatto named Pres Sams, the hired man on her father's farm near Jacksonville, Ill., is at home again. She was brought to St. Louis and turned over to her parents by Deputy Sheriff McCoy, of Jacksonville, who found her near Moscow, Ky. Sams fled to escape lynching. It transpires that the negro was a married man when he induced Miss Flack to wed him. The girl now bitterly repents her folly.

NEWS OF THE WEEK.
The first snowstorm of the season prevailed in England this week.

Six deaths and 73 new cases of yellow fever at Jacksonville Wednesday.

Robert Garrett manifested violent dementia while in care of his attendants, Monday.

A man named Hildebrand shot his wife dead at Wheeling pay-day night. He was drunk and they had a quarrel.

James O'Connor's livery stable, in New York city, was burned out, six horses being roasted alive and seventeen fine vehicles destroyed.

Peter Straubb, of Mattoon, Ill., while insane, imagined that spirits commanded him to torture himself, so he gouged his eyes out.

A fire at the Ohio Valley Foundry and Glass Works, Bellaire, Ohio, Saturday, did damage to the amount of fifty or sixty thousand dollars.

Minnie Katzenberger, aged thirteen years, of Chicago, confessed to attempting to kill her mother, brothers and sisters, by putting poison in their food.

A ruffian threw rotten eggs at Senator Blair of New Hampshire, while he was speaking on the tariff to a Republican meeting in Charlottesville, Va.

Monday's town elections in Connecticut show such substantial Republican gains as to indicate that Harrison will carry the state next month.

Isaac Lifter, a Harrisburg peddler, was attacked in a farmer's yard near Shippensburg by a pair of ferocious bulldogs, and was so terribly mangled that he will probably die.

Clerks in the Government departments have all received circular letters from the Democratic National Committee, asking them to contribute to the campaign fund.

Two abandoned women were murdered in Whitechapel, London, Saturday night, making the the fifth and sixth victims of the mysterious butcher, of whose identity there is still no trace.

The House has not had a quorum for a week past, and little business of public importance has been transacted. It is not thought that the House will again have a quorum present until after the election.

Hattie Flack, a white girl, of Jacksonville, Ill., who married her father's negro coachman, who was already married, has been returned home and the bigamist has probably been lynched.

Fifteen hundred miners of the Belleville, Illinois district, have quit work because the companies refused to give them two and one fourth cents a bushel top weight.

The body of a woman with the head, legs and arms missing was found on the Thames river in London, but it is not known whether this was another of the Whitechapel murderer's victims.

On account of the uncertainty caused by the passage of the Mills bill by the House of Representatives the firm of Painter & sons, of Pittsburg, has discontinued the making of cotton ties and abandoned that branch of its business.

Never was happier argument more felicitously stated than when Gen. Harrison said that Free Traders were studying maxims instead of markets. In a single phrase he exhibited the fallacy and the weakness of their whole argument.

WHEELING, W. VA., October 2.—The Baltimore and Ohio Railroad authorities to-day summarily discharged eighteen passenger conductors. The cause is unknown, the authorities refusing to talk, and the men being in ignorance.

Marsha! Bazaine, who surrendered the French Army at Metz during the Franco-Prussian war, died last week, an exile, at Madrid. He was condemned to be shot, but on account of his military services was sentenced for life and confined in some French fort, but escaped and lived quietly in Spain until his death.

A Curious Complication.
Miss Flack, the daughter of a St. Louis merchant who married Press Sams a negro, at Jacksonville, Ill., a short time ago, was arrested at Moscow in the house of Jim Gahlson, a negro brother-in-law of Press Sams. She refused to go with the officers until she learned that a warrant for her was in their possession. Miss Flack is a beautiful woman, 18 years old, tall and graceful. She is well educated, a skillful pianist and accomplished in other ways. Press Sams, her negro husband, left her last week for parts unknown, first pawning her clothing, valise and picture of her parents. Sams served four years in penitentiary for horse stealing. He has a wife at Union City, Tenn.
pres-sans-jacksonville-1888-10.A14:
NEWS BREVITIES.
Important News Items in Pithy Paragraphs.

The senate passed the bill forfeiting the Northern Pacific land grant.

About half the tobacco crop in Bracken county, Kentucky, was damaged by the late frost.

The annual reunion of the association of Eastern Illinois Veterans was held at Champaign.

Jacob Heber, a St. Louis basket-maker, shot and killed his wife and blew off his own head.

The president signed the Chinese bill and returned it, with a message of explanation, to congress.

The senate confirmed the appointment of Judge Lambert Tree, of Illinois, to be minister to Russia.

A new trial has been ordered in the case of ex-Alderman McQuade, one of the New York city "boodlers."

The Wisconsin Methodist conference found that the charges against Bishop Halsey were not sustained.

William George, a wealthy farmer of Basco, Ill., was swindled out of $1,200 by sharpers with a lottery scheme.

Radical socialists held a meeting in Chicago recently and decided to form an independent political organization.

A dividend of half of 1 per cent. has been declared by the Santa Fe directors. The last dividend was 1½ per cent.

It has been decided that the lease of the Pittsburg public school building recently given to a Catholic society was unlawful.

The papers transferred to Mr. Richard Smith, of the Cincinnati Commercial Gazette, have been signed.

The Iowa W. C. T. U. met at Des Moines in its fifteenth annual session, 500 delegates being present and Mrs. J. Ellen Foster presiding.

Campbell & Cutler's paint, oil and glass store at Kansas City, was burned Wednesday. The loss, $40,000, is covered by insurance.

John J. Connelly, an insane highway robber, hanged himself in his cell in the Salem (Mass.) county jail early Wednesday morning.

The Secular Union Congress, whose object is the total separation of church and state, opened its twelfth annual congress at Pittsburg Friday.

Skeletons of three men and four women, with other relics of the mound-builders, were found in a mound on the Wood river two miles east of Alton, Ill.

The court house, with most of the records, and the jail of Sac county, Iowa, were burned at Sac City. A prisoner named Charles Carlson is believed to have been burned, but his body has not been found.

Dr. Edwin L. Tons strangled himself to death at the Washingtonian home. He was once a reputable citizen of Chicago, but was ruined by the opium habit.

A rain and thunder storm swept over Columbus, O. Roofs were blown away and trees leveled. The damage at the exposition grounds is estimated at $10,000.

Peter Straubb, a Chicago machinist, gonged out both his eyes at Mattoon, Ill., in obedience to the commands of spirits with whom he was communing.

Mortimer Sackville West, the first Baron Sackville, is dead. The British minister to Washington is a sprout of the same family, but not on good terms with it, so it is said.

After eight years' wandering H. C. Cooley returned to Bevier, Mo., to find his wife married to another man. He made love to her again and they eloped from husband No. 2.

Several hundred head of cattle in Anglaiz and Allen counties, Ohio., are affected with pleuro-pneumonia and many have died. The herds affected have been strictly quarantined.

Several people have been arrested in London on suspicion of them being the White-chapel woman-slayer. Rewards aggregating £800 are offered for the capture of the right man.

The Grand Army encampment at Columbus has adjourned. Major Henry Warner, of Missouri, was elected commander-in-chief. Next year the veterans will meet at Milwaukee.

Several men are under arrest in London suspected of complicity in the horrible and mysterious murder of women in the White-chapel district. There have been two additional murders within the past two days.

The Sionx commission has left the Indians without getting enough signers to make the treaty. Delegations from the six Indian agencies will soon visit Washington and present their wishes to the president.

Premier Greenway, of Manitoba, is charged by the Winnipeg Free Press with having accepted money, to be used in the recent elections, from the Manitoba Central railway, in return for which he was to secure legislation for the road.

English grangers are forming societies and agitating the abolishment of the game laws. A sailor boy was recently sent to prison for two weeks for sucking an egg which he stole from a partridge's nest on Lord Bradbourne's estate.

Mrs. Sarah Jane Owens, widow of the late Commodore Owens, left her home in Chicago recently and went to Washington to make a plea for an increase of pension from $30 to $50 a month. She has been arrested and detained by the Washington police on a charge of insanity.

Hattie Flack, 19-years-old, daughter of a St. Louis commission merchant, who married and fled with a mulatto employed on her father's farm, has returned to her parents' home. The mulatto, who was already married, fled from his victim at Moscow, Ky., to escape lynchers.

POINTED PARAGRAPHS. Topics of the Times Given in a Terse and Spicy Manner.
Xenia, O., has a Democratic "Hickory club."

Flint glass workers' annual convention at Canton, O.

Fort Smith, Ark., had its sixtieth execution Friday.

Hillsboro, O., college will have a normal school attachnent.

The saloonists of St. Louis will open Sunday to test the new closing law.

William Landreth, murderer of his stepdaughter, was hanged at Portland, Ora.

Rev. Thomas F. Managan is spoken of to succeed the late Vicar General Conway, of Chicago.

Manager William C. Mitchell, of the People's theater, St. Louis, fell from a cable-car and was killed.

John J. Mahoney, the New York bookmaker, bets $20,000 to $10,000 that Cleveland will be elected.

The survivors of Company H, of the old Fifty-ninth regiment, held a reunion at Bethel, Clermont county, Ohio.

Senator Cullom's coachman, Joseph M. Chase, was found guilty of manslaughter in driving over Professor E. A. Paul.

Senator Ingalls says a letter in the New York Sun, purporting to have been written by him to W. W. Phelps, is a forgery.

At Salt Lake City, the church farm, valued at $150,000, was reclaimed in government proceedings against the Mormons.

Conductor John Dwyer and two other men were blown from a train near Monmouth, W. T., by a cyclone and fatally injured.

The notification committee of the Republican National convention called upon Levi P. Morton Saturday at Rheinbeck, N. Y.

Hon. E. S. Hammond, once a political power in Ohio, now resident of Washington, celebrated his eighteenth birthday Friday.

A high tidal-wave suddenly struck the ship City of Rome, July 1, and injured several persons, besides carrying off the ship's boom.

Charles Fossenden, of Youngstown, O., sues the New York, Pennsylvania & Ohio railroad for $50,000 equivalent for injuries in an accident.

It is getting to be so rare a thing to strike a water well in the gassy gas country that the fact of finding one is telegraphed from New Bremen, O.

William Gray, of Hampton county, South Carolina, put a bullet through the heart of Craddock Mew, whom he found in improper relations with Gray's wife.

Xenia, O., is in a peck of trouble over an effort to settle the affairs of her defunct National bank and the midnight depredations of the prowling chicken thief.

Capt. Andrews and his Dark Secret, on their way to England, were spoken on July 2. The captain had had a rough time of it in his little boat and felt very much used up.

Robert Bryan, aged sixteen, colored, hangs to a Henderson, Ky., tree. The mob that put him there objected to his summary manner of carving the life out of Riley Hancock, aged nineteen.

Joseph Meehr, worth $250,000, is at Long Branch, and has a detective always with him. He thinks his wife and mother-in-law are in a plot to put him in an asylum and get possession of his money.

Mrs. Elizabeth McEntyre, of New York, is under the delusion that her husband's spirit now inhabits a little boy. She makes love to all the youngsters, and has proved herself a source of terror to them.

Samuel Thoman, aged forty-five, eloped from Sharon, Pa., with Della Belton, aged sixteen, his niece. He was heavily in debt to merchants and farmers, and had an action of divorce pending against his wife.

The commissioners of Grant county, Indiana, have awarded to the Massillon Bridge company, of Massillon, O., the contract for the new bridge over the Mississinewa river at Marion. The structure will cost $19,000.

Three youths, Ed. Finley, H. Halliday and J. Morewood, supposed to be of Springfield, Ill., were murdered by Indians in Indian Territory, to avenge the death of a half breed, who, it is thought, had been killed by the boys.
W. H. Escue is in jail at Ironton, O., charged with using undue influence to secure a favorable verdict in a lawsuit. When Justice Belville decided against him he promptly mopped the floor with the law dispenser.

D. W. Earnhart, of Lebanon, O., is cited to appear before the honorable court and prove, if he can, that his Broadway club is not a weapon to knock the Dow law silly and lead drinkers down the broad way of destruction.

The three members of the firm of Shotwell, Clerihew & Lothman, which failed some days ago, were arrested in Minneapolis on a warrant sworn out by the cashier of a bank to which the firm is largely indebted, on a charge of swindling.

Blountsville, Ind., treated Elder Polly to a dose of spoiled eggs because he lectured on prohibition; then the hoodlums brought out anvils and celebrated the Fourth. Polly did not want so much as cracker to assist in the whooping up of the day of freedom.

Witnesses testified that Tom Ferguson, of Waverly, O., left his horse to struggle in the canal over an hour before it drowned, without an effort to get it out. He was fined $15, but whether the witnesses were fined for allowing the cruelty deponent sayeth not.

Young Ladies' Republican club at Vincennes, Ind., cut down a 100-foot tree, trimmed and dragged it to town, planted and run up the Harrison flag, and with disordered bangs, pounded fingers and wild enthusiasm voted the g. o. p. too sweet for anything.

Scott county, Kentucky, is the scene of a blue grass vendetta; 200 men, guided by Sheriff Hedger, are searching for Caleb

Ed Haley, H. Holliday and J. Marwood, all under 20 years, a few days ago.
A saloon passenger on the steamer Celtic from Liverpool, was taken down with small pox during passage. The ship will be detained at quarentine in New York.
Grand Duke Vladimier speaking at the banquet, said his stay in Berlin had convinced him that Emperor William was Russia's friend and was prepared to become her ally.
At Henderson, Ky., Robert Bryan, a 16 year-old negro, stabbed Riley Hancock, white, aged 19, Friday, killing him. Bryan was arrested, but was taken by a mob and lynched.
Judge Walter Q. Gresham sailed on the steamer Werra, Saturday afternoon, for Europe. He will be absent about two months, returning in time to assist in the Republican campaign.
The fire in the Century building, New York, was practically out by 8 o'clock Saturday morning. The loss is estimated at $230,000,000, principally by water, and fully insured.
All the securieties amounting to about $700,000 stolen from the Union Bank in Providence, R. I., June 23, by Teller Chas. A. Pitcher, have been recovered, and will be in possession of the bank in another week.
Governor Hill has called an extra session of the legislature for July 17, to provide appropriations to prevent prisoners in the State prisons from remaining in idleness after July 15, when the appropriations for the purposes of their employment will be exhausted.
William S. Davis, a flagman at Wychford Junction, R. I., Saturday, attempted to stop Charles Doane who was about to drive a horse across the track in front of the approaching train. Done struck the horse, and the animal knocked the flagman down and the train ran over him and killed him instantly.
Kari Kormanhaus and Charles Hendrix of Jersey City, quarreled Friday evening over an alleged insult to the latter's wife. Both men drew revolvers and kept up a running fire on the street until both fell, Henrix with a dangrous wound in the groin and a Kormanhaus with a bullet in his leg. During the shooting a child was shot in the ankle and will lose a foot.
Well informed persons at Vienna, Austria, deny the fact that an understanding has been arrived at between Austria and Russia regarding the eastern question. The Russians continue to erect military stores near the frontier, and are building steam mills and bakeries for the army around Warsaw, which place has been transformed into a first-class fortress. The Russian forces on the frontier are being increased.

Prescott Tallouse, a clerk in the dry goods store of E. L. Veezie, of Waterville, was Friday, detected in taking money from the money drawer. He was taken before Judge Stewart, where he owned up to various thefts from time to time, in all amounting to about $600. He was bound over to the September term of court. It is believed that the amount taken is much in excess of what he stated.

An Irish demonstration was held at Glasgow Saturday to protest against the imprisonment of Mr. John Dillon. Michael Davitt, who was one of the speakers, challenged Attorney General Webster to try Mr. Parnell if the law officers of the crown believed him guilty of the grave crimes alleged against him. He declared that the government were false to their oaths, recurrent to their duties, and traitors to English law if they did not put himself and Mr. Parnell in the dock.

The Amalgamated Association received official notice Saturday morning that the Linden Steel Company of this city and the Newport Iron Company of Newport, Ky., had signed the scale and would resume operations next week. The scale now has 18 signatures, including two of the largest firms in this city. The manufacturers, however, still assert that the lockout is not broken, and that the majority will stand firm until the workmen accept the proposed reduction.

A destructive wind storm struck the town of Edwardsburg, Indiana, on Diamond lake, about eleven o'clock Friday night. The wind struck with terrific force, overturning and carrying away many of the houses. There is not a business house in the place that is not damaged, and the town is almost a complete wreck. Please boats in the lake were lifted out of the water, and thrown on to dry land. No one was killed or seriously injured so far as known.

Preliminary arrangements have been made to organize a board of trade at Thomaston. Since the decline of ship building and dullness in the lime business, the town has fallen behind. The people also lost heavily in the Pacific Bank, Connotton Valley railroad and other "wild cat" swindles, and must move to recover the lead. Thomaston has the largest lot of lime rock quarries in Knox county. Two-thirds of the lime rock burned in this town and Rockland is dug in Thomaston, and is virtually Thomaston lime, although burnt elsewhere.

Late Friday night, 15 or 20 young men who had been drinking in a saloon owned by Thomas Tierney. Long Island City, quarrelled over local politics and Tierney, trying to pacify them, was set upon by some of the men and securely bound. The men left but reentered shortly and found the saloon closed. They forced their way into the bar room. Here policemen met them, and not

Another Henderson Mob.
Last Friday about noon as Riley Hancock, a white man, and Robert Bryan, a negro about 16 years old, were riding in a wagon near Smith's Mills in this Henderson they quarrellled and finally came to blows. Both fell out of the wagon, and in the encounter Bryan stabbed Hancock to the heart, killing him instantly, the weapon used being a physician's knife with a blade about four inches long.

The murderer was arrested, and after an examining trial a party consisting of the latter and two guards started with the prisoner intending to place him in jail at Henderson. About dark when within five minutes of the city the party was overtaken by a mob of fifty mounted men masked. The terrified negro was snatched from the guards, the latter being driven off, covered by a score or more of revolvers. Bryan was hurriedly taken to a neighboring, tree, where he was hanged and left dangling in mid-air. The murdered man was 19 years of age and a cousin of Jeff Hancock, the man who was murdered by a negro several weeks ago near the scene of the present lynching.

CONDENSED TELEGRAMS.
SAM PRICE, charged with being one of the most notorious "Wild Catters" in Roan county, Tenn., and also with being a member of a large gang of illicit distillers who infest that county, was captured on the 6th, by Deputy Marshal Fred Hill, at the point of a revolver. Price attempted to get to his gun before being captured but Hill was too quick for him.

EXPERIMENTS made at Newport, Ky., the details of which were made public, on the 7th, have resulted in the extraordinary discovery that aluminum, which now costs $20,000 a ton, and is produced only in France, can be obtained anywhere by a simple process and at less than one-bundredth part of the present expense.

THE New York syndicate who recently purchased the Warrior coal fields, comprising $300,000 acres of land near Birmingham, Ala., at $4.50 per acre, have sold the same to a syndicate of Liverpool, England, for $8 per acre.

THE Court of Claims have disallowed the claim of Julia A. Thomas, administratrix of the estate of Isog Greer, of Lauderdale county, Miss., for $20,000 for supplies taken during the war. They find that the claim was not presented within the prescribed time.

ABOUT ten days ago Officer McDaniels, in self-defence, shot a negro named Hooks, who belongs to a prominent negro family at Texarkana, Ark. At the time several open threats were made by friends of the wounded negro, and ever since muttered complaints have been heard because the white folks released the officer on $500 ball.

ROBERT BRYAN, a sixteen-year-old boy, stabbed Riley Hancock, white, aged nineteen years, on the 6th and killed him near Smith's Mill, Ky. Three men started to Henderson with Bryan, and just at dark were in the outskirts of the town when overtaken by fifty masked men who drove Bryan's guards off and lynched the murderer to the nearest tree.

A TERRIBLE tragedy occurred at Rising Sun, Yazoo county, Miss., on the 7th between S. H. Whitworth, McLean and Haskins on one side, and R. H. Ivey, W. H. McCarthy and Sam Austin on the other. The first three entered the store of McCarthy & Matthews armed with Winches and pistols, and some words between the parties brought on firing, in which Ivey and Sam Austin, je, were instantly killed, and W. H. McCarthy, and two others were mortally wounded.

A TERRIBLE rain and half storm visited Sharp and Independence counties, Ark., on the Mh. Sixty-five farmers in the vicinity Charlotte lost everything in the way of crops, corn, oats and cotton being entirely destroyed. The sufferers are narly all poor, and steps are being taken to aid them. The loss is variously estimated at from $8000 to $10,000 in the locality named.

A DYNAMITE bomb was exploded in the court-yard, Nicholasville, at midnight, which shook up the town and did considerable damage to the fine court-house, shattering all the plate-glass windows and doing damage to the circuit clerk's office. The books and records had to be removed. The explosion shook up the town, and alarmed men and women. All night ordinary bombs had been exploded, but when the sixty-per-cent. dynamite cartridge exploded it jarred the town like an incipient earthquake. The bomb was exploded by a couple of well-known young bloods. A lady recognized them as they flew. Rev. George O. Barnes, who preaches at the court-house when he is not sick, lays it on the Devil.

WILLIS COLEMAN, colored, while at a negro picnic on Hord's Hill, Maysville, had his right eye shot out, and may die. It is not known how the shooting occurred.

POST-OFFICES have been established at Pulah, Hickman County, and at Evans-
ton, Greenup County, and John D. Wilson
and Henry E. Evans commissioned post-
masters respectively.

The post-office at Percal, Elliott County,
has been abolished.

on the farm of Mrs. W. A. Clark, four

Louisville, was fatally shot at St. Paul,
Minn.

late Bishop Kavanaugh, died in Clark
County on the 4th. He had been in the
ministry more than sixty years, and was

idea of gravitation.

The great Scrugham defalcation case, at
Lexington, has been settled by the payment of $15,000 to the bank, which releases Scrugham's sureties.

The Mercer County bonds trouble has been settled, and the bonds are to be passed over to President Young, of the Louisville Southern road.

A POST-OFFICE has been established at Browning, Daviess County, with E. E. Dewy as postmaster.

War broke out in Scott County, on the 6th, which may prove a worse vendetta than the Rowan County war. Some ten days ago a constable, Sadocia Connellee, jr., was murdered in the vicinity of Sadieville while attempting to serve a civil process on Caleb Parker. Intense excitement has reigned in the county in regard to the murder, but the civil authorities seemed incapable, owing to the wild country in which the deed was done and the large number of friends of the murderer. The Governor was appealed to, but refused to offer a reward until the county officials had exhausted every means in their power. On the 6th, the sheriff, T. T. Hedger, summoned two hundred of the stanchest men in the country who went to Sadieville in charge of Deputy Sheriff James Ford and Colonel Geo. Robinson, a son of Ex-Governor Robinson, to scour the country for the murderer. There will be a desperate conflict before Parker is apprehended, and it is not unlikely that a bitter war will be waged.

HENRY FRANKE, a prominent tobacco buyer, of Paducah, was drowned in Mayfield creek, near Wickliffe, Ballard County.

The noise of a Kentucky water-spout, near Nicholasville, on the 4th, was heard ten miles.

There was more tobacco planted in this State this year than last.

The prospects for a large fruit crop in Kentucky is very promising this season.

JOHN WILSON, a farmer of Jackson County, sent his two little sons, aged six and four, to a neighbor's on an errand the other day. There was no one at home at the time, and the eldest child picked up a gun, aimed it at his little brother and fired. The ball passed through the lad's body, near the heart, and in half an hour the victim died. The brother attempted to carry the dying boy home on his shoulder, and was met half way by his father. Mr. Wilson was overcome with grief, and in his excitement drew a knife and attempted to slay the other son, but fortunately some men who witnessed the scene prevented the double murder. The little fellow was taken home, covered with blood, but never regained consciousness after the fatal shot, and expired soon after reaching his mother's arms.

A company dressed in the British uniform of 1776 appeared in a Fourth of July parade in Louisville.

The Louisville and Nashville road is determined to push on its road from Pineville, and the contract has been given out for the extension of the division from that place to Cumberland Gap. The contract was awarded to Messrs. Serpell and Morris, of Louisville, and a number of sappers and miners have left for Pineville to locate a camp and erect a barracks. The work will be pushed with vigor, and the contract stipulates that the roadbed shall be ready for the track by the first months of next spring. The road will cost $32,000 per mile. A large amount of heavy work in the shape of drilling and ballasting will have to be done, and some rough country passed through, but the contractors say they will be able to finish the work at the proper time.

In the law and equity court at Louisville Judge Sterling B. Toney refused to issue a writ of habeas corpus prayed for by J. J. Cornelison, who alleged in his petition that he was detained in jail without lawful authority. After the decision, Colonel Sam McKee, Cornelison's lawyer, brought suit against Judge Toney, under Section 401 of the Criminal Code, which inflicts a forfeiture of $500 on any judge refusing an application of this character. The entire case is an interesting one, and will attract attention.

SEVENTY-FIVE thousand pounds of hemp were destroyed by fire at Nicholasville.

ABOUT 3000 delegates, coming from all sections of the country, participated in the convention at Baltimore, called for the purpose of forming a National Association of Democratic clubs. Chauncey F. Black, of Pennsylvania, was elected President of the Association, which comprises 496 clubs.

MASKED men stopped a stage in California and robbed the express messenger of $10,000 in silver bullion.

At least six lives were lost and numerous houses were struck by lightning during an electrical storm in the Northwest.

FOUR passengers were killed and fifteen injured by a railroad accident near Helena, Montana.

CINCINNATI had a grand celebration of her municipal centennial and of the national holiday, all in one, opening a big exposition, with the aid of the venerable Mrs. James K. Polk, who, from her home in Nashville, gave the signal by telegraph for starting the machinery.

SAMUEL M. HENDERSON, sixty years old, of Trafalgar, Ind., shot and killed his divorced wife and then killed himself.

Two of Francis Scott Key's grandchildren unveiled at San Francisco on Wednesday the bronze monument to the memory of the author of "The Star Spangled Banner." It is the gift of the late James Lick.

FIRES swept through the best business block in Marysville, Cal., causing damage estimated at $200,000.

A STORM of hail and rain caused widespread damage in portions of Ohio, Illinois, Iowa and Minnesota.

INDEPENDENCE DAY ceremonies were in progress on the grounds of the Yallabusha Fair Association at Water Valley, Miss., when the grand stand, in which 400 spectators were seated, fell without warning. Fifty persons were seriously injured.

Boys threw firecrackers under a carriage containing two ladies, at Chicago, and the explosion so frightened the horse that he upset the vehicle, killing the two occupants.

Mayor Kenyon, of Gueda Springs, Kan., was murdered by the proprietors of an illicit whisky saloon he was endeavoring to suppress.

Six drunken farmers engaged in a free fight at Mansfield, Mo., and five of them were killed.

Delaware peach growers in convention recently, at Dover, estimated their crop at 12,000,000 baskets, of which the Pennsylvania railroad can transport 6,500,000 baskets.

County Judge Pulliam, of Hardinsburg, Ky., shot and killed a man engaged in litigation before him who took exception to some of his rulings.

Gus Bogles, a bootblack of Denison, Texas, nineteen years old, who murdered William Morgan in the Creek Nation a year ago, has been hanged at Fort Smith, Ark.

The entire business portion of Lake City, the county seat of Missouri County, Mich., has been destroyed by fire.

Citizens of Joliet, Ill., placed obstructions on the track of a railroad, to the building of which they objected, thereby derailing the construction train and killing the engineer and three Italian laborers in a house near Sault Ste Marie, Mich.

William Landieth has been hanged at Dallas, Oregon, for the murder of his stepdaughter, Simmie Ellis Antle, last January, under circumstances of peculiar atrocity.

A train ran into a land slide near Lafayette, Ind., and killed three train men.

At Henderson, Ky., Robert Ryan, a colored man, sixteen years old, stabbed and killed Riley Hancock, white, sixteen years old. Three men started with Ryan for the jail, when they were overpowered by a mob, who hanged the murderer.

SOUTH CAROLINA.
It has just been learned that at John T. Roddy's camp on the "3 C's" seven miles from Rock Hill, one negro was killed and three fatally injured by a bank caving in Tuesday.

Information is just received of a horrible crime committed in York county. Robert Wood, a white man of sixty years, with a family, is charged with brutally injuring and mutilating a white girl named Hill, aged only six years. A party of about fifty white men went at night to the house of the girl's mother, and though she was quite ill, forced her to make affidavit that Wood was the person who had injured the child. Wood has been notified to quit the county in five days, or take the consequences. He is supposed to have gone. If he remains he will be either lynched or very roughly handled.

GRADY SOLID FOR COLQUITT. He Also Favors a Revision of the Tariff with Incidental Protection.
ATLANTA, Ga., Jan. 24.—Mr. Henry W. Grady, in an interview to-night relative to the attitude he intended to take regarding Senator Colquitt, said: "I am going to support Mr. Colquitt for reelection just as earnestly as I supported him for his election. It is well understood that I differ with him on the tariff, but there is not very much difference after all. I stand on the Chicago platform as far as the tariff is concerned. I believe the tariff should be revised, but in such a way as to give incidental protection to American industries. However, I do not exactly agree with Senator Colquitt's position, but that will make no difference between the Senator and myself. He has made a good Senator, and I shall support him again.

"As for the difference existing in the Democratic ranks on the tariff, that question will not live when Senator Colquitt's election comes up. If the Democrats in Congress do not effect a compromise on this question, the Democratic National Conventions certainly will make a positive deliverance on the subject. I shall stand on the Democratic platform, no matter what it is for. I consider Democratic union and success very much more important than the establishment or the repeal of any theory of taxation."

Peter Coffee Convicted of Way's Murder.

NEW HAVEN, Jan. 24.—The case against Peter Coffee, charging him with the murder of Station Agent Way at Stony Creek on May 9, 1887, was given to the jury at 11½ A. M. to-day, and at 3½ P. M. they returned a verdict of murder in the second degree. Judge Torrance at once sentenced Coffee to State prison for life.

Way's body was run over just beyond the Stony Creek station by a freight train pushing there at about 11 P. M. May 9, 1887. In picking up the body the train hands noticed that it was cold; that but little blood was to be seen, and that the pockets were empty, indicating that Way, who had been paid off that day, was robbed and murdered and his body placed on the track to give the impression that he committed suicide.

Buying a Telegraph Plant Cheap.

BALTIMORE, Jan. 24. — The Postal Telegraph Company's property in this State was sold at public auction to-day to James Nelson Jamison of New York, representing the American Telegraph and Telephone Company. The price paid for the property, which includes all the wires, poles, rights, and franchises, and office furniture, was $80,000, which is $60,000 less than the original cost. The wires will be used as part of a telephone line between Baltimore and New York.

The Maine Ice Crop is All Right.

AUGUSTA, Jan. 24.—The outlook is that the crop of Kennebec ice will not only be a large one, but that it will be housed better than for several years. The thickness and quality of the ice are all that could be desired. The expense of getting it this winter is much less than it has been for years.

Panama Lecks Begun.

PANAMA. Jan. 16.—The canal company has engaged another contracting firm, that of Erzinger, Dephieux & Co., to build the locks which were lately determined upon. These men arrived on the Isthmus on Dec. 20. Their work has already been begun. Good progress is reported from Bohio-Soldado, at which station will be situated the first lock from the Atlantic side.

Now that the rainy season is over there is every likelihood that more activity will prevail along the line of the canal than during the past season.

Messrs. Croges and Marolles, chiefs of the Darien expedition parties, which left here about a month ago to select and mark out the territory ceded in Darien to the canal company by the Colombian Government, returned last week. They gave good reports of the parties, and said that they were achieving their object without hindrance of any kind. They returned to Darien on the 12th.

Halo and Hearty at 96.

RED BANK, Jan. 24.—Joseph Field, a farmer of Middletown, will be 96 years old on his next birthday. He was born at the old Field homestead in Middletown on Sept. 28, 1792, and has lived in the vicinity ever since. In early life he bought 150 acres to which he has added little by little until now he owns more than 400 acres of the best farm land in the State. Mr. Field was not married until 1867, when at the age of 75 he married Uretta, a daughter of John Heddon. She lived only a few years but left three children, Joseph, Uretta, and Rebeca. This hearty old man can be seen every day doing farm work and doing as much as any man on his place. He frequently walks to this town, 2½ miles, and it takes a good pedestrian to keep up with him. He has always been temperate in all things. He is supposed to be worth $300,000.

Labor and Wages.

For two days the men at work for the Knick-erbocker Ice Company and the Wolf Ice Company at Athens have been considering the matter of striking for an advance of twenty-five cents per day and for the payment of time checks every night. The wages paid were $1.50 and $1.75 per day, and the demand was made for $1.75 and $2. Yesterday morning at about 10 o'clock, after the quarter-day punch had been finished, the men laid down their tools, and work was stopped. No violence was resorted to. The companies refuse to pay the advance demanded, and the runs are now idle.

Ice cutters, to the number of 140, employed by the Drivers' Union Ice Company at Wenham Lake, Salem, Mass., struck yesterday for an advance of fifty cents to $2 per day. Their demand was refused.

Killed Because he Did Not Take Care.

POUGHKEEPSIE, Jan. 24.—Gustav Olsen, an expert bridge builder, was killed here to-day by being knocked from the new bridge being built over the Hudson, and falling to the ground below. The men were about to quit work on account of the high wind. They had a timber hoisted up, but not yet swung into place. He was unwilling to stop until the timber was in place, and attempted to manage it himself. He made a miscalculation, and was struck on the back of the head by the timber as it swung around. He rebounded against several timbers in the bridge work as he fell and every bone in his body was broken.

Lynched a Mexican.

CORPUS CHRISTI, Jan. 24.—Santos Salizer, a Mexican, was lynched on Sunday night near Collina, in Neuces county, for the supposed murder of Jacob Stafford, whose body was found riddled with bullets back of his house on Saturday. The tracks of a horse that Salizer rode corresponded with tracks found near the body, and on this evidence the Mexican was hunted down and hanged by ranchmen and cowboys.

Obituary.

James J. Lyons, who was with Macy & Co. for fifteen years as architect and superintendent of construction, died in Pasadena, Los Angeles county, Cal., on Jan. 6, aged 64. Mr. Lyons was obliged to leave Macv's last year on account of ill health. His travels in Europe did not benefit him, and he went to California with the hope of regaining his health. He had been a prominent architect in San Francisco, and many public buildings there are of his designing. Mr. Lyons leaves no family. His remains, which have been brought on from the West, will be buried to-morrow from St. Vincent de Paul's Church, Brooklyn.

Alexander M. Rosa, long a prominent builder, died very suddenly of heart disease at 1:30 o'clock Monday afternoon at his home, 55 West Fifty-second street. He was born in New Jersey in 1811.

Mr. Richard F. Kemble, of the class of 1818 of Columbia College, died at Cold Spring on Monday in his 88th year. He was the oldest living graduate. His nephew, Mr. Gouverneur Kemble, is Secretary of the Dock Board.

Lady Sackville, a sister-in-law of Sir Lionel Sackville West, British Minister at Washington, died suddenly in England yesterday of heart disease.

Frederick C. Brightly, author of Brightly's Digest and other notable law books, died in Philadelphia yesterday, aged 76 years.

William Laverack, one of the oldest and best known merchants of Buffalo, died yesterday, aged 78 years.

LATER.
A COMMUNICATION was transmitted to the United States Senate on the 24th from the Commissioner of Internal Revenue showing that the amount of revenue collected on liquors since the present system of internal revenue taxation went into effect on September 1, 1862, down to June 3, 1887, was $1,348,626,099.

The brewers of Milwaukee on the 24th informed their employees that in a few days every union man would be discharged.

VISCOUNT DAS NOGUEIRAS, Portuguese Minister at Washington for ten years, died on the 24th.

A fire on the 24th in O. G. King's shoe house at Newark, O., caused a loss of $100,000.

SANFORD TANNER, a rich bachelor of Freeborn County, Minn., was confidenced out of $22,000 by sharpers on the 24th.

ANOTHER blizzard was raging in Dakota on the 24th, and at Neche the mercury went down to sixty below and the wind reached a velocity of forty miles an hour.

By an explosion of gunpowder on the 24th at Brest, Russian Poland, eleven persons were killed and thirty injured.

The Ohio Wool-Growers' Association met at Columbus on the 24th and adopted resolutions condemning the proposition to place wool on the free list.

The Governor of Mississippi on the 24th vetoed the bill providing for the holding of a Constitutional convention.

The Republicans of the District of Columbia met on the 24th and, owing to a quarrel, two sets of delegates were chosen to attend the National convention, one favoring Mr. Blaine and the other Mr. Sherman.

ANTON HEEBE, who died in Dubuque on the 24th, was the owner of the first brewery in Iowa.

The discovery was made at Victoria, B. C., on the 24th of a powerful Chinese society whose object was to murder at $500 a head.

THE Indiana Wool-Growers' Association met at Indianapolis on the 24th and condemned the proposition to place wool on the free list.

MILLBURN FITE, the oldest colored man in Southern Wisconsin, died at Racine on the 24th, aged ninety-eight years. He was a slave for seventy-two years.

SANTOS SOLIZER, a Mexican, was lynched on the 24th at Collins, Mex., for the supposed murder of Jacob Stafford.

Bills were introduced in the United States Senate on the 24th to amend the pension laws; to change the time of meeting of the long session of Congress to the first Monday in October, and of the short session to the second Monday in November; to provide that publications of the second class may be transmitted through the mails free of charge to subscribers who live in another county, but received their mail in the county in which the publication is issued, and for the admission of Montana as a State. In the House a bill was introduced authorizing the President to discontinue any customs district where the revenues are not equal to the expenses.

Out of Fuel. BROWN'S VALLEY, Minn., Jan. 19.—We have been blockaded for three weeks. Unless a train comes in with fuel within two days there will be serious suffering here and all about. There is more suffering as yet in the country than in town. The opinion is general that the railroad authorities have been very remiss in thus delaying the opening of the road. Men are working toward us from Morris, but none are put on this end of the line. The "Shoofly" Flies the Track. PLYMOUTH, N. H. Jan. 23.—The "Shoofly" train, bound south on the Boston, Concord and Mortreal R. R. ran off the track at Warren's summit at 3 o'clock this morning demolishing one car and badly shaking up the passengers. No one was hurt in the accident caused by a broken rail. This makes the fourth derailment of trains since Saturday night. All trains are from three to four hours late. Death of Col. Moulton. NEW YORK, Jan. 24.—Col. Charles William Moulton, brother-in-law of Gen. Sherman and John Sherman, died at an early hour this morning. The funeral will take place from his old home at Glendale, Ohio, on Thursday. Col. Moulton was a faithful officer in the army during the civil war and as a lawyer stood high in the profession. He leaves a wife and four children. Shattered by Dynamite. CHATHAM, Canada, Jan. 24.—The house of Isreal Evans, license inspector, was shattered by dynamite early this morning. No one was hurt, but the house was badly damaged. The police have arrested a man with a loaded revolver, fuse and caps for dynamite cartridges in his possession. Three others are also detained on suspicion of being implicated in the affair. An Abortionist's Victim. RAPID CITY, Jan. 19.—Mrs. Rosanna Peepin, aged thirty-three, died here Tuesday, undoubtedly from the effects of an abortion. It is reported a boat's crew are fast in the ice near the east end of the island and beyond assistance. A LIVING DEATH. PECULIAR OUTCOME OF THE ENVIRONMENTS OF OUR GREAT CITIES.
Victims of Paralysis Dragging Their Feet Along the Pavement—Patients Who Are as Helpless as New Born Infants—Sad Case of a Journalist.

On these sunny mornings, when the atmosphere is cool and bracing, one sees here and there on the streets a man crawling along aided by a crutch or a cane. He is usually bent forward, his progress is slow, difficult and painful. His feet drag with a shuffle on the surface of the pavement. His hair is gray, although his countenance may not indicate more than middle age. There are evidences of pain in his features. There are wrinkles and contractions that are the cicatrices of wounds incurred in fierce life struggles. The eyes express a commingling of weakness an despair. His shoulders droop, and his entire figure has a bagginess suggestive of a collapse. On his shrunken lips are hints of a pleading helplessness.

When he speaks it is with hesitation and a muffled tone. His utterances come with difficulty; they are low, choked, broken. His speech halts at short intervals as if at a loss for the proper word. Often he cannot find it, and frequently an unwanted and strange term, wholly without meaning, will thrust itself in the hiatus. Possibly one arm dangles at his side, loose and limp as rope. Possibly one leg is dragged along as if it were a foreign body. Perhaps one side or the other of his mouth is drawn up with a line that spreads out fan shaped into a series of scar like shrinkages. His glance, like his gait, is ...abbling and uncertain. Over his face is spread an expression that is a combination of imbecility and hope. He is an object with qualities so peculiar, so individualized, that one easily recognizes him as the victim of some one of the numerous forms of paralysis.

These specimens taking the morning air, assisted by cane or crutch and shuffling along the sidewalk, are getting to be a frequent exhibition. Whether or not characteristic of other points, they are getting to be an increasing feature of Chicago.

The men who no longer crawl out to catch the glow and warmth of the summer sun are nerveless as new born children. Their limbs are inert as masses of gelatine. They are powerless to move their muscles, and have to be lifted, turned, taken up and down like babes. They must be fed, and the wants of nature cared for as if they were puling infants in the nurse's arms.

This new disease is a peculiar outcome of the environment of our great cities. The atmosphere of this region is fused with a malaria which exhausts, prostrates, paralyzes those whose overworked bodies are forced to inhale it. Its victims are not the old who have reached the allotted span of their life, nor those enfeebled by age or heredity, but the men with active brains, intense energy, boundless ambition and restless effort. It is in the nature of a rot which affects not the green, the immature, but the ripened fruit. It attacks the men who labor by day and dream of work by night; it is a sting which pierces not the drones, but the workers in the human hives.

The idler slowly disintegrates and disappears. He passes from a lethargic life into death with as little consciousness and suffering as attend the natural demise of a mollusk. He is an implement that rusts from disuse; the tireless brain worker is a machine, driven at a high rate of speed, with no stoppages for repairs, which carries a tremendous pressure, and some day explodes and is blown into fragments.

Over a quarter of a century ago there came a young man from an eastern state, who in time located in Chicago. He was finely educated, ambitious, industrious, energetic and ready and willing to devote himself to any honorable employment. He soon secured a situation as principal of one of the public schools.

Further on he gave up teaching and connected himself with journalism. He was for several years a valued attache of this journal, during which time he showed himself capable, indefatigable, prompt, and the possessor of a high order of intellect. Of a religious nature, he later accepted an offer to take charge of a prominent denominational weekly issued in this city, and became its chief writer and managerial assistant, and for many years filled his place with credit to himself and the periodical with which he was connected.

Such was Leander Stone, principal of a public school, reporter on The Chicago Times and afterward one of the powers that controlled the great Methodist journal, The Northwestern Christian Advocate. The face and figure of no man in Chicago were better known than those of Leander Stone during all these years.

A few months ago, having just passed into a ripe middle age and in the very height of his popularity and usefulness, he felt one day a numbness in one of his arms. It extended slowly till the whole arm was involved, and then it crept into the other arm, and so on and on, a little at a time, till it had permeated and possessed his entire limbs and torso. His head alone escaped. The last time I saw him, all below his neck was a dead mass so far as motion is concerned.

Like one of Dante's damned, he was imprisoned in ice to his chin. And yet the savage destiny that has thus imprisoned him did not have the mercy to deprive the inclosed mass of sensation. Along its nerves travel incessant poignant pains, which are beyond reach and beyond

CRIMES AND CRIMINALS
A German Shepherd is Murdered for His Money.
HIDING OUT FROM THE LYNCHERS.
RALEIGH, N. C., January 28.—[Special.]—News has been received here of a terrible lynching at the town of Plymouth, the county seat of Washington county, night before last. The mob, composed mainly of mounted men, marched to the jail and took therefrom Patterson Spruill, John Blount and Matthew Blount, all colored. The doomed men were taken to a piece of woods a mile from town, and were tied to trees. The lynchers then opened fire upon them with all sorts of weapons, from Winchester rifles to shotguns, and did not cease firing till all the men were dead and riddled with bullets and shot. This lynching is the result of a very brutal murder which was committed in the afternoon of the 23d of last December. While a man named Ed. Dawman, an itinerant jeweler, was passing through the country near the town of Creswell, four negroes, three of whom were those lynched, met him and presently knocked him in the head, robbed him and threw the body in a shallow pit, where a teamster discovered it, seeing the knees sticking above the ground. Christmas day all four men were arrested. One confessed the crime. All were taken to jail at Plymouth. Violence was feared, as public feeling ran very high, and special precautions were taken. The people in the section where the murder was committed, which is some miles from Plymouth, were particularly stirred up, and it is probable that they were the lynching party. Everything was conducted quietly and with system. The men would have been tried for their lives at the spring term of court. The evidence against them was regarded as conclusive. It is the first lynching in the state in many months.

A German Shepherd is Murdered for His Money.

Corpus Christi, Texas, January 23.—[Special.]—News reached this city last night that Jake Stafford, a German, was murdered and robbed near Collins, Texas, this county. Stafford was a peaceable man, and engaged in the sheep business.

Last Thursday, at three o'clock, he left Collins for his home, some few miles in the country. His wife became alarmed by his not coming that night. A search was begun in the morning, and his body was found Saturday, in a water hole, with three bullet holes in it, one through the body and two through the head. Stafford only had nine dollars on his person before starting home. No money or valuables were found on him, thus proving that robbery was the cause of his death.

Santosear Salizar, a Mexican of bad character, was arrested on suspicion, and rumor reached here this morning that Salizar was hung last night by a mob.

WYTHEVILLE, VA., July 11.—The negro who was charged with committing a criminal assault on a Mrs. Metcalfe, of Pulaski county, was taken out of the hands of the officers last night and hanged. The particulars as your correspondent is able to gather them are as follows:

Late yesterday afternoon Judge Holbrook, county judge of this county, received an imitation that a mob was forming for the purpose of storming the jail. He so informed the sheriff and ordered him to remove the prisoner, William Henry Smith, to Lynchburg as quietly and secretly as possible to avoid suspicion. Accordingly Sheriff Harkrader early in the evening placed the prisoner under guard of his deputies and spirited him to an unfrequented spot out of town to await the arrival of the 11 o'clock train. Just before the train arrived the guard conducted him to the depot and boarded the train on its arrival without seemingly arousing suspicion. But a number of the mob had come on the train from Rural Retreat, and before any defence could be made the negro had the noose around his neck and was being dragged from the car. The officers were powerless and made no further resistance. The negro was taken about 200 yards from the depot and hanged to a tree on the top of Boyd's Hill and his body riddled with bullets. He was found about an hour afterwards by some citizens and brought to town. It is rumored that he confessed his horrible crime before he was executed, but this is doubted by the officers. The dastardly deed for which the negro paid the awful penalty was committed in Pulaski county on last Thursday, when it was reported in the papers that the negro had been lynched, but the officers of Pulaski county, evading the lynchers, and by travelling all night in a buggy succeeded in bringing the negro safely to Wytheville and lodging him in jail at 4 o'clock on Friday morning. The woman is reported to have since died, as she was in a delicate condition at the time of the deed. The community here is perfectly quiet, and it would not be possible to realize from appearances that anything unusual had happened.

vim-smith-wytheville-1888-06-30.A3:
Hung Without Trial.
WYTHEVILLE, Va., July 11.—At 12 o'clock last night a body of masked men took Win. Smith, colored, who was charged with having committed a criminal assault on a respectable white lady, a Mrs. Midkiff, in Pulaski county, from the custody of Sheriff Harkrader, at the depot in this place, and hung him in a grove about four hundred yards distant. After hanging Smith the lynchers riddled his body with bullets. Those participating in the affair were from Pulaski county. The men had been in this neighborhood since yesterday morning. Sheriff Harkrader had received information of their presence and intention, and was about to board the train with a view of taking Smith to Lynchburg, when the mob appeared and took possession of the accused. Smith was given time to pray, and made a confession of his crime.
