VIRGINIA NEWS.
Mr. John B. Lightfoot, a prominent citizen of Caroline county, died in Port Royal on Tuesday.

Col. W. W. Williamson has purchased the Scriven property, near Warrenton, for six thousand dollars.

E G. Elam, a former merchant of Petersburg, was killed by a lightning stroke in Buckingham county Tuesday.

R. P. Halstead, a well known citizen of Norfolk, a veteran of the late war, and a member of Pickett-Buchanan Camp, died yesterday morning.

Col. Wm. P. Craighill has submitted his estimates for next year as follows: James river, $400,000; harbor at Norfolk, $100,000; approaches to Norfolk harbor, $100,000; Currituck sound, etc., $20,000; New river, $20,000.

Mrs. Sarah Brunet, of Norfolk, who died last Friday, left $5,000 to the Freemason Street Baptist Church in that city, $5,500 to the Southern Baptist Theological Seminary, $1,000 to the home mission board and $1,000 for the Home for Aged and Indigent Females.

Argument in the trial of W. H. Godsey, clerk of St. Charles Hotel, in Richmond, for the murder of Dave Glass, a negro waiter, closed last night, but there was no verdict. The jury was held over till to-day. They are said to be 10 for acquittal and two for conviction.

Henry Smith, the negro who committed the outrage on Mrs. Midhiff, in Pulaski county, a few days ago, was lynched near Wytheville by a mob Tuesday night. He was taken from the cars while being removed for greater safety, hanged to a neighboring tree and his body riddled with bullets. The parties to the lynching are unknown, but are supposed to be from Pulaski.

A severe thunder storm passed over the lower end of Middlesex county Monday afternoon, and a large hall, built by the Good Templars and Masons about two years ago, was struck by lightning and burned to the ground, with all the furniture. The crash was so severe that pieces of weather-boarding and window facings were torn off and scattered around for several hundred feet, and hogs that were near by were instantly killed.
vim-smith-wytheville-1888-06-30.A8:
AN OUTRAGE IN PULASKI.
AN AGED LADY ASSAULTED BY A NEGRO—THE VILLAIN LYNCHED.
A special from New River to the Lynchburg Virginian says: A brutal outrage was committed in this vicinity yesterday by a strange negro man upon the person of Mrs. Midkiff. The negro called at her house in the forenoon and asked for something to eat. She gave him some bread and meat which he ate out in the yard. He then asked for some water and followed her into the house where she went to get it. There he suddenly clutched her by the throat and overpowered her. After accomplishing his purpose he fled to the railroad and took an east-boundt rain. Information of the outrage was telegraphed to stations along the line and the brute was arrested at Christiansburg and brought back to Churchwood on the next train, where he was turned over to Deputy Sheriff Morgan. Last night a mob of twenty-five persons called at Morgan's home and took the negro away from him by force. They then carried the miscreant before his victim for identification. She, however, was so frightened and distraught that she could not positively identify him. The lynchers took him out in the woods near by when they beat him unmercifully with sticks but finally decided not to lynch him. They took him back and turned him over to the deputy sheriff again.

This morning he was taken to Newbern, where the county court is in session, and his case, and also that of his would-be lynchers, committed to a special grand jury.

Our Radford correspondent writing about the same affair says that negro was a 'tramp,' one of a party of ten just out from Pocahontas.—The other negroes in the party were found at New River after the outrage and some of them volunteered to go with the officers and identify the one who had stopped at Mrs. Midkiff's, which they did at Bangs's where he had been arrested on the information sent by telegraph.

A later dispatch from Christiansburg says the negro was arrested at Bangs's depot and taken in the direction of Radford. This was the last that has been seen or heard of him. He never reached Pulaski county jail. It is said that he was hanged by a body of men and his body riddled with bullets and afterwards sunk in New River.—William Jefferson is now serving twenty years in the penitentiary for a similar offence committed near here about two years since.—The people thinking justice was too tardy took this last matter into their own hands.
vim-smith-wytheville-1888-06-30.A13:
Some Religious Occurrences.
There were some occurrences reported last week, which, because of their religious bearing, are peculiarly fit for Sunday contemplation, and it is the more desirable that we should put them together here in their logical relation because, for the most part, they were scattered about as minor items of news in the newspapers.

The case of the Rev. Mr. PHILIPS, the faith cure pastor of Jersey City, is one of the most interesting and at the same time one of the most perplexing recorded during the week. It seems that, although the chapel over which he presides is supported and his own salary paid by Mr. JOHN ELSEY, a wealthy convert to the faith cure doctrines, Mr. PHILIPS has persisted in preaching from the text that "it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven." The inference might be that the pastor's independence of character and unswerving devotion to truth as it is presented by Scripture are stronger than his regard for his self-interest. If that were so he would, of course, be deserving of commendation as a high and noble spirit. But

what shall we say when we are told that at the very time when he was so preaching the Rev. Mr. PHILIPS was striking for a raise of salary from $800 to $1,000 a year? That looks very much as if he were trying to frighten Mr. ELSEY into compliance with his demand by threatening him with hell fire, and, so looking, it looks very badly; though, as he is a handsome young man, the unmarried women of the congregation are, of course, standing by him.

There were several serious and some curious church quarrels reported. For instance, the Baptist church at Bellwood, Georgia, has become a very bear garden because of a difference of opinion between the sexton on one hand and the pastor and deacons on the other as to the moral character of sleight-of-hand tricks introduced as a part of the diversions at a church festival. The sexton, it seems, refused to act as doorkeeper on conscientious grounds, but the others had no such scruples, and yesterday the telegraph reported that the flock was rent asunder with dissensions as to the matter, several of the deacons having been found guilty of lying, and members having been expelled on various charges. Yet the whole lamentable affair is the result of a discussion over the moral nature of what really has no moral nature at all.

How much better is the outcome of the trouble in the Baptist church at West Newton in Massachusetts! There the dissension was caused by accusations of misconduct against the pastor, for which five members were dismissed from the church as malicious slanderers. But on Thursday the pastor came out like a man, confessed that the charges were true, and relieved the innocent brethren excluded. He did wrong in the first instance, but he followed the admonitions of Scripture, and earned just commendation by confessing his fault, praying for forgiveness, and stepping down and out. He did not refuse to face the music, after the manner of the Reformed Church pastor at Passaic in New Jersey, who recently ran off to parts unknown when his false pretences to piety were exposed, but acknowledged his fault like a man of courage and conscience. Nor did he attempt to brazen it out by browbeating his accusers and persisting in a lie.

Three cases illustrate the difference of opinion as to the office and propriety of prayer. On Thursday a little girl attending a picnic at Lancaster in Pennsylvania was abducted by a tramp, and when she was found and he caught by a large searching party the first impulse of the crowd was to hang the wretch to the nearest tree, but, we are told, "wiser counsels prevailed, and the whole crowd joined in a prayer and praise meeting for the recovery of the child." after which the tramp was carried to jail. That was a sensible, a legal, and a truly plous proceeding. "Vengeance is mine, saith the Lord, I will repay;" but gratitude to God must be expressed as a bounden duty. Yet, when a negro was lynched at Wytheville, Virginia, on Wednesday, the crowd did not offer up thanks for their success in finding the brute, though they allowed him a few minutes in which to pray for his own soul. The lynchers, for their part, were, of course, anxious that he should go straight to hell.

But prayers may be inopportune and out of place, as, in our opinion, were those of the Salvation Army women who on Tuesday forced their way into the most fashionable saloon in the town of Atlanta, and held a vociferous prayer meeting there against the protests of the proprietor and his undoubtedly legal rights. Instead of bringing peace, they brought war, and were very properly arrested and locked up.

Theological controversies are always unprofitable as a method of advancing religious truth. They are more enjoyed by the devil than by the angels of light. As an illustration we have only to refer to the efforts of two Catholic boys of Jersey City to convert a Protestant playmate by religious argument. The Protestant resisted, and fought his ground in words so obstinately that on Thursday the others resorted to blows, a frequent consequence of such controversy, and having thrashed the youngster roundly, his father has sworn out a warrant for their arrest. But it is to be said in their excuse that they were young in polemics, none of the three being more than 10 years old.

How good men are sometimes the victims of a cruel misunderstanding is shown in the case of the Buffalo Methodist minister who was thrashed as an insolent masher by an outraged husband, who mistook him for another man. It is true that the father of the assailant has apologized to the preacher, but the incident was exceedingly disagreeable, all the same. It shows how careful people should be in establishing identities. Because there are elderly masher, it cannot reasonably be inferred that every elderly man is a masher. We do not wonder that the parishioners of the Rev. Mr. Dalby are indignant, and that they are not so ready as this good parson to let the young man off as having simply blundered. It is a serious matter to thrash a reputable minister as a masher because of mistaken identity. But it is to be said in extenuation of the blunderer that his wife is a "beautiful little brunette" and he is very proud of her, and has a manly disposition to defend her against insult.

Enrolling Women.

The action of the Presbyterians in World's Convention at London in unanimously approving of a proposition to establish orders of deaconesses, shows how rapidly Protestant prejudices against the organization of women for religious work have been disappearing during recent years.

This has been in part the result of a change in religious sentiment, but probably it is still more due to the change of opinion as to the proper sphere of woman's activities which has taken place within the last generation. Women having become more prominent in secular affairs, it is natural that the Church, of which they are the mainstay, should consider methods for utilizing their demonstrated practical abilities and their fervid zeal in the work of religion also. The Presbyterians, though the most conservative of all the Protestant sects, therefore follow the example of the Episcopalians in taking a step which a few years ago would have been denounced as tending Romeward, but is now approved and justified as sensible and logical. Their Council has simply declared that feminine piety and energy should be put in methodical use in the Church instead of being allowed to go to waste, or to be expended in unorganized and desultory effort. Though the Protestant deaconess or sister, with her peculiar garb, has long been a familiar object in Germany, it was not until recent years that she appeared in England and this country, and then only after a bitter fight with Protestant prejudice. VIRGINIA NEWS.
Gathered From Our State Exchanges. The Lexington Gazette boasts of a horse.
The Lexington Gazette boasts of a horse of remarkable intelligence in that city. It says that the animal got out of his stable and went to where a public hydrant is located. A party of gentlemen standing on the opposite corner noticed the horse at the hydrant and the water running at full head. One of the party crossed the street and cut the water off. As soon as the horse was left alone he commenced to pull at the hydrant lever with his mouth. He pulled first one way then the other until finally, finding which was the way to open the valve, the lever was pushed all the way back, the water rushing out, much to the satisfaction of the horse, which drank heartily.

The Alexandria Gazette says that the funeral of Mr. Cornelius Cox, who was killed in the railroad accident on Thursday morning last, took place this evening from his late residence on north Columbus street and was very largely attended. The services were conducted by Rev. J. M. Nourse, and Messrs. G. A. Mushbach, Frank S. Harper, J. S. Beach, T. W. Robinson, A. T. Ramsay, I. M. Kell, all members of the Bachelor's club, acted as pall-bearers. The remains were temporarily deposited in a vault in the Methodist cemetery to be removed hereafter to the family lot in the Congressional cemetery in Washington. The Bachelor club, of which the deceased had long been a member, sent a beautiful floral tribute.

The wife of William Jones, the negro who was hanged by a mob at Wytheville Wednesday night, and who lives with the family of Mr. J. B. Pollard of this city, on West Salem avenue, received a letter from the sheriff of Wythe county announcing how her husband had met his death. She took the matter very philosophically, as far as is reported, and seemed to think that under the circumstances Jones met with his just deserts. Many people in this city, white and colored, knew Jones, and the general verdict is that he suffered a just punishment for his crime, although the summary processes involved in his sudden taking off were not, of course, wholly approved. — Roanoke Times.

The Shenandoah Valley tells this fish story: On Friday, Uncle Jacob Spreaker, aged 70, caught with a dip net, near the New Market depot bridge, a German carp which measured 18 inches long, and weighed 3 lbs. and 9 ozs. The fish was alive when brought to town, where it attracted much notice on account of its large size. The man who can beat Uncle Jake, will have to be wide awake.

The Jonesville Herald says: A destructive wind storm swept over this part of the county Saturday night, the 7th instant, about 10 o'clock, destroying large quantities of growing corn, blowing down trees, etc. We hear of no loss of life or injury to stock, but in some places, particularly along the river, the loss to the corn is severe, the wind breaking the stalks off.

Lynchburg Advance: Alice Jefferson, the colored woman who is charged with the murder of her infant child, over whose remains an inquest was held yesterday, has mysteriously disappeared from the city, and all trace of her has been lost. The police, however, are resolved to leave nothing undone to bring her to trial for the alleged crime.

Speaking of the recent disaster on the Virginia Midland railroad, the Alexandria Gazette says:

"This is the first time in the history of this road that a passenger has been killed on it, notwithstanding frequent accidents have occurred, and this is decidedly the most serious one."

The Southern Republican, heretofore published in Halifax county, and edited by Mr. Stovall, has suspended publication for the lack of patronage. It was one of the very few Republican papers published in the State.

The Liberty (Bedford) Index states that the tobacco shipments to foreign points last week exceeded by several thousand pounds any previous week's output in the history of tobacco manufacture in Liberty.

The Scottsville Courier reports that a few days ago they had a tremendous hail storm near that town, which beat down a great deal of corn.

Bell Boyd is lecturing all over the State, and her effort is very highly spoken of.

For some time Gustave Johnson has been punishing his son, 10 years old, in an inhuman manner for trifling causes. ILLINOIS. White Woman Marries a Negro, and, as Usual, She Lives in Terre Haute. Special to the Indianapolis Journal. MARSHALL, Ill., July 16.—A remarkable wedding took place here this afternoon. Samuel Rush, a slender negro stripling of twenty-two years, black as the ace of spades, was married to Mrs. Annie Armstrong, a large, finely-formed white woman, aged thirty-six. Both are residents of Terre Haute, and Rush gave his occupation as that of fireman at the car works. Young as he is, this is his second marriage. Brief Mention.
A sheriff is having trouble at Morris, to prevent the lynching of William Bailey, a negro, who assaulted a frail thirteen-year-old girl.

The Rev. A. Kinney Hall's resignation as rector of St. John's Episcopal Church, Decatur, has been accepted. Failing health is assigned as the cause of the resignation. He will probably go to Indiana.

A week ago Gov. Oglesby received a letter from a widower in one of the western counties of the State soliciting assistance in obtaining a wife. The Governor did not expect to hear anything more on the subject, but during last week not less than a half dozen letters have reached him, some of them written evidently in the way of jest and others in sober earnest, offering to enter into matrimonial negotiations. The Governor is somewhat puzzled, and threatens to throw up the agency.

He Had to Marry the Girl.

BUFFALO, July 16.—A romance of mesmerism was told by Edward Shaw about the singular marriage of Louis B. Kline, an acquaintance

who recently left Barnum's show at St. Louis and then traveled with the Howard Magnet Combination. Said Mr. Shaw: "Professor Kline is a Pennsylvania boy, who has lived in New York and distinguished himself by mesmeric feats. Three weeks ago he was in Sault Ste. Marie, a little city in Michigan, with some other professional people. He was invited to attend a parlor entertainment, at which he was asked to exhibit his mesmeric powers. One of the subjects, Miss Mamie Leroy, could not be released, and some doctors who were summoned could not account for her condition. The spell was finally broken, but the girl refused to leave Kline, and when he finally escaped she became insensible. Kline was sent for and his presence gave her relief. Her father demanded that he break the spell or marry the girl. After trying every means of relief a justice was called in and tied the knot. Mamie is a handsome blonde, but her husband is greatly grieved, because he was engaged to marry a New York girl whom he dearly loved."

The curiously mated couple were the guests of Mr. Shaw this week.

Another firm, Brown & Co., signed the amalgamated scale, and there is great probability of a break in the ranks of the manufacturers.

Idle persons in Washington are talking about a vacancy in the pension office. They say the president is dissatisfied with certain official acts of General Black.

The published story that General Sheridan is liable to leave his bed is denied by the general's brother, who says the sick man is still too weak to raise his head.

A twelve-year-old boy named Pascal Porter has blossomed out as an exhorter, and has paralyzed the religious people of southern Indiana with his fervid eloquence.

A sheriff is having trouble at Morris, Illinois, to prevent the lynching of William Cailey, a negro, who assaulted a frail 13-year-old girl.

Jefferson Ray, aged 21, while walking in his sleep, was mistaken for a midnight assassin and fatally shot by his brother, a farmer on the border of the Choctaw nation.

Threats are heard among the Burlington strikers of vengeance upon the officials who set the traps into which the leaders have fallen, but no organized scheme of violence is anticipated.

G. M. Rider was hanged at Marshall, Mo., for the murder of R. P. Talant who was killed for his intimacy with Rider's wife. It is nearly two years since the murder was done.

Because of dissatisfaction among members of the Western Iron Manufacturers' association it is reported that its disolution is probable.

Sam Jones, the revivalist, in a harangue at Chautauqua declared Cleveland would be re-elected, but that the issue in 1892 would be prohibition.

Speaker Carlisle appointed a committee of five to investigate the causes and evils of excessive immigration and it will report at the next session of congress.

The surface of the water in the Chicago river was set on fire by a boy dropping an ignited match into it. Sewer gases and other nauseous refuse caused the ignition.

General Sheridan appears to be growing better continually and enjoys quite an appetite.

Emperor William is willing to have his mother hold the titles of Empress and Queen Frederick.

Private Joe Fifter made the opening speech of the Illinois campaign at Springfield Monday evening.

Francis A. Hoffmann, Jr., has returned from Washington and feels jubilant over the prospects of democratic victories this fall.

The house of representatives by a vote of 120 to 102 rejected the proposition to strike wool off the free list in the Mills tariff bill.

Judge Gary of Chicago deferred action on the will of Mrs. Emory A Storrs, the evidence as to her sanity not being technically satisfactory.

Serious trouble is threatened in the Skeena river region of British Columbia by an uprising of Indians against the white settlers.

Raymond, the artist who killed himself lately at Trinidad, Colorado, was a victim of the cocaine habit.

Attempts have lately been made to bribe customs inspectors in Washington territory to admit smuggled opium.

White caps have appeared in Lee county, West Virginia, and unmercifully flogged a number of degraded women.

Robert Garrett has returned from Europe in excellent health and is devoting himself to the affairs of his dead brother's estate.

Charles Marks, a United States marshal, was killed near Bartelsville, Indian Territory, by a Creek half-breed wanted for the attempted murder of the mayor of Geuda Springs.

M. H. De Young, said the Chinese question had sunk out of sight on the Pacific.

Charles Lynde was shot and severely wounded at Parso s, Kansas, by a Mrs. James, who objected to becoming his mother-in-law.

The New York legislature has assembled in extra session to provide an appropriation for the penal institutions of that state.

The farmers of Crawford county, Illinois, have decided to raise no more wheat, barley, or rye for three years. This is a direct blow at the life of the chinch bug.

John Rose and his son-in-law, S. S. Hall, of Stanton, Kentucky, settled an old quarrel according to the code of honor. Hall was killed instantly, and Rose was seriously injured.

Ex-President Hayes provided at the prison conference proceedings at Boston, Thursday. R. H. Dawson, of Alabama, delivered an address in which he said the system of leasing convicts should be abolished.

Mrs. A. R. Parsons, in an interview with a Chicago Times reporter, stated that she knew nothing of the dynamite plot which Inspector Bonfield claims to have discovered, but she hopes that such a plot is going on. She is not only willing that Governor Oglesby and Judges Gary and Grinnell be killed, but gives it as her determination to do the killing herself as soon as she feels certain she can succeed in an attempt.

A competent authority states that the armed groups of anarchists have increased by 100 per cent since the bomb was thrown into the ranks of the police at the Haymarket. This means that instead of 2,500 equipped with repeating rifles and bombs there are now 5,000 fully armed.

The Anarchist Trio.

CHICAGO, July 18.—The course to be pursued in prosecuting the would-be assassin of Grinnell, Gary and Bonfield was decided this morning. It was semi-officially announced that the anarchist trio will be taken about noon before a justice and the case continued ten days. That would give an opportunity of presenting the murderous conspiracy with the least possible delay to the grand jury, which assembles Monday.

A HORRIBLE CONFESSION.
William Patterson, the Murderer of Jennie Bowman, Said to Have Acknowledged His Crime, Which Was the Fourth Murder He Had Committed.

Louisville, Ky., Feb. 10.—John Crow, a colored prisoner in the jail here, told a sensational story yesterday to the effect that William Patterson, condemned to death for the murder of Jennie Bowman, had made a confession to him. Before getting his reprieve of a month Patterson was in an agony of fear, and exchanged confidences with Crow. He confessed to the murder of Jennie Bowman and to three other murders. One was a young white girl whom he had assaulted, and the next was an old colored woman who knew of the first murder. The next victim was a gambler, whom he killed about two years ago, and whose slayer was supposed to be a young white man, who was convicted and is now in the penitentiary. Patterson denies the story.

On the Verge of a Lynching.
LOUISVILLE, June 17.—A strange story was made public to-day in connection with the Governor's action on the application of William Patterson for a pardon. Patterson is a negro who, with another, in broad daylight attacked Jennie Bowman, a servant girl, in a fashionable suburban residence, last year, and beat her in such a horrible manner that she afterwards died. Both were captured, and Patterson denied his guilt, while the other confessed. The latter was hanged, but retracted on the scaffold his statement that Patterson was with him at the time of the murder. A tremendous effort has been made to secure Patterson's pardon, although he was convicted and his sentence affirmed in the highest court in the state. A petition was sent to Governor Buckner, who gave him a respite of one month, as he had not had time to examine the case.

The Legislature was then in session, and the Governor respited him again until June 22. He announced a couple days ago that he could not again interfere with the sentence. To-day it was learned that a well organized plot had been laid for a few men to lynch Patterson in case he had been pardoned. The plan was for one or two to go too the jail at a time and then seize the keys, unlock the door and hang the prisoner. It was thought this could be done so secretly and quietly that the authorities would not have a chance to interfere in time. Less than a dozen prominent citizens who had taken great interest in the case had fully arranged the plans and in fact they came very near taking this action. When the first respite was granted, they actually held a meeting to make the arrangements when some of the cooler heads persuaded them that the Governor would not interfere.

DIED PROTESTING HIS INNOCENCE. A Negro Hanged in Louisville for a Crime He Says He Did Not Commit.
Louisville, June 22.—William Patterson, a negro, was hanged in the jail yard shortly after daybreak this morning. His conduct on the scaffold was the most vigorous protest of innocence possibly ever heard from a man executed by the law. He concluded by saying:

"I have never seen my so-called victim, and either before or after her death could not distinguish her from Queen Victoria herself. I know that no earthly power can now save me from this," glancing at the noose, "but I swear I am as innocent of her death as I am that of Marie Antoinette."

The execution was a most bunglesome affair. The noose had not been properly adjusted, and when the trap was sprung the knot slipped under his chin.

He struggled for four minutes.

On June 21 a year ago Jennie Bowman, a servant-girl, was murdered while protecting her employer's house from robbery. There were evidence that two persons had committed the crime. Albert Turner, a negro, was arrested and confessed, implicating Patterson. Turner was hanged one month after the crime.

Patterson, however, fought his case through all the courts, making a final appeal to the Governor.

PATTERSON STRANGLED.
Shocking Scenes at the Execution of a Murderer.
REMARKABLE OCCURRENCE.
Four Minutes After the Drop Falls the Victim Speaks—Slowly Strangled to Death—Belief in His Innocence by Many.
LOUISVILLE, Ky., June 22.—William Patterson (colored) was hanged this morning at 6:10 o'clock, in the yard of the Jefferson county jail.

He was convicted with another colored man, Albert Turner, for assaulting and fatally beating Miss Jennie Bowman on April 23, 1888. Miss Bowman was a domestic employed by a family who lived in a fashionable suburb, and the crime was committed about 10 o'clock in the morning.

The family were all absent from the house at the time, and no one witnessed the murder. Turner and Patterson were arrested on suspicion, and Turner immediately confessed. Patterson protested his innocence.

On April 27th, a mob surrounded the jail bent on lynching the two negroes. The State militia was called out and guarded the prisoners for three days, keeping the mob at bay, when the excitement subsided, and the crowd dispersed.

Turner pleaded guilty, but on the scaffold said Patterson was innocent. He was hung on July 1. Patterson was tried, convicted, but appealed his case, and the lower court was sustained. The Governor respited him three times, but refused to interfere further.

Patterson protested his innocence on the scaffold. He was slowly strangled to death, and four minutes after the drop fell said: "Curse them!" and then, "Lord save me!" His struggles were frightful. Many people believe firmly in his innocence, and there were strong attempts to secure his pardon. Missing from a Lancaster Picnic.
LANCASTER, July 12. - The Memorial Presbyterian and Lutheran Sunday schools of this city pionicked to-day at Penryn Park. With the former school was Bertha Beck, aged 5, who was no companion by her mother. The little girl disappeared shortly after 12 o'clock and had not been found up to a late hour this evening. When last seen she was near the lake, and it is generally believed that she fell in, although the water has been dragged and dynamite bombs exploded without effect. A large party are to-night exploring the hills in the hope that she wandered away.

A STRANGE STORY.

The story of the little girl's recovery is one filled with interest and romance, and it will be a long time before the occurrence is erased from the memory of the public. Early on Friday morning, a special train, byinging twenty men from Lebanon, arrived at the park. This was a party of searchers that had been organized by the management of the park and railroad company, and they were at once put to work on a search that continued throughout the whole day. Between 12 and 2 o'clock p.m. all the boats on the lake were manned and men, with rakes in their hands, making searches in the water, kept rowing about. This was all to no purpose, however, and the child was still undiscovered.

The first person to make his appearance on the picnic grounds on Friday morning was Rev. Thomas Thompson, of the Presbyterian Memorial church, of this city. He had attended the picnic of the day before, and so interested did he become in the search for the child that he remained in the woods until a late hour at night. He slept at a farm house near the park and was up early in the morning ready to do all in his power to solve the mystery of the child's disappearance. When he went to the grounds everything was quiet, no one being astir. While the reverend gentleman was walking] around the park he came across a strange old man, whom he afterwards learned to be William Smith, a resident of the neighborhood, and the man who it has since been found caused the little child's disappearance. SMITH, THE VILLAIN.

When Mr. Thompson met Smith he was wearing a broad-brimmed black slouch hat and in his hand carried a basket the contents of which was covered with a handkerchief. Smith seemed to be wandering around the grounds, but he appeared very garrulous and anxious to talk and he and Mr. Thompson soon became engaged in a conversation. Quite naturally their talk dritted upon the disappearance of the little girl on the night before. Smith said he knew where the child was and could find her. Mr. Thompson asked him why he did not do so at once and stop any further trouble or annoyance. Smith said he needed help and Mr. Thompson asked him what kind. The old mar, in a business like way, said that Mr. Jackson, the superintendent of the park, would pay a large sum of money for the return of the lost child and he desired to get some of it. Mr. Thompson cut the old fellow rather short during that conversation, yet he had a belief that the man knew much more than he was willing to tell.

SUSPICIONS AROUSED.

Soon afterwards the special train came in from Lancaster bringing a large crowd of people to attend the picnic of the Reformed Sunday schools. The grounds were soon filled with a lively crowd of pleasure seekers, and the principal subject of talk among them was the lost child. Old Smith hung around and during the morning he approached Mr. Thompson several times and always referred in his conversation to the missing girl. He spoke of the case of Charlie Ross, the missing Philadelphia boy, and seemed to be familiar with it. This increased the suspicion of Mr. Thompson. Later Smith spoke to a number of people about the missing girl. He said he had a magic glass in his basket by the aid of which he could locate the child. He exhibited this glass, which was a small, old-fashioned mirror, to quite a number of people. At last everybody began to mistrust him, and the majority of the people on the grounds thought he was either a crank or he knew something of the missing girl. He was surrounded by crowds wherever he went, and he always produced his magic glass.

LOOKING INTO THE MAGIC MIRROR.

He spoke to so many people on the subject of the girl that finally some became interested in his talk. He said that if he could find any one in the woods who could look into his glass and see the lost child he would be able to find her, but he must have a dark place to do his work. About four o'clock in the afternoon a party went into a passenger car which was standing on the siding, along with the old man, to see what he would do. They were Mrs. Beck, the missing child's mother, Harry C. Moore, Joseph Shirk and Emanuel Wolf, of this city. The old man lifted the cloth off the basket and drew therefrom a black shawl and the magic mirror. The car was made quite dark and Smith then said that he wanted some one who could look in the glass and see the lost child and then everything would be right.

Those present were each taken away and in private were given a look at the glass, but none were able to see the vision. Finally Harry W. Buckins, of the Examiner, who was on the ground, was called into the car. The old man took him aside and Buckins upon looking in the glass told him that he saw the outlines of a child sleeping in the woods. Of course the reporter saw nothing of the kind, but it is not always necessary to tell the exact truth in cases of this kind. The old man asked Buckins in which direction from the lake the child was lying and whether he could lead him to her, but these questions staggered the reporter. Superintendent Neff, of the railroad, next took a peep at the glass and also said that he could see the child, but he could not lead the way to it.

Smith then said that he must find some one who was familiar with the mountains, but such a man was not to be bad. He said further that the men who look in glasses and find things are now all dead. The old man still continued to talk about the reward and by this time everybody was watching him. At about 6 o'clock in the evening, Smith met Joseph Shik, of this city, and George Hauer, of Lebanon, who is telegraph operator at the park, near the lake. He at once took them into his confidence, saying that he would find the girl and they would capture and divide the reward. The three then started and walked down the railroad towards Mt. The Manheim Sun had a representative at White Oak on Monday evening when William Smith, the alleged abductor of Bertha Beck, arrived there from Lebanon. The Sun will publish the following:

There were a hundred people at the station, and when Smith got off the cars Geo. Harman, one of Smith's bondemen, said: "Bill, you better sink the glass under the ground a hundred feet. It got you in jail and has given you lots of trouble."

Smith replied, "I think more of the glass now than ever I did. It found the lost girl."

Henry Steinman spoke to a Sun man saying, "Yes, I went his bail because he is an innocent man. I saw him in the harvest field at 12 o'clock on Thursday and at 2 o'clock my daughter Mazie was out after raspberries and talked to Smith and went into his house when it rained and saw him there. The railroad conductor must be wrong when he says Smith rode on his train on Thursday."

From the lake at Penryn runs a narrow path towards Mount Hope. The best theory is that Bertha lost herself in this pathway and strayed into the thorns where she was discovered.

A Sun reporter interviewed Smith on Tuesday morning. The man had come to Manheim to see his old friend M. J. Burkholder, the merchant who kept store at White Oak. He wore a cheap straw hat with a blue ribbon band. He was clean shaven and his white goatee carefully arranged. His eyes blinked continually as he spoke freely to the newspaper man.

"When did you see Bertha Beck?" asked the reporter.

He answered in German slowly and deliberately. "Not until Swenk from Lancaster had arrested me and Superintendent Jackson like a tiger started the cry of 'lynch him!' 'hang him!'"

"But you knew you were arrested for stealing the child?"

"Yes, I knew that too well. On Thursday morning about 9 o'clock when the wheat was dry enough I went into the field to work. The rain chased me out and I got wet. I went home and changed my clothes, and then carried a letter to the postoffice at Graybill's mill for my daughter. On my way there I saw half a dozen of people. Then I went down to the station at White Oak. The last train brought out John Sayler, Jr., and he told me that the girl was lost. That was the first I knew of it."

"Did you then go to the park?"

"No, I went home and wanted the imagination glass, not 'airth spiegel,' that's the German name for it; but my family would not give it to me, so I had to wait until morning. I got up early. Something made me go. I could not stay. I bought a ticket at White Oak for Penryn. When I got on the grounds I did not stand around like a steer, but was there for business, to see if anyone could see the lost child in the glass."

Smith then related his experience with the persons who looked in the glass and was particularly severe on the young man who said he saw the girl but couldn't locate her because he was not acquainted with the woods. He is strong in his condemnation of Superintendent Neff's conduct.

"Why didn't you see where the child was?"

"because I am not the proper subject and can't see anything in the glass. I don't have the power to locate things. When I went over I expected to find some of Freeman's hands who knew the grounds who would have the power to locate. In the morning I had a number of the men to look in the glass. I was disgusted with the outcome of the matter and was about to go home when I met Shirk at the tool house. He looked in the glass and said that he saw the child, not in the lake but beyond the lake. I did not see the child. He started off and I followed him. He had gone some distance and they said the child was found I wanted to find a good place to cross the stream. That's what I was looking for when Officer Swenk came up and told me it was all right now. He began asking me if I hadn't stole the girl and then I just found out what they were up to.

"When I got back they wanted to lynch me. Neff had a rope and held me by the throat. Jackson was one of the worst among them. When I saw the child she could not talk, but would nod yes to anything they asked her."

Smith had not read any of the newspapers, and when the story as published was related to him he laughed at it and said it was not correct. He denied the account of the interview about the location of the child and said many of the words were put into his mouth. He did not go there for money. He wanted to show the people what he could do with his glass which he made fifteen years age. In all that time Smith never found anything, still he believes in the glass, but he declares that he will never use it to save anyone, not even from death.

LEBANON, Sept. 20.—The case of William H. Smith, of White Oak, Lancaster county, charged with kidnapping Bertha Beck, of Lancaster, from Penryn Park, July 12th, was attached yesterday afternoon.

SUPPOSED LYNCHING.
A NEORO'S MYSTERIOUS DEATH IN DIN- WIDDIE.
Some Particulars of the Case-News and Personal Notes-A School Commencement.
[Correspondence of the Richmond Dispatch.] Harrington VA. June 21, 1889
PETERSBURG, U.S.A., June 21, 1889.

From all the facts that can be learned in the case there seems to be no doubt that the negro William Stokes, whose dead body was found Sunday morning last in the road near Marmora, Dinwiddie county, came to his death by lynching. Stokes was about twenty-five or twenty-seven years of age, and was a comparative stranger in the neighborhood, having appeared there about the lst of April, seeking employment. He obtained work on the farm of Mr. J. M. Abernathy. No one could definitely ascertain where he came from, and different locations were at times reported as his home. The last report was that he came from the vicinity of Norfolk. It is stated that while in Mr. Abernathy's employment he several times broke into that gentleman's house with intentions, it is believed, other than robbery, but was driven out. He was finally discharged from Mr. Abernathy's employment. It is further alleged that Stokes subsequently forced an entrance into the house of a colored tenant on the same farm, and his conduct was such that assault on the colored man's daughter was suspected. Previous to this stokes had been warned that it would be better for him to leave the county. His response was to the effect that this was a game at which two could play.

The prevailing impression is that Stokes was taken from his prison-house and shot by unknown parties. The affair was so well conducted that there is not the faintest suspicion as to the identity of any person engaged in it. Nor is it known whether the lynching party was composed of white or colored people. It is understood that the matter has been brought to the attention of the County Court, by whom it will be brought before the grand jury with the view of an investigation, but it is not likely that anything definite will be developed. The affair occurred some fifteen miles west of this city, near the Appomattox river.

Dargan are very gratifying to the many friends of these gentlemen in this city. Dr. Rosebro is at present pastor of the Tabb-Street Presbyterian church here. A Mysterious Murder in Virginia.
Intelligence was received here on Monday of a murder committed in Dinwiddie county, under peculiar circumstances. It seems that on Saturday a colored man, named Wm. Stokes, was arrested on a warrant charging him with breaking into the dwelling-house of Mr. Abernathy, near Marmora, in the above-named county. He was placed in charge of Special Constable Grosham, who carried the prisoner before a justice of the peace for a hearing, but in consequence of the absence of some of the witnesses the case was continued until Monday. After the case had been continued, the constable carried the prisoner to his (Gresham's) house and placed him in a corn-crib, but gave a bed and made him as comfortable as possible. Monday morning when Constable Gresham went to his crib, he found the doors of the crib open and the prisoner gone. About one hour afterwards Mr. Gresham was informed that there was a dead man down the road, and he went off to look after the matter. Upon viewing the body Constable Gresham identified it as that of Stokes, his prisoner. An examination of the body developed the fact that the deceased had been shot in the back and also in the back part of the neck. A coroner's inquest was held, and the verdict of the jury was that the deceased came to his death by being shot by some one to them unknown.

William Stokes, colored, in the employ of J. M. Abernathy, of Dinwiddie County, Va., was arrested recently charged with a criminal assault. The constable locked the prisoner up in a log crib on his place, intending to keep him there until he could carry him to the county jail. PETERSBURG.
THE RECENT HOMICIDE—SPECULATIONS AS TO THE REAL CAUSE.
The Dinwiddie Lynching Case-No Evidence Before the Grand Jury-General and Political.
[Correspondence of the Richmond Dispatch.]

August 21, 1888.

The recent homicide in Dinwiddie county, of which the general particulars have been published in the Dispatch, has caused a great deal of comment both in this city and in the county. Mr. A. C. Pyne, who was killed by Mr. Gouldie Elam in the presence of the lady whom they were escorting home, was widely and popularly known. Mr. Elam has been a resident of the county all his life. While it is given out that the immediate cause of the trouble between the two gentlemen was an unpaid bill of Mr. Elam's, for which Mr. Pyne had become responsible as an act of friendship, the general belief is that there was another and more exciting cause, which will probably be developed upon the trial. The grand-jury term of the County Court of Dinwiddie met yesterday and Elam was indicted for the murder of Pyne. The case was continued until the next term of the court for trial and the accused was committed to prison. It is said that the strongest evidence against Elam was given by Miss Judith Barker, the lady who was with the two gentlemen at the time of the fatal difficulty. It is believed that at the trial facts will be developed that will assign other causes than that mentioned for the deplorable tragedy.

THE DINWIDDIE LYNCHING CASE.

The grand jury of Dinwiddie county yesterday made every effort to prove the identity of the parties alleged to have been engaged in the lynching of the negro William Stokes, near Marmora, on Saturday night, the 16th of June. But no evidence could be obtained to identify any person, and the matter was therefore dismissed. Stokes had been arrested by the neighborhood constable on the charge of entering the house of a colored man—a tenant on the farm of Mr. J. M. Abernathy—with the intention of committing an assault. He had previously on one or more occasions forced an entrance in the night-time into the residence of Mr. Abernathy, on whose farm he was employed, and his conduct was such that it was believed his intentions were more serious than that of robbery. He had been warned to leave the neighborhood, but refused to do so, saying that he could meet force with force if necessary. When arrested he was locked up in a farm-house for safekeeping until he could be taken to the county jail. On the following morning he was found dead in the road a short distance away, and an examination showed that he had been shot to death. By whom the lynching was done was unknown at the time, and has ever since remained a mystery. The affair was wrapped in the utmost secrecy, so much so that not the faintest suspicion attaches to any one.

Columbus, Tex., Jan. 1.—The colored boy, William Washington, who was suspected of the murder of Mrs. Mary Miller near Ellinger, was captured by Shariff Townsend and his deputies at New Ulm in the adjoining county, and brought to Ellinger yesterday under a heavy guard. Washington has made a full confession to Sheriff Townsend. He says he knew Mrs. Miller was alone with the children. Just as she had put out the light he entered the room and grabbed her about the waist. Washington says she struck him and screamed. He struggled with her and attempted to cut her throat in the bed room, but she got loose and ran out into the yard. He pursued and caught her just as she entered a field adjoining the house. He says he threw her down, cut her throat and afterward accomplished his purpose. She was dead, he declares, when he left her. Washington will be lynched before many hours. It is proposed by some that he be slowly tortured to death. The general feeling is that hanging or shooting is an inadequate penalty for his awful crime.

COMMISSIONER CARROLL D. WRIGHT submitted to the Secretary of the Interior at Washington on the 29th the third annual report of the Bureau of Labor, which relates entirely to strikes and lock-outs for the six years ended December 31, 1886. During that period there were 3,903 strikes, involving 1,318,624 employees, and 1,047 of the strikes were successful. The total loss to employers was $34,164,914, and to employees, $59,948,882. In 1887, the report says, there were, according to the best information obtainable, 853 strikes.

The business failures during the past year show a decrease of 200 in number, but an increase of $53,000,000 in liabilities, as follows: 1887, number 9,634, liabilities $167,560,944, average $17,392; 1886, number 9,834, liabilities $114,644,119, average $11,651.

Advices of the 30th ult. report the loss of the sloop Lizzie Ella near Cape Blas, Fla., with her crew of five men.

John McKenna, a plumber, fell sixy feet into a well, at Lexington, Ky., on the 30th ult., but escaped unhurt.

The Kelly family, accused of horrible murders at Oak Creek, Kan., were captured on the 30th ult. and lynched in Texas. The son was hung, and the mother and daughter shot while the posse was endeavoring to capture them. The old man escaped.

Executions took place on the 30th ult. as follows: William Finchum, at Harrisonburg, Va., for the murder of his brother; Gus Edmunson, at Somerville, Ala., for killing his wife; Albert Peters, at Marianna, Ark., for the murder of William Johnson, and John Strickland, at Conway, S. C., for killing his mother.

A document advocating the use by working-men of the bomb, the torch and the bullet was circulated at New York on the 30th ult., the closing sentence being "Brothers, remember Chicago and your oath."

A TRAIN fell through a trestle on the 30th ult. near St. Petersburg, Pa., the cars falling thirty feet. Six persons were seriously injured and the wreck was destroyed by fire.

A TIDAL wave of monstrous proportions swept upon the headlands outside of Portland (Me.) Harbor on the 30th ult., and the great mass rose sixty feet above high-water mark, carrying everything before it.

WILLIAM HERRING, who recently killed his wife and her paramour at St. Francis, Ark., was lynched on the 30th ult.

PAYNE, STECK & Co., of New York City, wholesale jewelers, failed on the 30th ult. for $100,000.

DURING the absence of her husband on the 30th ult. the young wife of John Miller, a wealthy farmer living near Ellinger, Tex., was taken from bed by a negro, carried to a field near the house, assaulted and murdered.

A FURIOUS snow-storm prevailed in the Northwest on the 30th ult., and all railway travel was greatly retarded.

THE Michigan Commercial Travelers' Association held its fourth annual session in Detroit on the 30th ult.

THE Kansas Temperance Union, in convention at Topeka on the 30th ult., passed resolutions to continue earnest work for constitutional prohibition and declared against third party agitation.

A PASSENGER train jumped the track on the 30th ult. near Great Bend, Pa., and rolled down the bank, sixteen of the passengers being injured.

On the 30th ult. the skeletons of fourteen murdered persons were found in a cavern near the ranch of John La Blant, a Sioux Indian, at Willow Creek, D. T. La Blant had fled.

LAURA WEBSTER, aged eighteen, of San Francisco, had on the 30th ult. been asleep for seventy days. Her physicians administered liquid food to her through a tube.

A TERRIFIC gale was raging on the 30th ult. on the New England coast, and many vessels had been wrecked, but no lives lost.

An explosion of natural-gas on the 30th ult. at Lima, O., killed Eugene O'Neil and caused the destruction of property worth $10,000.

DURING a row on the 30th ult. in a justice's court at Sumter, S. C., Judge Haynesworth was shot dead and two other men were fatally wounded.

The people of the town of Clarksville Ind., on the Ohio river, were on the 30th ult. preparing to elect delegates to Congress. They would demand admission as a Territory under the old Virginia charter, which it was claimed was still in force.

PERSONAL AND POLITICAL.

The Union Labor party of Indiana will hold a State convention at Indianapolis March 7.

The funeral of Daniel Manning, ex-Secretary of the Treasury, occurred at Albany, N. Y., on the 27th. President Cleveland and several members of the Cabinet attended from Washington.

CAPTAIN CYRUS VIGUS, the oldest citizen of Cass County, Ind., died on the 27th, aged ninety-four years. He was a veteran of the war of 1812.

The Kansas State convention of the Prohibition party, held in Topeka on the 27th, decided to begin a vigorous campaign during the coming year, and to put a full State ticket in the field.

M. D. BABCOCK, inventor of the Babcock fire extinguisher, from royalties on which he was at one time receiving $10,000 a month, died in the almshouse at San Francisco on the 24th, aged seventy years, of softening of the brain.

JOHN S. MARMADUKE, Governor of Missouri, died of pneumonia on the evening of the 28th at Jefferson City, aged fifty-four years.

JUDGE RAPALLO, of the New York Court of Appeals, died on the 28th in New York City.

JOHN J. LITTLETON, editor of the National Review, of Nashville, Tenn., who was shot recently by Joseph R. Banks, died on the 28th.

W. W. CORCORAN, of Washington, the noted philanthropist, celebrated his nineteenth birthday on the 27th.

The Prohibition convention at Topeka, Kan., on the 28th elected delegates to the National convention and voted down an anti-monopoly plank.

J. W. JACKSON, aged eighty years, a wealthy pioneer resident of Chicago, on the 29th was married to Mrs. Sarah Golden, aged fifty-five years. Both had previously been twice married.

LIEUTENANT-GOVERNOR ALBERT P. MOREHOUSE was sworn in as Governor of Missouri at Jefferson City on the 29th to finish the unexpired term of the late Governor Marmaduke.

MRS. EUNICE BOSWORTH TAYLOR, wife of Congressman E. B. Taylor, of Ohio, was stricken with apoplexy in the streets of Washington on the 29th and died in a few moments.

THE Kentucky Legislature convened on the 30th ult.
